### Chapter ten: How the life of the newborn is arranged according to the years of nurturing of each planet.

Something must be said regarding the arrangement of the natural life of the newborn, and how each of the planets governs it from its beginning until its end. The order is as follows: the Moon, which is closer to the Earth and said to be faster than all other planets, is the first of the planets in order when starting from the lowest spheres. It governs the life of the newborn from its beginning for four years, which are called its "years of nurturing" <note>original: "anni nutritionis"</note>. This period is regarded as the time of nursing and early growth. 

Next, Mercury governs for 10 years, which are its years of nurturing. Then Venus governs for seven years. Then the Sun governs for 19 years. Then Mars governs for 15 years. Then Jupiter governs for 12 years. Finally, Saturn governs for 30 years, which are its years of nurturing. If the person lives past these <note>a total of 97 years</note>, the cycle of governance returns to the Moon, then to Mercury, and so on through the rest of the planets as stated. Therefore, in whichever period one of the aforementioned governors is well-placed <note>astrologically favorable in the birth chart</note>, it will well-arrange the life of the newborn during that time, and vice versa. It will add to or diminish the years of the person’s life during that time according to its own condition and nature.

### Chapter eleven: Which days and nights each planet possesses, why they are named after them, and concerning unequal hours and masculine and feminine hours.

Each of the planets has its own day and its own night assigned to it. Thus, when a certain day or night is assigned to a specific planet, the first hour of that day or night will belong to that planet from which the day takes its name. The second hour will belong to the planet that follows it in the order of the planets. 

For example, Sunday belongs entirely to the Sun because the first hour of Sunday is the Sun's. Monday belongs to the Moon because its first hour is the Moon's. Tuesday <note>Latin: "Dies martis"</note> belongs to Mars because its first hour is Mars'. Wednesday <note>Latin: "Dies mercurij"</note> belongs to Mercury because its first hour is Mercury's. Thursday <note>Latin: "Dies iouis"</note> belongs to Jupiter because its first hour is Jupiter's. Friday <note>Latin: "Dies veneris"</note> belongs to Venus because its first hour is Venus'. Saturday <note>Latin: "Dies sabbati"</note> belongs to Saturn because its first hour is Saturn's. 

Therefore, I say that the first hour of Sunday is the Sun's; the second is Venus', who follows it in the order of the planets. The third is Mercury's, who follows Venus. The fourth is the Moon's, who follows Mercury. Then the cycle begins again from the highest planet: the fifth hour is Saturn's, from whom one starts after the Moon. The sixth is Jupiter's, who follows Saturn in order. The seventh is Mars', who follows Jupiter. Again, the eighth is the Sun's, who follows Mars. The ninth is Venus', who follows the Sun. The tenth is Mercury's. The eleventh is the Moon's. The twelfth is Saturn's, who, as was said, follows the Moon. Thus you have the 12 hours of the day, whether they be equal or unequal <term>unequal hours: also called "seasonal hours," these are calculated by dividing the total daylight into 12 equal parts, meaning an hour in summer is longer than an hour in winter</term>.

->Concerning the equal and unequal hours of the night.<-

Just as each planet has its own day assigned to it, so too does each have its own night assigned to it and named after it. For the entire night that follows Sunday is said to be Jupiter's, because the first hour of that night is Jupiter's; the second is Mars'; the third is the Sun's; the fourth is Venus'; the fifth is Mercury's; the sixth is the Moon's; the seventh is Saturn's; the eighth-

<column-break/>

-is Jupiter's; the ninth is Mars'; the tenth is the Sun's; the eleventh is Venus'; and the twelfth is Mercury's. Thus you have the twelve hours of the night, whether they be equal or unequal.

->Concerning masculine and feminine hours.<-

Among the hours of both night and day, some are masculine and some are feminine. The first hour of any day and the first hour of any night is masculine; the second is feminine; the third is masculine; the fourth is feminine; the fifth is masculine; the sixth is feminine; the seventh is masculine; the eighth is feminine; the ninth is masculine; the tenth is feminine; the eleventh is masculine; and the twelfth is feminine. 

Therefore, you must consider the hour of birth for a male to see if it was a masculine hour; if it was, it contributes to the well-being of his masculinity. If it was a feminine hour, it is unfavorable for his masculinity, for it makes the newborn somewhat effeminate. If it is a feminine hour at the birth of a female, it contributes to the well-being of her femininity and makes her natural in her feminine character. If it was a masculine hour, it makes her decline somewhat toward masculinity and creates, in a certain way, the nature of a "virago" <note>original: "viraginis," a woman of masculine spirit or strength</note>, though not entirely.

### Chapter twelve: Regarding the forms or figures that the signs give to those born.

<margin>The forms that the signs give to the newborn.</margin>

We have spoken of the forms or figures that the planets give to those for whom they are significators. It remains to say something else regarding the assistance of the figures or forms themselves, which seems to pertain in some way to what is called the "root of life." For just as the planets grant their figures to the newborn, so do the signs. One does not give a complete form to the newborn by itself, but both work together, one with the other. A planet could not give an appearance to the newborn by itself without the sign, nor the sign by itself without the planet—just as a mother cannot bear a child without a father, nor a father without a mother. A person cannot be born without some sign ascending <note>referring to the Rising Sign or Ascendant</note>, nor can someone be born without some planet being the lord of the sign then ascending. Thus, it is necessary that both participate with each other in the birth of any person. 

Consequently, the signs modify the influence of the planets, so that the person's appearance is not exactly what the planet would give. Likewise, the planet modifies the sign, so the figure is not exactly what the sign would give; sometimes one assists the other. These are the figures that the signs give to humans:

Sign and star consider.</margin> Some resemble their fathers; some resemble their grandfathers or great-grandfathers, on both the maternal and paternal sides. And we see different people practicing one and the same art at the same time and in the same way; yet some of them grow rich by it, while others are impoverished by the same trade. Sometimes those who know the art better and spend less, living in misery, do not grow wealthy, while others do the opposite. We see some who are not very wise, yet people listen to their words and believe them, regarding them as wiser than those who are actually wise; and vice versa. We see some who remain always healthy, some always sickly, some half-healthy; some who are helped in their illnesses by medicines and the care of doctors, and some who are harmed by them. We see some who abound in riches but lack children; some who abound in children but lack riches; some who abound in both; some who lack both; some who abound in these things for a time, and some who lack them for a time. Some who at one time abound in children yet see their deaths and grieve for them. Others who leave their children behind after death, and the children inherit their goods. Similarly, there are some men who perform the duties of women, and certain women who perform the duties of men, fighting and doing many things that pertain to men. Such was a certain Maria of Crema, who carried men's weapons like a man—such as hunting spears—and hunted wild boars; and the daughter of <unclear>Gircauensis</unclear> who was named Fredona; and many others. There are some who are excellent singers and have clear-sounding voices, and some who know nothing of singing. And some who know very well how to play musical instruments and use them, and some who neither know how nor could learn, yet they know other things better than other men. We see some who rejoice on one day and are sad on another, even without a manifest cause. And some who rejoice on a day when others are sad, and some who are sad on a day when others rejoice. Some rejoice on a good day and are sad on a bad one, and some are sad on a good day and rejoice on a bad one. We see some who are stutterers, some who are talkative; some wise men who have few and poorly ordered words, and some who have many and well-ordered words; and some who have many but poorly ordered words, among both the wise and the unwise. And we see many other circumstances happen to men of which it would be difficult to make individual mention. However, concerning where these things come from and why, I shall—God willing—make mention of them to you and explain them in the treatise on <term>nativities<note>The study of birth charts and the destiny of individuals based on their time of birth.</note></term>. And although the work may seem lengthy, it will be of such great utility that it will not generate boredom in your reading or studying. Some unusual and almost unheard-of things will be said there, such as these: for we see that no face of a man is so similar to the face of another that there is not some dissimilarity as well as similarity between them.

### Thus ends the first part of the third treatise.

### Here begins the second part concerning those things which happen to the planets in themselves and what happens to one from another.
### Chapter one concerning those things which happen to the planets in themselves.

<summary>This page concludes the physical descriptions of the Zodiac signs and introduces a philosophical inquiry into the "accidents" of human life—the unpredictable variations in appearance, wealth, health, and talent that seem to defy simple hereditary or natural logic.</summary>
<keywords>Zodiac, physiognomy, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, heredity, Maria of Crema, human diversity, astrology, nativities</keywords>

<meta>The previous page concluded a series of physical descriptions associated with the Zodiac signs and began discussing "accidents"—unforeseen variations in nature. This page transitions from the "accidents" of human traits to the astronomical "accidents" of the planets, specifically their varying speeds, sizes, and orbital positions.</meta>

In this second part of the third treatise, we must speak of certain "accidents" <note>In medieval science, an "accident" refers to a non-essential quality or an observable phenomenon, such as a planet's change in brightness or speed.</note> that happen to the planets within themselves and in relation to one another. I shall speak to you as one who has already been introduced to this subject, and not as a complete beginner. First, I will tell you, following in the footsteps of the philosophers, about those things that happen to the planets within themselves. These accidents include: when a planet is ascending in the circle of its **apogee** <term>aux<note>From the Arabic 'awj', meaning the highest point or apogee; the point in an orbit where the planet is furthest from the Earth.</note></term>; when it is descending in that same circle; and when it is neither ascending nor descending. Al-Battani <note>original: "albabitius," the 9th-century astronomer whose work helped refine the Ptolemaic system</note> said that the significance of these planetary events is that when a planet is ascending toward its apogee, it appears smaller in light and size, and slower in its course.

<margin>Since it is further from the Earth, it appears smaller in light.</margin>
For when a planet is in that part of its <term>eccentric<note>A circular path where the Earth is not exactly at the center, explaining why planets seem to change distance from us.</note></term> furthest from the Earth—where its apogee is located—it then appears smaller in light and in the size of its body, and it seems slower in its course. This is not because it actually travels a shorter distance in one day than another (for it always travels along the path of its <term>epicycle<note>A smaller circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the eccentric), used to explain retrograde motion.</note></term>), but it appears this way because of the distance of the various parts of the epicycle.

<margin>Here, at the opposite of the apogee.</margin>
And when it is at the opposite of its apogee—that is, in the part of its eccentric that is closest to the Earth—it then appears larger in light and in the size of its body, and faster in its course.

<margin>In the further part of the eccentric, the planet moves slower.</margin>
<margin>In the closer part, it moves faster.</margin>
In the further part of its eccentric, its course seems slower because of the larger spans of the degrees <note>the arc or "compass" of the degrees</note> in that part compared to the other. In the closer part, however, its course seems faster because of the smaller spans of the degrees in that area; this is because it traverses smaller spans in less time than larger ones, even though it is always moving at a constant rate, as I have said.

<margin>Speed and slowness are described in relation to the eighth sphere.</margin>
Therefore, the course appears faster in relation to the eighth heaven <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which serves as the background for planetary movement.</note> just as it does in its own eccentric. In the further part, the course appears slower in relation to the eighth heaven because it traverses the larger spans of degrees in that part more slowly than it does the smaller ones.

<margin>The degrees of the eccentric are larger on the side of the apogee than on the opposite side.</margin>
The degrees of the eccentric are indeed larger on the side of the apogee than on the opposite side. This occurs because of the displacement of the center of the eccentric from the center of the Earth (which is the center of the eighth sphere). Some have thought that the "apogee" was the furthest point of the epicycle, but they were perhaps using the term loosely or were mistaken. True apogee belongs only to the furthest point of the eccentric and not the epicycle. In the epicycle, we consider only the **furthest distance** and the **nearest distance**. The furthest distance is that part of the epicycle which is above the line of the eccentric. The nearest distance is that part of the epicycle which is below the line of the eccentric. Thus, "apogee" and "distance" differ from one another in this way.

<margin>Apogee is not considered in the epicycle.</margin>
Furthermore, it is clear that apogee is not considered in the epicycle because the epicycle orbits the entire eccentric. Thus, it is sometimes at the apogee (the furthest part of the eccentric), sometimes at the opposite of the apogee (the closest part), and sometimes between these locations.

<margin>The apogee of the eccentric always remains fixed in one sign and one place; thus, apogee is considered only in the eccentric.</margin>
The epicycle travels through all the signs, but the apogee of the eccentric remains fixed in one sign and one place; therefore, apogee is only considered within the eccentric. The apogees are as I describe to you in this present work: The apogee of the **Sun** and the apogee of **Venus** are in the very same degree: the 18th degree and 50th minute of Gemini. The apogee of **Mars** is in the 2nd degree and 51st minute of Leo. The apogee of **Jupiter** is in the 15th degree and 30th minute of Virgo. The apogee of **Saturn** is in the 1st degree and 5th minute of Sagittarius. The apogee of **Mercury** is in the 18th degree and 10th minute of Libra. However, the apogee of the **Moon** is not distinguished in the same way as the apogees of the other planets, for its apogee is not subtracted from its mean motion in calculations. This is due to the motion of the center of its eccentric in a small circle whose center is the center of the circle of the signs <note>the Ecliptic</note>. 

When a planet is in the middle of its circle—so that there is as much of the circle of fixed stars above the planet as there is below—whether it is before or after the apogee, it then appears equal in body and light; in all other places, it appears either larger or smaller. When it is traveling toward the apogee and there are 90 equal degrees or less between it and the apogee, it begins to appear smaller in light and body; it continues to diminish little by little until it reaches the apogee, which is the furthest part of the eccentric. Once it begins to move away from the apogee, it begins to appear larger; it continues to grow as long as it is in view until it is 90 equal degrees away from the apogee (as measured on the circle of signs), at which point it appears "equal" as mentioned before. From that point onward, it grows visibly larger in light and body until it reaches the opposite of the apogee, which is the part of the eccentric closest to the Earth.

If the planet's **corrected argument** <term>argumentum equatum<note>A mathematical value representing a planet's position within its epicycle after adjusting for various orbital irregularities.</note></term> is from one degree up to six signs, its power or course will be increasing. If it is from six signs up to twelve, its course will be decreasing. If it is exactly at six or twelve signs, the planet's course is neither increasing nor decreasing. Here, within the epicycle, we consider **direct motion**, **retrograde motion**, **station**, and the speed or slowness of the course. When a planet is in that part of the epicycle above the eccentric, it is called **direct**. When it is in the part below the eccentric, it is called **retrograde**. When it is at the points where the line of the eccentric touches the circle of the epicycle, it is called **stationary**. And when it is between those two points of contact—at the peak of the epicycle's diameter furthest from the eccentric line—it is called slow in course. But because this work is not dedicated to the study of that, I will cease speaking of it further and return to my original purpose.

And when the **equation** <term>equation<note>original: "equatio," a mathematical correction added to or subtracted from a planet's "mean" position to find its "true" position.</note></term> of any planet is added to its mean course, it then increases the course or the number. And when the equated equation is subtracted from the mean course of the planet, it then decreases the number or the course. And when **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, or **Mars** travel faster than their mean course, they are called "increasing" in their course or number; when slower, they are called "decreasing." Now, the mean course of **Saturn** in one day is 2 minutes and 35 seconds. The mean course of **Jupiter** is 4 minutes and 59 seconds. The mean course of **Mars** is 31 minutes and 26 seconds. And when any of them travels exactly as much as its mean course, its course is said to be "equal," which is to say it is neither increasing nor decreasing. 

And when the **Sun**, **Venus**, or **Mercury** travel in one day more than the mean course of the Sun—which is 59 minutes and 8 seconds—it is called "increasing" in course; and when it travels less than 59 minutes and 8 seconds, it is called "decreasing." And when the Sun is near its **apogee** <term>aux<note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note></term>, either 90 degrees before it or 90 degrees after it, its course is said to be "equal" or "mean." And when it is less than 90 degrees from it, its course is "slow." And when it is distant from it, either before or after, by more than 90 degrees, its course is called "swift." And when it travels at 59 minutes and 8 seconds, its course is called "equal." And when the **Moon** travels in one day more than 13 degrees, 10 minutes, and 35 seconds, it is called "increasing." And when it travels less than 13 degrees, 10 minutes, and 35 seconds, it is called "decreasing." And when it travels exactly 13 degrees, 10 minutes, and 35 seconds, then its course is called "equal."

### Chapter Two: That the planets are Northern and when they are Southern.

It happens to the planets that they are sometimes **Northern** and sometimes **Southern**. A planet becomes northern when it passes its **node** <term>genzahar<note>original: "genzahar," from the Persian/Arabic word for the nodes of the moon or planets; the points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note></term>—that is, the place in which the line of the planet's eccentric orbit cuts the path of the Sun. Hence, when it passes from the south into the north, its transition is through the point of contact of its eccentric with the Sun's eccentric. And as long as it remains in that part of its eccentric which is on the northern side of the Sun's path, it is called "Northern," until it comes to the other point of contact which is opposite that transition, and returns to that part of the eccentric which is on the southern side of the Sun's eccentric; in that entire half, it is called "Southern." And when it has passed the aforementioned first point of contact up to three full signs, it will be a "northern ascending" planet; and from three signs up to the sixth, it will be "northern descending." And when it has passed the said point of contact again, returning to the south, up to three full signs, it will be "southern descending"; and from three up to six full signs—which is the place of its node from which it begins to be northern—it will be "southern ascending." These are the things that happen to the planets within themselves.

### Chapter Three: Concerning those things that happen to planets in relation to one another, namely one from another.

In this chapter, we must treat those things that happen to one planet from another according to their properties—that is, in relation to one another. And first, we must consider those things that happen to **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, **Venus**, and **Mercury** from the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> and regarding the luminaries. **Ptolemy** said that when a planet sees itself "face to face," then the planet is said to be in the **Almugea** <term>Almugea<note>original: "almuguea," an astrological configuration where a planet's distance from the Sun corresponds to the distance between their respective planetary "houses" or home signs.</note></term> of the planet. "Almugea" sounds like "face-to-face vision"; this word of Ptolemy's seems somewhat Arabic; it is to be understood in this way: when a planet is "western" from the Sun, it is said to be in the Almugea of the Sun. And be careful not to be deceived by Ptolemy saying "western"—do not understand it to mean that the planet sets after the Sun, as "western" is understood elsewhere. But by "western" from the Sun, Ptolemy meant

<column-break/>

that the planet should be on the western side such that it sets *before* the Sun sets. And Ptolemy understood when he said "face to face" that this means the distance between the planet and the Sun should be as great as the distance between the **House of the Sun** <note>The zodiac sign Leo.</note> and the House of that planet. I understand this as: when the planet is distant from the Sun by as much as the distance between its own House and **Leo**, which is the House of the Sun. 

For example: let us suppose that **Saturn** is distant from the Sun by as much as the distance between **Leo** and **Capricorn**, which is the House of Saturn. That is, let the Sun be in any one sign, and let Saturn be in a sign that is as distant from that one as **Capricorn** is distant from **Leo**—namely, that one of them be in the sixth sign from the other, just as **Capricorn** is the sixth sign from **Leo**. And let there be as many signs, degrees, and minutes between them as there are between those two signs, with one of them included in the count and the other excluded, which is five full signs; then Saturn will be in the Almugea of the Sun. 

For example: let us suppose the Sun is in the 12th degree of **Leo** and Saturn is also in the 12th degree of **Pisces**. Now Saturn is in the sixth sign from the Sun, counting the sign in which each of them is located—namely: Leo, Cancer, Gemini, Taurus, Aries, and Pisces. Now Saturn is distant from the Sun by as much as the distance between **Leo**, which is the House of the Sun, and **Capricorn**, which is the House of Saturn, such that five full signs fall between them. For from the 12th degree of **Pisces** to the 12th degree of **Leo**, there are five full signs: namely, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo; just as five full signs fall between **Leo** and **Capricorn**, which are Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. <note>The author is calculating the distance through the zodiac to show the symmetrical relationship.</note> For from the 12th degree of Leo to the 12th degree of Cancer is one full sign. From the 12th degree of Cancer to the 12th degree of Gemini is one full sign, making two signs. From the 12th degree of Gemini to the 12th degree of Taurus is one full sign, making three signs. From the 12th degree of Taurus to the 12th degree of Aries is one full sign, making four signs. From the 12th degree of Aries to the 12th degree of Pisces is one full sign, making five full signs. For a sign is not counted as "its own" in the sign where it begins, but in the second sign from itself. 

Similarly, for **Jupiter** to be in the Almugea of the Sun, there must fall between it and the Sun as many signs, degrees, and minutes as there are between **Leo** and **Sagittarius**, which is the House of Jupiter, and this is four full signs; that is, Jupiter must be in the fifth sign from the Sun. For example: let the Sun be in any sign—let us say **Gemini**. It is necessary now that Jupiter be in **Aquarius** so that it is distant from the Sun by four full signs, neither more nor less. For **Aquarius** is the fifth sign from **Gemini** in the same degree and minute. Let the Sun then be in the 3rd degree of **Gemini**; now, from the 3rd degree of Gemini to the 3rd degree of **Taurus** is one full sign; from the 3rd degree of Taurus to the 3rd degree of **Aries** is one full sign, making two signs. And from the 3rd degree of Aries to the 3rd degree of **Pisces** is one full sign, making three signs. And from the 3rd degree of Pisces to the 3rd degree of **Aquarius** is one full sign, making four full signs, and thus Jupiter will be in the fifth sign from the Sun. 

Similarly, for **Mars** to be in the Almugea of the Sun, it must be in the fourth sign from the Sun, so that three full signs fall between them, just as they fall between **Leo** and **Scorpio**, which is the House of Mars; and as was said, with one included and the other excluded as in the others. Let us suppose the Sun is in the 4th degree of **Aries**; it is now necessary for Mars to be in the 4th degree of **Capricorn**, since between the 4th degree of Aries and the 4th degree of Capricorn there are three full signs: for from the 4th degree of Aries to the 4th degree of **Pisces** is one full sign; and from the 4th degree of Pisces to...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary configurations and "accidents," specifically finishing the explanation of almuguea (a relative positioning of planets) and moving into the definitions of planetary "joining" (aspects) and the cycle of oriental/occidental phases relative to the Sun.</meta>

the fourth degree of Aquarius is one whole sign <note>The text is explaining how to count distances in the zodiac; from the 4th degree of one sign to the 4th of the next is exactly 30 degrees, or one full zodiacal sign.</note>; and thus there are two whole signs. And between the fourth degree of Aquarius and the fourth degree of Capricorn is one whole sign, and thus there are three whole signs: and so **Mars** will be in the fourth sign from the **Sun**. In the case of **Venus**, however, **almuguea** <term>almuguea<note>original: "almuguea," from the Arabic "al-muwājahah," referring to a specific configuration where a planet is as many signs away from the Sun or Moon as its "house" (domicile) is from the Sun or Moon's house.</note></term> is not considered in the same way as in other planets, because she does not distance herself from the Sun as far as her house is from the house of the Sun. But she is said to be in the **Sun’s** *almuguea* when she sets before the Sun sets, and is at her furthest elongation from the Sun so that she cannot move any further away from him. Concerning **Mercury**, it must be said that for him to be in the Sun’s *almuguea*, he must be in the second sign from the Sun, so that one whole sign falls between him and the Sun, just as one whole sign is between Leo <note>The house of the Sun</note> and Virgo, which is the house of **Mercury**. Suppose that the Sun is in the 9th degree of Capricorn and the 12th minute: now it is necessary that **Mercury** be in the 9th degree of Sagittarius and the 12th minute, because between the 9th degree and 12th minute of Capricorn and the 9th degree and 12th minute of Sagittarius is one whole sign. The **Moon**, however, is not said to be in the Sun’s *almuguea* because the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> are not said to be in the *almuguea* of luminaries; and also because it would be necessary for her to be far from the Sun by only one sign, and when she is in the Sun’s *almuguea* she ought to receive it; and since she can receive *almuguea*, it could bring about or confer sensitivity.

### On almuguea.

In the *almuguea* of the **Moon**, it must be considered: and you must know that just as a planet which is in the Sun’s *almuguea* is "occidental" <note>Setting in the west</note> from the Sun—that is, it sets before the Sun sets—so it is necessary that, conversely, a planet which is in the **Moon’s** *almuguea* be "oriental" <note>Rising in the east</note> from her: such that it sets after the Moon and not before her, and the Moon sets before it and not after. And **Ptolemy** <note>original: "ptholomeus," the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> said: when a planet is as far behind the Sun as its house is from the house of the Sun, and as far ahead of the Moon as its house is from the house of the Moon, or is safe from their rays, then it is in *almuguea*.

### On the almuguea of other planets.

The sages did not care to mention the *almuguea* of the other planets, because they did not believe there was great power in them; nevertheless, each of the other five planets has its own *almuguea*. For the *almuguea* of the three **superior planets** <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> is considered like the Sun’s *almuguea*, and that of the two **inferior planets** <note>Venus and Mercury</note> is considered like the Moon’s *almuguea*. And any of them can be in the *almuguea* of another when it is as far from it as its house is from the house of the other which is nearest to it; and the lower planet always receives *almuguea* from the higher, except for **Saturn**, who receives his *almuguea* from **Mercury**.

### Chapter four: On the altitifal of planets.

There is another state of the planets toward each other, namely a bodily or aspectual joining or application, which **Al-Qabisi** <note>original: "alchabid⁹," referring to Al-Qabisi (Alchabitius), a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> calls **altitifal** <term>altitifal<note>From the Arabic "al-ittiṣāl," meaning "joining" or "application" (aspect).</note></term> or continuation. For a bodily joining occurs when a planet joins another planet in the same sign. An aspectual joining occurs when two planets are in two different signs looking at each other in a **trine**, **sextile**, or **square** aspect, and the "light" <note>faster-moving</note> planet has fewer degrees in its sign than the "heavy" <note>slower-moving</note> planet has in its own, provided there are six degrees or fewer between them—that is, between the rays of one and the body of the other. For example: suppose **Venus** or **Mercury** is in the 4th degree of Aries, and **Mars**, **Jupiter**, or **Saturn** is in the 10th degree of Gemini, Cancer, or Leo ahead of it; or is in the 10th degree of Aquarius, Capricorn, or Sagittarius behind it; then **Venus** or **Mercury** joins that planet through an aspect until it reaches its aspect degree by degree. And the same thing is to be

<column-break/>

understood concerning bodily conjunction: such as if **Venus** or **Mercury** is in the 4th degree of Aries and any of the superior planets is in the 10th degree of that same Aries; now the light planet joins the heavy one by body, and it is always said to be "joined" to it until it completes its joining with it at the exact same minute; but after it has passed it by one minute, it is said to be "separated" from it. What I have told you about **Venus** and **Mercury**, understand for all others: for the light always joins the heavy, and the less heavy joins the heavier, until it reaches **Saturn**. For **Saturn**, being heavier <note>slower</note> than the rest, joins no other planet, as has been said elsewhere, but all others join him. **Al-Qabisi**, however, said that a planet is not called "joined" to another unless it joins it degree by degree, whether that joining be bodily or by aspect; he understood this to be the very act of perfecting a matter. And **Masha'allah** <note>original: "Alstahala," referring to Masha'allah ibn Athari, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note>, in whom the sages placed great trust, said that from the moment a planet casts its rays upon the planet to which it is joined, it is a joining, unless another planet prohibits their union. Furthermore, one planet joins with another, and they signify thereby the effects of things. Whence, because one planet casts its rays upon the rays of another and is distant from it only as much as their **orbs** <note>The "aura" or range of influence surrounding a planet</note> combined, it is said that one "seeks the joining" of the other; and it signifies the effect of the thing questioned unless another planet destroys or impedes it, and that is called a "heavy joining." And when the distance is only as much as the orb of one planet, it is called a "joining" absolutely, and unless something interferes, as was said, it signifies the effect of the matter. And when the orb of the light planet touches the body of the heavy one, it is said that the heavy one is "in the degrees" of the light one. And all these things are considered both in aspect and in bodily conjunction.

### Chapter five: When planets are called oriental and when occidental.

**Saturn** and **Jupiter**, from the moment they emerge from under the rays of the **Sun**, as **Al-Qabisi** says, are called **oriental** <note>Rising in the morning before the Sun</note>; and they are said to increase in strength until they are 30 degrees away from the Sun. This is like a sick person who, after a **crisis** <note>The turning point of an illness</note>, increases in strength and prosperity until he resumes his former vigor and returns to the state he was in before he began to be ill, and remains more secure. Then, from those 30 degrees until another 30 <note>i.e., 60 degrees from the Sun</note>, they are called "strong orientals," because they are then in the greatest security from the Sun that they can ever be; for they do not fear him then in anything, just as a man does not fear sickness who has escaped from it and has already resumed all his strength; indeed, after a perfect recovery and resumption of power, he is sometimes fleshier and stronger than usual, if his **complexion** <note>The balance of his bodily humors</note> is well-disposed to receive it. And when they have passed the Sun by 60 degrees—that is, when the Sun is that far distant from them—they are called "orientals going toward weakness" until they reach an elongation of 90 degrees from the Sun, and then they are called "weak orientals" until they reach **retrogradation** <note>When a planet appears to move backward in the sky</note>. And after they have begun to move retrograde, they are called "retrograde orientals" until they are in opposition to the Sun, degree for degree. And after they have passed the degree of opposition to the Sun until they reach **direction** <note>Resuming forward motion</note>, they are called "retrograde occidentals." Then, from the degree of direction until the 60th degree after direction, they are "strong occidentals"—not that they are truly strong, but less weak. Then, from said 60 degrees until their distance from the Sun is 30 degrees, they are called "occidentals going toward weakness." Then, until they reach the beginning of **combustion** <note>Getting so close to the Sun that their influence is "burned up" or hidden</note>, they are called "weak occidentals." And after they have begun to enter under the rays of the Sun until they reach his degree, they are called "combust occidentals." And all these degrees are considered according to the **zodiac** <note>The belt of the heavens</note> and its degrees, and not according to the **eccentric** or the **epicycle**.

# Chapter six: regarding the two lower planets, when they are oriental and when they are occidental.

**Venus** and **Mercury**, when they separate from the **Sun** and are themselves retrograde, are called "weak orientals." From the moment they begin to move direct until they are near the **Sun**—such that there are as many degrees between them and the **Sun** as there were between the **Sun** and them when they began to retrograde—they are called "strong orientals." Then, until the midpoint of those degrees remaining between that aforementioned place and the rays of the **Sun**, they are called "weak orientals." And from the moment they begin to enter beneath the rays of the **Sun** until they are in the same degree as the **Sun**, they are called "combust orientals" <note>original: "orientales combusti"; combustion occurs when a planet is so close to the Sun that its influence is "burned up" or hidden by the Sun's light.</note>. Then, until they have traveled through all the other degrees of combustion, they are called "combust occidentals" moving toward their appearance. And from the moment they begin to appear from beneath the rays of the **Sun** in direct motion until the 15th degree after their appearance, they are called "strong occidentals." Then, until the midpoint of the degrees between that place and their first station <note>The "station" is the point where a planet appears to stand still before changing direction.</note>, they are called "occidentals moving toward weakness." Then, until the beginning of their retrogradation, they are called "weak occidentals." Then, until they come to the rays of the **Sun**, they are called "retrograde occidentals," or "most weak." And after they have begun to enter beneath the rays until they come to the degree of the **Sun**, they are called "combust occidentals."

Every planet, from the moment it emerges from beneath the rays of the **Sun** until it joins another planet either by body or by aspect, is said to be "in its light." This is what it means for the planets of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> to be "in their light." Therefore, you ought to consider this in nativities <note>birth charts</note> or interrogations <note>horary questions</note> and see whether the significator of anything is in its light, and it will be good or bad accordingly. For if it signifies good and is in a good place in its **epicycle** or its **eccentric** <term>epicycle and eccentric<note>In Ptolemaic astronomy, these are the circular paths and off-center circles used to explain the complex movements of planets.</note></term>, it will signify that good as a completed thing when this occurs. And if the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are "strong orientals" and are approaching their furthest distance or their **apogee** <note>original: "augem," the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>, or if they are in fast motion—especially if they are northern—all matters will become better, more perfect, faster, and with less labor. If, however, they are "weak orientals" or moving toward weakness, or are descending in any of the aforementioned circles, they signify the effect of the matter, but with labor, insistence, delay, worry, and with some degree of diminution; this is true in nativities just as in interrogations. If they are occidentals, they will likewise diminish the good. And if they are "weak occidentals," they will diminish the signified things even more. And if they are retrograde or combust, they will diminish them even more still, and they will give what they were meant to give only with labor, insistence, worry, and anguish—especially if, along with this, they are southern.

# Chapter seven: on the leadership or the *hayz* of the planets.

**Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a famous 10th-century Arabic astrologer whose introductions to astrology were standard textbooks in Medieval Europe.</note> said that a planet is said to be in its **leadership** <term>leadership<note>original: "duxtoria," likely a Latinization of a term referring to a planet's guiding power or "dexterity."</note></term> when it is in its **hayz** <term>hayz<note>original: "ayz," a condition of dignity where a planet is in a sign and "half" of the day/night cycle that matches its own gender and nature.</note></term> or in its "likeness." This means a masculine planet in a masculine sign, and a feminine one in a feminine sign; and a diurnal planet by day above the earth and by night below the earth; and a nocturnal planet by night above the earth and by day below the earth. Thus, by day it is oriental to the **Sun**, and by night occidental to the **Moon**. And so that the planet may be in one of the angles of the **ascendant** <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a chart</note>, and one of the luminaries is in one of the angles in a square aspect to that planet. For example: let the fifth degree of **Taurus** be the ascendant (which is then the first house); it is then necessary that the planet be in the fourth house or the tenth from the ascendant, so that it is in an angle of the ascendant—specifically in the fifth degree of the sign forming that house—so that three entire signs fall between those houses and the ascendant,

<column-break/>

and some luminary is in a square aspect to that planet; that is, so that 90 degrees fall between them—specifically between the planet and the luminary.

He also described **leadership** in another way, interpreted as "safety" or "security." This is when a planet is oriental to the **Sun** by day, and occidental to the **Moon** by night. "Oriental to the Sun" means it rises before him; "occidental to the Moon" means it sets before her; specifically, so that there are 60 degrees between the planet and the **Sun** or **Moon**. And likewise, the luminary must be in its own *hayz*: the **Sun** by day above the earth and by night below the earth, and the **Moon** necessarily must be by night above the earth and by day below the earth. For this reason, the wise have said that a planet should be safe from the rays of the luminaries. When a planet enters beneath the rays of the **Sun** so that it is covered by them, it is "combust" until it emerges from beneath his rays and appears.

When it begins to enter beneath the rays, it is said to "begin to be burned" or to have "fallen into combustion." This **leadership** <note>Here used to mean the zone of influence</note> is beneath the rays near the **Sun** by 12 degrees when moving toward him (if it is one of the lower planets) or separating and receding from him by two degrees or less. Or, if it is one of the superior planets and the **Sun** is moving toward it and is within 12 degrees, or has left it behind by two degrees or less, it is "oppressed." And when it is with the **Sun** in one degree, so that there are 16 minutes or less between them—both in latitude and longitude, which is rarely attained—it is shown to be "united." Then it is made stronger, as if it were in the "furnace" of the **Sun**, which is "in his heart" <term>cazimi<note>original: "in corde ipsius," meaning "in the heart of the Sun." An astrological condition where a planet is so close to the center of the Sun that it is fortified by the Sun's power rather than burned by it.</note></term>. Many of those who treat the stars, especially in my time, have disagreed on this, saying that when a planet is distant from the **Sun** by 16 minutes or less, it is "alone" and is in the "heart of the Sun." I have followed them, but not simply; for a planet to be in the "path" or the "heart of the Sun," it must be distant from the **Sun** by at least 16 minutes in both longitude and latitude. This was the intention of the philosophers, because if a planet is distant from the **Sun** in longitude by less than 16 minutes, but in latitude by more than 16 minutes, it is nonetheless combust, since the difference of latitude in combustion is as sensible as that of longitude.

**Alchabitius** said that when a planet has passed that same union—namely, for the three superior planets, if they remain 2 or 3 degrees behind the **Sun**, or for the inferior planets if they have moved 5 degrees away from it—it is said to have "escaped," whether they are direct or retrograde. The philosophers said this with great caution and for certain certainty, so they might not be deceived in anything. I, however, believe a planet has escaped once it is separated from the **Sun** by 2 degrees or more, whether it is in front or behind. A planet is said to have "escaped" in the likeness of a sick man whom the fever has left, yet he has not yet recovered his health so that he might be called "cured," nor is he entirely free; however, he is out of danger until he recovers, after which he is called "liberated." 

Thus it is with a planet: when it enters combustion, it is like one who begins to fall ill. When it is in the final stage of combustion, it is like a sick man when the **paroxysm** <note>The peak or sudden attack of a disease</note> is in a state where the fever is about to come on and is already as if in the making. And when it is separated from the **Sun** by up to 2 degrees, it is like a sick man who has reached a **crisis** <note>In medieval medicine, the "crisis" was the turning point of a disease, after which the patient would either recover or die.</note>, which is not yet complete—like the sweat, sleep, discharge, and similar things that produce a crisis. And when it is from those 2 degrees up to the other three—namely, the completion of 5 degrees—it is like a sick man whose crisis has arrived and is now complete. And when it is from those 5 degrees of distance from the **Sun** until it emerges from beneath the rays, it is like a sick man whose illness ceases and is manifestly diminished; and it is entirely liberated from combustion just as a sick man is entirely liberated from illness, but has not yet resumed his former strength; nevertheless, he is safe from that sickness.

### ¶ Chapter 8: Regarding the three superior planets from the time they appear from beneath the sun's rays.

And after **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** have appeared from beneath the rays of the **sun** and are entirely out of <term>combustion</term> <note>original: "combustionem"; combustion occurs when a planet is so close to the Sun—usually within 8.5 degrees—that its own light and influence are "burned up" or obscured by the Sun's power.</note>, so that they may be seen in the east before the **sun**, they are called "oriental on the right" until they reach the point opposite the **sun**. Their strength increases until they are distant from the body of the **sun** by 30 degrees. And from there for another 30 degrees—so that the total distance from the body of the **sun** is 60 degrees—they are "strong orientals." From those 60 degrees onward, they are orientals moving toward weakness until they come to their first <term>station</term> <note>The "station" is the point where a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing its apparent direction.</note> and begin to <term>retrograde</term> <note>To move backward through the zodiac, contrary to the usual order of the signs.</note>. From the first station onward, until the **sun** is opposite them in a direct line, degree for degree, they are "retrograde orientals." But after the **sun** has passed them by opposition, they are "retrograde occidentals" until they come to the second station and begin to move "direct" (forward) again. From that point until the **sun** approaches within thirty degrees of them, they are "strong occidentals." From there onward, until the **sun** approaches within fifteen degrees, they are called "occidentals moving toward weakness." Afterward, they are "weak occidentals" until they enter beneath the rays of the **sun**. From then on, they are "combust occidentals" until they are united with the **sun** in the same degree. And when they are in opposition to the **sun**, they are called "opposites." When they have passed the opposition, they are called "oriental on the left." This is a significant hindrance to them, for they begin to fear that they will again come into combustion; they are like a person being pursued who begins to grow weary in flight and sees the one following him already cutting off his path, seeing that the pursuer is faster and drawing near, fearing he cannot escape the other's hands.

->¶ Regarding Venus and Mercury when they separate from the sun.<-

**Venus** and **Mercury**, from the time they separate from the **sun** and are retrograde, are "orientals" until they come to their first station and begin to move direct. From the point of moving direct until they are as far away as they were when they began to retrograde, they are "strong orientals." Then, until they approach the **sun** within twenty degrees, they are "weak orientals" until they enter beneath the rays of the **sun**. After they are beneath the rays, they are "combust orientals" until they are united with the **sun**. And **Alchabicius** <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician whose work was a standard textbook in Medieval Europe.</note> said that from then on they are "combust moving toward appearance" until they are seen. From the moment they separate from the **sun** in direct motion, they are called "strong occidentals" until they come to retrogradation. And from the time they begin to retrograde until they are again united with the **sun**, they are called "weak occidentals." And he said that when a planet has emerged from beneath the rays of the **sun** and has been joined to no other planet, it is said to be "in its own light." This is the state of the planets in relation to the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>.

### ¶ Chapter 9: Regarding the conjunction of planets according to latitude.

Hitherto mention has been made in the preceding sections regarding the <term>conjunction</term> <note>A conjunction is when two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky.</note> of the planets, and that mention was regarding their conjunction according to <term>longitude</term> <note>Longitude measures distance along the ecliptic, essentially East to West.</note>, considering that conjunction from east to west or vice versa. Now, however, it remains to speak of their conjunction according to <term>latitude</term> <note>Latitude measures how far north or south a planet is from the ecliptic (the sun's path).</note>; this is the kind that occurs between them from south to north or vice-versa, or toward either side. A conjunction of latitude is when one of the planets is joined to another according to its latitude; for example, if one planet were joining another by its physical body and both were in the same degree, their conjunction would be by

<column-break/>

latitude and equal, whether that conjunction or <term>application</term> <note>The movement of a faster planet toward an aspect or conjunction with a slower one.</note> is northern or southern, because the latitude of each of them would be on one and the same side. And if their conjunction is by opposition, their latitudes will be equal in this way: namely, that the latitude of one is ascending in the north and the other is ascending in the south. And although this statement may seem difficult to understand, it is simple in itself; for when a planet goes to its furthest distance, it is then "ascending in the north." And it is necessary for this—that one be joined to another by opposition—that one be in one quarter of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an epicycle is a small circle the planet moves on, which itself moves along a larger circle.</note> and the other be in its own epicycle in the quarter opposite to it. All conjunctions that occur by any other means than this are conjunctions of longitude and not of latitude. And that way is when one planet is northern ascending in the north and the other is southern descending in the south. Nor is it a conjunction of latitude. Nevertheless, the wise men of this art, and especially those who use an <term>almanac</term> <note>A set of tables used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies.</note>, do not care much about this conjunction of latitude in their judgments; this does not seem appropriate to me, especially in great matters such as <term>nativities</term> <note>Birth charts.</note>, universal questions, the revolutions of the years, and similar things.

### ¶ Chapter 10: Regarding the void of course of the planets.

After one planet has been joined to another and their conjunction has been perfected, and after the perfection it has been "translated" (passed on)—so that one of them is separated from the other and after the separation it is joined to no other planet—it is called <term>void of course</term> <note>original: "vacuus cursu"; a condition where a planet makes no further major aspects before leaving its current zodiac sign.</note>, because it then runs solitary. And it shall remain "void of course" until it is joined to another or seeks its conjunction, as has been said elsewhere; and this is a certain hindrance to it. And **Alchabicius** said that as long as any planet is solitary in any sign and no other planet <term>aspects</term> <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle (like 90 or 120 degrees) between planets that allows them to "see" or influence each other.</note> it, that sign is said to be "feral" or "wild"; and this is likewise a great hindrance to it and very <unclear>bad</unclear> for a <unclear>person</unclear>.

### ¶ Chapter 11: Regarding the translation of the nature of the planets.

It was the opinion of certain philosophers that one planet transfers the nature of one to another absolutely. For they said that when a light planet is separated from a heavy one and joins another—whether heavier than it or lighter—it transfers the nature of the first to the second. This seems somewhat obscure to me to admit so simply; for it does not seem likely that although one planet is joined to another, it would give it its power or commit its nature or disposition to it, unless it joins it by some of its <term>dignities</term> <note>original: "dignitatum"; essential strengths or "honors" a planet has based on its position in certain signs or degrees.</note>, according to the saying of the philosopher: "A planet gives nothing in a place where it promised nothing." Therefore, if a planet does not give it its nature or power, it does not seem that it could carry the nature of another to a high place. And even if it did give or commit it to itself, by the same reasoning it does not seem that it would give it to another unless it were joined to the same by some of its dignities. And I believe that this was their intention, although they did not express it. But if a light planet were joined to a heavy planet by some dignity of the heavy one, the heavy one would commit its nature and disposition to it, and it could carry it with itself until it joined another planet which it found in some dignity of its own; and it would commit to that one what it had received—unless perhaps that power were lost by the conjunction of another, even if it did not commit it to itself. For it is not likely that someone gives to a stranger in a foreign land what he acquired for himself. Nevertheless, since they were wiser than I, their words are to be upheld, whatever their intention may have been. And they said that a planet carries the nature of a planet to another according to such an example...

¶ Suppose the **Moon** was joined to **Venus** in one sign and in one degree: for example, let her be in the 4th degree of **Taurus** <note>original: "tauri"</note>. And when she was separated from **Venus**, she was joined to **Mars** in the 6th degree of that same **Taurus**, or in whatever other degree he might be. Now, **Mars** is "heavier" <term>ponderosior</term> <note>In medieval astrology, "heavy" planets are those that move more slowly through the zodiac (like Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars), while "light" planets move quickly (like the Moon, Mercury, and Venus).</note> than **Venus** or **Mercury**, which are "lighter" than him. In this way, the **Moon** "transfers the nature" <term>transfert naturam</term> of **Venus** to **Mars**, or to whichever planet she first finds or is first joined to. For **Venus** had yielded her disposition and nature to the **Moon**, and the **Moon** herself committed to the one she first found and was first joined to that which had been committed to her by **Venus**. 

And they said that there is another mode of the translation of a planet's nature to another: as when a lighter planet joins a heavier one, and that heavier one is joined to another even heavier than himself; then that middle-weight planet, being between the light and the heaviest, transfers the nature of the lighter to the heaviest. ¶ For example, **Mercury** was joined to **Venus** in the 10th degree of **Pisces** <note>original: "piscis"</note> or in any other degree; and after separation from **Venus**, he was joined to the **Sun** in the 12th degree of **Pisces** or any other; and the **Sun** likewise is joined to **Mars** in the 14th degree

of the same **Pisces** or in any other, provided the degrees are related to one another. In this way, **Mercury** transfers the nature of **Venus** to the **Sun**, and the **Sun** transfers it to **Mars**. But if neither of those two heavier ones is joined to any other planet alone, but instead both are joined at the same time and once to a single planet, then that third planet is said to "return the light" <term>reddit lumen</term> of those two to that place in the circle which he himself "gazes upon" <term>aspicit</term> <note>To "gaze upon" or "aspect" means the planet is looking at another part of the zodiac through a specific geometric angle, like a square or a trine.</note>. And this is called the "return of light" according to such an example: **Mercury** was separated from **Venus** at the 10th degree of **Pisces** or wherever; and after separation from **Venus**, he was joined to the **Sun** and **Mars** in the 12th degree of the same **Pisces** or wherever; and these were then joined to **Jupiter** in the 13th degree of the same **Pisces** or wherever, but **Jupiter** is joined to no other planet. In this case, **Jupiter** transfers the light of **Venus** to that place in the circle which he himself gazes upon: namely, to the 13th degree of **Taurus** before him by a <term>sextile aspect</term> <note>A sextile aspect occurs when planets are 60 degrees apart, considered a harmonious relationship.</note>.

# ¶ Chapter 12: Regarding the return of light of the planets and its cutting off.

Since we have spoken of the translation of the nature of the planets, it remains to speak of the return of their light and its "cutting off" <term>abscissio</term> <note>original: "abscisione"; "Abscission of light" occurs when a planet's intended connection to another is interrupted or "cut off" by a third planet getting there first.</note>. This occurs if one planet seeks a conjunction with another, but they are not yet joined together, and another planet besides those two joins first with the one whom the first was seeking; that third planet then "returns the light" of the third to the first. It is called the "return of light," and it is also called its "cutting off." ¶ For example, let it be posed that the **Sun** was in the 12th degree of **Cancer**, and **Saturn** in the 18th degree of **Libra**, and **Jupiter** in the 15th degree of **Gemini**. Now, the **Sun** is seeking a conjunction with **Saturn** from a fourth [square] aspect; but **Ju-**

...similarly, **Jupiter**, which is closer to the junction of **Saturn** than the **Sun** is, joins him by a trine aspect <note>A trine aspect occurs when two planets are 120 degrees apart, considered a very harmonious relationship.</note> and cuts off the **Sun's** light from **Saturn**; this is called the "cutting off of light" <note>original: "abscissio luminis"</note>. There is also the "returning of light" <note>original: "redditio luminis"</note>, which occurs when **Saturn** returns the light to the **Sun** that he had already begun to receive from him, but instead receives the light of **Jupiter**, who is closer to him. For instance, if **Jupiter** is at the 15th degree of his sign, the **Sun** is at the 12th degree, and **Saturn** is nearby; in such a case, the matter being asked about in an astrological question might be destroyed or lose hope.

This is much like the way certain merchants or others who buy and sell things behave. One person asks another to sell him something and hopes to obtain it in the way he requested, not believing anyone else will interfere. But then someone else comes in from the side and offers the seller a bit more than the first person promised, thus taking the item for himself. He frustrates the first person's goal or causes someone else to intervene, so that the first person is denied and the second person acquires it. This is a very important concept to consider in astrological questions, as a matter is often frustrated even after it seems to be progressing directly.

You should also know that the "return of light" is considered according to the **aspect** <note>The geometric angle between planets.</note>. However, the "translation of nature" or "virtue" is considered both by physical conjunction <term>corporalem coniunctionem</term> <note>When two planets occupy the same degree and sign.</note> and by aspect, though most often by physical conjunction.

### Chapter 13. On the prohibition of conjunction and why things are sometimes not completed.

**Prohibition** <note>original: "prohibitio"</note> of conjunction is the reason why matters are sometimes not brought to completion. This happens in two ways. The first is when three planets are in one sign at different degrees, and the "heaviest" <note>In medieval astrology, "heavy" (ponderosus) refers to slow-moving planets like Saturn or Jupiter; "light" (leuis) refers to fast ones like the Moon or Mercury.</note> planet is at a higher degree than the others. If one of the other two seeks a conjunction with that heavier planet, but there is another planet in the middle between them, the one in the middle "prohibits" the union. Because it is at a lower degree, it prevents the first from reaching the heavier planet until the middle one has passed through the conjunction and left it behind. 

¶ For example: the **Sun** was at the 10th degree of **Capricorn**, **Mars** was at the 14th degree of the same sign, and **Jupiter** was at the 16th degree. The **Sun** sought to join **Jupiter**, but **Mars**, being between them (closer to **Jupiter** than the **Sun**), prohibited the **Sun** from joining **Jupiter**. **Mars** himself joined him first, and thus **Mars** did not cease to prohibit the **Sun's** union with **Jupiter** until he had passed him. Only then could the **Sun** join **Jupiter**. Therefore, if the business being questioned had not been totally destroyed yet, it could only be completed once the **Sun** and **Jupiter** finally joined.

¶ The second mode occurs when two planets are in one sign and a "light" planet joins a "heavy" one by body, while another planet also joins that same heavy one by an aspect from the same degree. In this case, the planet joining by body in the same sign cancels the conjunction of the one looking on by aspect. The physical conjunction <term>coniunctio corporalis</term> is stronger than the aspectual one.

¶ For example: **Venus** was at the 4th degree of **Aries**, **Mars** was at the 9th degree of **Aries**, and the **Moon** was at the 4th degree of **Aquarius**, wishing to join **Mars** by aspect. The **Moon** would have joined him if nothing else interfered, but **Venus**, joining **Mars** physically, prohibited the **Moon's** conjunction with **Mars** for the reason stated above: that a physical union destroys an aspect, but an aspect does not cancel a physical union. It would be different if the planet in aspect were at a higher degree in its sign than the one joining by body. For example, if **Venus** was at the 4th degree of **Aries**, **Mars** at the 9th, and the **Moon** was at the 6th degree of **Aquarius**, then the **Moon** would 

<column-break/>

join **Mars** and cancel **Venus's** union with **Mars**, because the **Moon** "sees" him from a closer degree than **Venus** was joined to him.

You should also know that if any planet is joined with the Lord of the sign it is in, or with the Lord of its **exaltation**, or the Lord of its **term**, **triplicity**, or **face** <note>These are the "Essential Dignities," specific segments of the zodiac where certain planets have increased power or "home-field advantage."</note>, whether by body or aspect, that Lord "receives" the planet. It takes up the planet's disposition and nature and virtue. 

¶ This is certainly true if it joins the Lord of the **house** or **exaltation**, or joins the Lord of two of the other minor dignities (such as the Lord of the **term** and **triplicity**, or **term** and **face**, or **face** and **triplicity**). But if it joins only the Lord of the **term** alone, or **triplicity** alone, or **face** alone, that Lord does not "receive" it, because a single minor dignity does not have enough power to create "reception" without the help of another.

¶ The planet that "receives" another commits its own disposition to it, even if they are "enemies" by aspect or conjunction. 

¶ For example: the **Moon** was at the 3rd degree of **Aries**, and **Mars** (the Lord of **Aries**) was at the 8th degree of **Gemini**, **Cancer**, or **Leo** ahead of her, or in **Aquarius**, **Capricorn**, or **Sagittarius** behind her. In this case, the **Moon** was joined to **Mars** by aspect, and he "received" her from his own house, committing his virtue and disposition to her. Or, if the **Moon** was at the 3rd degree of **Aries** and the **Sun** (the Lord of the **exaltation** of **Aries**) was at the 8th or 9th degree of those signs, the **Moon** joined the **Sun** by aspect; he received her from his exaltation and committed his strength to her. Or, if the **Moon** was at the 3rd degree of **Aries** and **Jupiter** (the Lord of the first **term** and the **triplicity** of **Aries**) was at the 5th degree of those signs, the **Moon** joined **Jupiter** by aspect; he received her from his term and triplicity and committed his virtue to her just as if he had received her from his house or exaltation. 

¶ This is the "commitment" or "giving" of the virtue and disposition of the planets. But if the **Moon** joined **Saturn**, who is the Lord of the triplicity of **Aries** but holds no other dignity there, he would not receive her, because he has only one minor dignity, which cannot create a perfect reception. 

**Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a famous 10th-century Arabic astrologer whose "Introduction to the Art of Judgments of the Stars" was a standard textbook in medieval Europe.</note>, however, suggests that if a planet is in any dignity of another planet and joins it, that Lord gives and commits its nature to it. I do not reject his opinion or say it should be cast aside, since he wrote the fundamental introductory text and his authority is greater than others. He said that when a planet is in any of its own dignities and is joined to another planet by body, it will give that planet its strength. Similarly, if a planet is in a place where another planet has some dignity and they are joined, it gives its strength or nature. 

¶ For example: **Jupiter** was at the 9th degree of **Aries** and **Mars** was at the 5th degree of **Aries**. **Mars** joins **Jupiter** and receives him from his own house; thus he commits his strength, disposition, and nature to him. And since **Jupiter** also has the dignity of triplicity there, he now holds both dignities: the one he has by triplicity and the one **Mars** gives him from the house. This mixture that **Mars** creates is called "reception," which the philosophers call <term>alcobol</term> <note>From the Arabic 'al-qabul', meaning 'reception' or 'acceptance'.</note>.

### Chapter 14. On the return of virtue when a planet returns it to the one who gave it to him.

<summary>This page defines the astrological concepts of "prohibition" (interference between planets) and "reception" (the sharing of planetary power). It uses a vivid merchant analogy to explain how one planet can disrupt the influence of another and cites the authority of Alchabitius on the nuances of planetary dignities.</summary>

<keywords>prohibition, reception, alcobol, Alchabitius, planetary dignities, cutting off of light, return of light, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, Moon, Aries, Capricorn, astrological aspects</keywords>

--- Page 73 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the "translation of light" discussed previously to the concept of the "return of virtue" (redditio virtutis). It explores how the strength or weakness of a planet's position (whether it is in a "strong" house or moving "backwards") determines if an astrological prediction will come to fruition or fail. It also introduces the concept of "refrenation," where a planet's influence is stopped before it can complete an action.</meta>

When one planet joins another and gives or commits its <term>virtue</term> <note>Virtue refers to the specific power or influence a planet holds based on its position.</note> or its <term>disposition</term> to it, and that planet which receives it is <term>retrograde</term> <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky, usually a sign of weakness or reversal.</note> or <term>combust</term> <note>Too close to the Sun, which "burns" and weakens the planet's influence.</note>, it cannot hold that virtue. Therefore, it returns it to the one who gave it, because it is too weak to keep it due to that retrogradation or combustion. Now, if both planets are in <term>angles</term> <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a chart, which are considered the strongest, most active positions.</note> or in the houses following the angles <note>Known as succedent houses (the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th).</note>, that "return" will be good and useful and bring profit. And if the planet joining the other is in an angle, and the one it joins receives it—whether in an angle or a succedent house—the return will bring profit and utility.

<column-break/>

| | | |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **House 12:** Pisces | **House 11:** Aquarius, Jupiter (4) | **House 10:** Capricorn, Mars (4) |

For example: suppose **Jupiter** was in **Aries** at the 10th degree, but he was retrograde or combust. Suppose he was in an angle, specifically the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The 1st house, representing the person asking the question or the start of an event.</note> of that same sign, **Aries**. Then, suppose **Mars** was at the 4th degree of **Capricorn** in the angle of the 10th house, or in **Aquarius** at the 4th degree in a succedent house. **Mars** joined **Jupiter** by aspect and received him into his own house, committing his disposition and virtue to him. But **Jupiter**, being retrograde, could not hold that virtue, so he returned it. This return was good and useful because **Mars** was in an angle or a succedent house, meaning he was strong enough to keep the virtue returned by **Jupiter**. In the end, all the power remained with **Mars**, so that the matter in question would succeed through his virtue and power.

C However, if the planet that is joined (the "light" planet or the one to whom the virtue is returned) is <term>cadent</term> <note>Falling away from an angle, specifically the 3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th houses, which are considered weak and unstable.</note> from an angle, or if the "heavy" planet that returns the virtue is in a cadent house, the return will be useless, bad, and harmful. For example: suppose the Ascendant was the 14th degree of **Taurus**, **Jupiter** was at the 4th degree of **Aries** (falling from an angle), and **Mars** was at the 3rd degree of **Cancer** (likewise falling). **Mars** received **Jupiter** and committed his disposition to him; but because **Jupiter** was falling from an angle, he could not keep the virtue committed to him by **Mars**, so he returned it. But **Mars**, also falling from an angle, could not hold the virtue returned by **Jupiter** due to the weakness of his position. This resulted in harm rather than benefit. It is like a man who had a <term>burden</term> <note>original: "fassez", a bundle or heavy load.</note> on his shoulder that he could not carry. He gave it to another, but that person gave it back because he also could not carry it. That return was not useful but...

<column-break/>

...destructive to the matter in question. If a question was asked about a thing, it would be annulled because of the weakness of **Jupiter**, who could not hold the virtue committed by **Mars**, and because **Mars** was too weak to receive it back and bring the matter to a conclusion. This failure was caused by the weakness of both.

I have, however, found some who seemed different from others, holding an opinion that they did not believe the "return of virtue" or disposition was a real thing. Such was the tyrant **Ezzelino da Romano** <note>original: "yallinus de romano", a notorious 13th-century ruler often used as a historical example of a "bad" client or skeptic.</note>. There was a certain astrologer of his named **Salionus**, whom I believe agreed with him more out of fear than out of actual belief. I believe this because **Ezzelino** held one of his brothers in chains, and **Salionus** feared he might kill him. He used to say that the **Moon** and any light planet simply took on the nature of whatever planet they joined, and that every heavy planet gave its virtue to a lighter one whether it "received" it or not. He held many other erroneous opinions.

### Chapter Fifteen: Concerning the Refrenation of the
### Planets.

One planet is <term>refrained</term> <note>original: "refrenatur", literally "reined in" like a horse.</note> from a conjunction with another in this way: when one planet wants to join or apply itself to another and believes it will complete that conjunction, but before the conjunction is finished, it turns <term>retrograde</term>. Thus, the conjunction it sought—and which it seemed certain to complete—is not finished. It is like someone holding the reins of a horse that wants to run, stopping it from going where it intended. In such a case, the planet is said to be "refrained" from joining the other. For example: **Jupiter** was at the 16th degree of **Pisces**, and **Mars** was at the 7th degree of the same sign, wanting to join **Jupiter**. But when **Mars** reached the 14th degree of **Pisces**, he became retrograde. That retrogradation "reined him in" from reaching **Jupiter**, so he could not complete the conjunction. Everything signaled by that conjunction was annulled. If a person seeking a matter hoped to complete it while **Mars** was moving forward, they would still have doubt and a <term>gnawing of conscience</term> <note>original: "remorsum conscientie", a feeling of anxiety or intuition that the plan will fail.</note> that the thing might not be finished. There would be more hope than suspicion until **Mars** actually turned retrograde; then, they would despair of completing the planned matter. This is properly called "refrenation," which **Alchabitius** <note>An influential 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work was foundational for European medieval astrology.</note> calls *alidichee* <note>original: "alidichee", a technical term for planetary frustration.</note>.

### Chapter Sixteen: Concerning the Contrariety of Planets.

Sometimes <term>contrariety</term> happens to the planets in this way: when a "light" planet is at many degrees in a sign, and a "heavy" planet is at fewer degrees than the light one, and a third planet (even lighter than the first) is at even fewer degrees than the heavy one, moving toward the heavy one to join it. But before they can join, the one that was at the most degrees turns retrograde. In that backward motion, it joins the heavy planet before the lighter one can reach it. Afterward, leaving that heavy planet while still retrograde, it joins the other light planet. This destroys the conjunction of the first light planet that was moving forward, and it destroys the matter signaled by that conjunction even if...

Mars was in the same sign at 15 degrees, seeking a <term>conjunction</term> <note>A conjunction occurs when two planets reach the same degree of the zodiac, merging their influences.</note> with Saturn and wishing to be joined to him. Then, while still moving backward, he joined with Mars and did not permit Mars to join with Saturn. And this is called **contrariety**, since the opposite of what should have happened occurred.
