### Chapter seventeen: on the frustration of the conjunction of the planets.

**F**rustration of the conjunction of one planet by another happens in this way: namely, when one planet wishes to join another more ponderous than itself and seeks its conjunction in a particular sign, but cannot join it there because that ponderous planet moves into another sign. Furthermore, some other planet <term>aspects</term> <note>Forms a specific geometric angle (like a square or trine) that allows planets to "see" and influence each other.</note> that sign, so that the one who first wished to join the other instead meets the rays of the aspecting planet before it can join the ponderous one. Thus, it joins the aspecting planet through an aspect because the rays of the one watching were at the beginning of the sign. It was necessary for the one seeking the conjunction to first join with the observer rather than joining the intended planet by <term>body</term> <note>original: "per corpus"; a "body" conjunction is a physical meeting in the same degree, whereas an aspect is a meeting by light/angle.</note>, and so that conjunction is destroyed and frustrated. To make this easier for you to understand, I will give you an example of this matter, because the text is very difficult.

A question was asked about a marriage with Libra <term>ascending</term> <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the question, representing the person asking.</note>, and Venus

And the person signified by Mars showed good intentions toward the person signified by Venus regarding completing what they sought, making a good promise and intending to do what was asked. But while those words were still being spoken, some other factor appeared that the first person had not considered—perhaps something that seemed more useful to him, or something he did not know how to say, as often happens. And so he abandoned the matter that had been long considered and instead completed that which had newly and unexpectedly happened to him.

### Chapter 18: on the abscission of light of one planet from another.

**A**bscission of light <note>original: "abscisio luminis"; also known as "frustration" or "cutting off," where a third planet interferes with the relationship between two others.</note> from one planet by another happens in this way: for example, if one planet wishes to join another more ponderous one, and a different planet is in the sign following the one where the ponderous planet is located. Before the first can join the one it desires (which is more ponderous than itself), that third planet—which is the most ponderous of them all—becomes retrograde. By moving backward, it joins the planet that the first, lighter planet wished to join. This most ponderous planet now "cuts off" the light of the light planet from the other (which is less ponderous than itself) and does not permit that conjunction to be completed. Thus, the matter about which the question was asked is destroyed.

For example: Mars was in the 24th degree of Aries and the Sun was in the 15th degree of Sagittarius, seeking a <term>conjunction</term> <note>A conjunction occurs when two planets reach the same degree, but here it refers to a "conjunction by aspect," where the Sun "reaches out" to Mars from another sign.</note> with Mars and wishing to be joined to him by <term>aspect</term> <note>An aspect is a specific angular relationship between planets; here, the Sun and Mars are in different signs but "looking" at each other.</note>, and he cast his light upon the light of Mars. Meanwhile, Jupiter was in the 3rd degree of Taurus and, in the meantime, became <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "retrogradus"; appearing to move backward in the sky.</note>. Jupiter joined with Mars during that retrogradation before the Sun could complete his conjunction with Mars. Thus, Jupiter "cut off" the light of the Sun from Mars, and so that conjunction was destroyed and nullified. In such a case, if a question were asked about some matter that seemed likely to be completed through the conjunction of the Sun and Mars, it would be ruined because of the conjunction of Jupiter with Mars.

There is also another way the light of planets is cut off from one another: namely, when some planet seeks a conjunction with another that is more <term>ponderous</term> <note>original: "ponderosior"; in medieval astrology, "weight" refers to the speed of a planet's orbit. Slower planets are "heavier," faster ones are "lighter."</note> than itself, and that ponderous planet in turn seeks a conjunction with another even more ponderous than itself. Before that first "light" planet can join the second "ponderous" one, that ponderous one joins the third, even heavier planet. Now, that third one cuts off the light of the second from the first light planet; and so the cause which was signified by that conjunction is destroyed, just as was said above. For example: Mercury was in the 10th degree of Aries (or any other sign), seeking a conjunction with Venus, who was in the 20th degree of the same sign. Mars was in the 22nd degree of the same sign. Venus joined with Mars first, and so Mars cut off the light of Venus from Mercury, with whom Mercury would have joined.

### Chapter Nineteen: In which places the
### planets become strong, and in which they are weak, and in which
### they become fortunate or unfortunate.

There are certain places in which planets are comforted and become strong, and some in which they become weak; some in which they become good and <term>fortunes</term> <note>original: "fortune"; beneficial planets like Venus and Jupiter that bring good luck.</note>, and some in which they become evil and <term>infortunes</term> <note>original: "infortune"; challenging planets like Saturn and Mars.</note>. The places in which they become strong and fortunate are these: namely, when they are in aspects with the good planets and fortunes—in a <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, considered very harmonious.</note> or <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect of 60 degrees, considered helpful.</note> or at least a <term>square</term> <note>An aspect of 90 degrees, usually difficult but here considered strengthening if other conditions are met.</note>—and especially if the aspect includes <term>reception</term> <note>A cooperative state where one planet is in a sign or "house" ruled by the other.</note>, for then they are made into fortunes even if they were naturally "evil" planets. Also, when they are in places where the evil planets are <term>cadent</term> <note>original: "cadentes"; falling away from the powerful corners of the chart, thus weakening their influence.</note> from them, so that they do not join with them, nor the others with them. Also, when they are separated from the infortunes and joined to the fortunes, or are positioned between two fortunes, or are between the rays of two fortunate planets. 

For example: Jupiter was in the 10th degree of Aries, Venus was in the 20th degree of Sagittarius, and the Moon was in the 15th degree of Leo. Now, the Moon was separated from Jupiter by a trine aspect (which occurs between Aries and Leo) and was joining Venus similarly by a trine aspect (which occurs between Leo and Sagittarius). 

Likewise, they are strong when in the houses in which they <term>rejoice</term> <note>original: "gaudent"; a planet "rejoices" in a specific house where its nature is most naturally expressed.</note>: namely, Saturn in the twelfth (as was said elsewhere), Jupiter in the eleventh, Mars in the sixth, the Sun in the ninth, Venus in the fifth, Mercury in the first, and the Moon in the third. Likewise, they are strong in the signs in which they rejoice upon entering: namely, Saturn in Aquarius, Jupiter in Sagittarius, Mars in Scorpio, Venus in Taurus, and Mercury in Virgo. Also, when they are in the <term>angles</term> <note>The four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th.</note> or <term>succedents</term> <note>Houses that "follow" the angles: the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th.</note>

<column-break/>

of the angles. And when they are united with the Sun as was said elsewhere: for a planet is not "united" unless it is next to the Sun, within less than 16 minutes before or behind, to the right or to the left; for a planet is not <term>in the heart of the Sun</term> <note>original: "in corde solis"; also known as "Cazimi," this is considered a position of immense strength where the planet is shielded by the Sun's power.</note> unless it is as I have said. Even if it were in the same minute as the Sun in terms of longitude, but far from it by more than 16 minutes in latitude, it would nonetheless be <term>combust</term> <note>original: "combustus"; literally "burnt up" by the Sun's heat, making the planet weak and hidden.</note> and could not be called strong for that reason. 

Planets are also strong when in a trine or sextile aspect to the Sun, or a trine or sextile to the Moon, provided she is then fortunate. Also when they are fast in their course, increasing in light and in number. And when they are in their <term>dignities</term> <note>Essential strengths based on a planet's position in the zodiac.</note>: in their houses, <term>exaltations</term>, <term>terms</term>, <term>triplicities</term>, or <term>faces</term>. Or when they are in their "similitudes" mentioned above: that is, a masculine planet in a masculine sign, a feminine planet in a feminine sign; a diurnal planet by day above the earth, and by night below the earth, and vice versa. Or when they are "received" or are in <term>bright degrees</term>. 

They are also strong when they are ascending toward the north and are ascending in the circles of their <term>apogees</term> <note>original: "augium"; the highest or furthest point in a planet's orbit.</note>. Also when they are <term>direct</term> <note>Moving forward normally through the zodiac.</note> or in their "second station" (which is when any of them is about to turn direct). And when they are emerging from under the Sun's rays; or when Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are <term>oriental</term> <note>Rising in the east before the Sun.</note> from the Sun and not very far removed from him, so that they do not go toward weakness. 

Masculine planets are strong in masculine quadrants, which are from the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The 1st house.</note> to the tenth house, and from the seventh to the fourth. Feminine planets are strong in feminine quadrants, which are from the tenth to the seventh, and from the fourth to the ascendant. The Sun similarly rejoices in masculine quadrants, except when he is in Libra, for that is his <term>fall</term> <note>original: "casus"; the sign where a planet's influence is most diminished.</note>. Venus, Mercury, and the Moon should be <term>occidental</term> <note>Setting in the west after the Sun.</note> from the Sun, so that they set in the evening after him. The Moon should be in feminine quadrants, and should be below the earth by day and above the earth by night. She should be in a feminine sign and a feminine place, or be in the exaltation of the Sun. These are the places in which planets become strong and fortunate, provided they are otherwise free from impediments.

### Chapter Twenty: Why and in which places planets become weak.

**H**aving spoken of strengths and fortunes, we must now speak of debilities and misfortunes. This occurs in many ways: whether through a physical conjunction with <term>malefics</term> <note>The "evil-doers," usually referring to Saturn and Mars, which were thought to bring hardship or restriction.</note> or being in an <term>aspect</term> <note>A specific angular relationship, like a square or opposition.</note> with them without <term>reception</term> <note>A state where one planet is in a sign ruled by the other, creating a hospitable "host-guest" relationship. Without this, the planet has no support.</note>; or by being so close to malefics or their rays that they are between them, or between a malefic planet and its rays, within a distance less than the <term>term</term> <note>Original: "terminus." Each zodiac sign was divided into five unequal sections called "terms," each ruled by a different planet.</note> of that planet. For example, if Jupiter were in Aries and Saturn were near him (or his rays) by less than six degrees—which is the term of Jupiter in Aries; or if Venus were there and Saturn were near her (or his rays) by less than eight degrees—which is the second term of Venus in Aries; or if Mercury were there and there were less than seven degrees between him and Saturn (or his rays)—which is the third term of Mercury in Aries. You should understand this in the same way for any planet and any term of any planet in any sign.

Planets are also weakened if they are in the terms of malefics, or if they are in the houses of malefics without being "received," or if malefics are "elevated" over them—that is, if the malefics are to the north of them in the tenth or eleventh places from them (specifically in a square or a trine aspect from behind). This is even worse if the malefics do not "receive" them; however, if they do receive them, the reception lessens their malice.

Weakness also occurs if they are under the Sun's rays or in <term>opposition</term> to it (which are called "combust" or burnt degrees), or in a square aspect without reception, or if they are with the <term>Head or Tail of the Dragon</term> <note>The North and South Nodes of the Moon, where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path. They were associated with eclipses and dramatic shifts in fortune.</note>. Or if they are joined to the <term>censahar</term> <note>A medieval term derived from Persian/Arabic referring to the lunar nodes or the "dragon" that causes eclipses.</note> so that they are between 12 degrees before or less, or 10 degrees after or less, from the Head, the Tail, or their *censahar*. Among the planets, the Sun and Moon are most hindered by their *censahar* when they are 12 degrees or less from the Head or Tail, for there they suffer an eclipse, which is a great detriment to them. Planets are also weakened if they are "obsessed" (besieged) by malefics or their rays.

Among the other misfortunes of planets is when a planet is <term>retrograde</term> <note>Appearing to move backward through the zodiac.</note>; or "falling" from the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The rising sign. A planet that cannot "see" the ascendant by a traditional aspect is considered weak and unable to act.</note> so that it does not aspect it; or if it is slow in its course; or in its first "station" (when it is about to become retrograde); or if it is in "dark degrees"; or if a masculine planet is in feminine degrees or a feminine sign; or if it is under the earth by day and above the earth by night; or if a feminine planet is in masculine degrees or a masculine sign; or if it is above the earth by day or under the earth by night.

Further weaknesses include: being in the signs opposite their own houses or <term>exaltations</term> <note>Signs where a planet is thought to have its greatest dignity or "honor." Being opposite these places is like being in exile.</note>; being "meridian" (in the south) or descending toward the south; falling from the <term>angles</term> <note>The four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th.</note> or their <term>succedents</term> <note>The houses that follow the angles: the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th.</note>; or being in houses that "fall" away from the ascendant. They are also weakened in the <term>Via Combusta</term> <note>The "Burnt Path," traditionally the section of the zodiac from 15 degrees Libra to 15 degrees Scorpio, considered a volatile and unlucky area.</note>, which is from the middle of Libra to the middle of Scorpio; or if joined to another planet that is retrograde, combust, or otherwise hindered; or if they are not received; or if the three higher planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars) are "occidental" (set in the west) from the Sun in feminine parts; or if the three lower planets (Venus, Mercury, the Moon) are "oriental" (rising in the east) from the Sun in masculine parts.

And if the Sun is in feminine signs or feminine parts—unless it is in the ninth house, which is the house of its "joy," because it signifies religion, as <note>original: "pho."</note> Porphyry testifies. Or if the Moon is "combust"; or in the degrees of its "fall"; or joined to planets that are in their fall; or in opposition to the Sun. Or if she is joined to malefics, or in opposition or square aspect to them without reception, or besieged by two malefics or their rays. Or if she is at the Head or Tail of the Dragon as was said; or if she is in Gemini with respect to Mercury; or in the terms of malefics; or falling from the angles; or joined to a planet falling from them; or in the "Burnt Path"; or slow in her course; or at the end of a lunar month

<column-break/>

without being received; or in smoky, dark, putrid, or <unclear>acemena</unclear> <note>Likely referring to "empty" or "featureless" degrees where the planet has no power.</note> degrees.

Because of this, the sages have said that when the Moon is hindered in this way, it can hardly produce anything from the aforementioned impediments; thus, it is not good to begin any work from which one hopes for a good result, nor any journey or pilgrimage; nor is it praised in <term>nativities</term> <note>Birth charts.</note>. If someone is born when the Moon is hindered by any of these impediments—which rarely happens—even if the birth itself is otherwise good, it diminishes the good signified by the birth according to the quantity or quality of the impediment. If the birth was already bad, it increases the evil for the newborn. The same applies to journeys or pilgrimages: if the journey was meant to be good, it diminishes the goodness; if it was bad, it increases the malice according to the nature of the impediment.

### Chapter Twenty-One: On the obsession of planets and signs.

**S**ometimes a planet is "obsessed" (besieged), and this happens in two ways. One is called "veneration," and this obsession is good. This is when a planet is between two "fortunes" (benefics) or their rays, having one fortune (or its rays) before it and one fortune (or its rays) after it, such that it separates from one and joins the other.

In a similar way, a planet is said to be "obsessed" in a bad way and for a bad purpose: when a planet is between two malefics or their rays, having one malefic before it and another malefic after it.

Just as a planet is said to be obsessed, so too can a sign be called obsessed, as <note>original: "Alchabitius"</note> Al-Qabisi says. He said that if the Sun or another fortune aspects a planet or sign that is "obsessed" from a trine or sextile aspect—provided they fall within ten degrees of the planet or sign—it dissolves that malice or obsession. A sign is called "obsessed" (in a good way) if one of the fortunes or its rays is before it and another fortune or its rays is after it. A sign is called "obsessed" (in a bad way) if one malefic or its rays is before it and another malefic is after it.

### Chapter Twenty-Two: How one planet loves another, and how it is loved by another, and how they hate each other in turn.

**T**he ancient sages said that some planets love each other, and some of them hate each other. For they said that Jupiter loves all planets and is naturally a friend to all, and they all love him and are all his friends, except for Mars. Venus loves all planets and all love her, except for Saturn. Saturn loves Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon, and they love him; but he hates Mars and Venus, and they hate him—and Venus hates him even more than Mars does. Mercury, when he is joined to those who love Saturn, loves him; when he is joined to those who hate Saturn, he hates him.

Mars loves only Venus, and she loves him; he hates the others, and they hate him—but Jupiter and the Sun hate him more than the others. The Sun loves Jupiter and Venus with a perfect love, and they love him; he hates Mars, Mercury, and the Moon, and they hate him. Mercury loves Jupiter and Venus, and they love him; he hates Mars, the Sun, the Moon, and Saturn, as I said. The Moon loves Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus, and they love her; she hates Mars, the Sun, and Mercury. The Head of the Dragon loves Jupiter and Venus, and they love it; it does not care about the others. Its Tail loves Saturn and Mars, and they love it; it hates Jupiter, the Sun, Venus, and the Moon, and they hate it. And again they say...

¶ Just as enmity sometimes falls between the planets, so 
too does friendship fall between them; namely, when a 
planet agrees with another planet in nature, quality,

all these friendships is the agreement in nature.

Venus and the Moon agree in coldness and moisture; and 
Venus is the lady of the Moon's exaltation; and thus do 
Jupiter and Venus agree in benevolence and the bestowing of good 
and fortune and timing.

<meta>This page continues the astrological discourse from the previous page, transitioning from the concept of planetary "reception" and enmity into a systematic classification of the seven planets based on their celestial spheres (circles) and their influence over the stages of human endeavors.</meta>

**Divisions**: for divisions are named and considered here according to the successive order of the circles of the seven planets. In this way, the first division is considered according to the motion of the three **superior planets** <note>In the medieval geocentric model, these are the planets furthest from the Earth: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note>, which are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, as you will find sufficiently determined below in the treatise on <term>nativities</term> <note>original: "natiuitatibus"; a birth chart or horoscope.</note>. The second division is considered according to the planet located in the middle of the others, which is the **Sun**. The third, indeed, is considered according to the motion of the three **inferior planets** <note>The planets between the Earth and the Sun: Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note>, which are Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.

¶ The first division of the planets—namely the superior ones—is threefold and triform, primarily regarding individual things here below; and this is according to the three diversities of motion: namely the first, second, and third. For the first motion moves *above* the center. The second moves *from* the center. The third, however, does not move above the first, nor from the first, nor above the center, nor from the center, but *towards* the center.

¶ Hence, the first division of the superior planets considers and refers to the first motion, which presides over the middle motion because those planets approach the first motion and are distant from the third motion, which is toward the middle motion. And one considers those divisions of motions over particular individuals whose durability is expected, such as the building of houses and the like, which have a beginning, and whose middle does not hurry, and whose end is far removed from its beginning; and these are attributed to **Saturn**, who has an affinity above the others with the first motion.

And the middle of these things is attributed to **Jupiter**, because just as Jupiter is the middle among the other superior planets and located in their midst, and his motion is moderate among those motions, therefore the middle of those things is attributed to him, and also their completions are attributed to him and considered according to him. And because he is closer to Mars (to whom the end of things is attributed) than Saturn is, and closer to Saturn (to whom the beginning is attributed) than Mars is, therefore the middle and the completions of things are attributed to him and considered according to him.

¶ The end, however, is attributed to **Mars**, because he is placed at the end of the first division, and because the end brings about the destruction of things; and for this reason, battles, wars, and contentions are attributed to him, since those things contribute more to consumption, diminution, and destruction than others.

¶ For the *beginning* indicates that things exist; the *middle* indicates their perfection; and the *end* indicates their destruction. And because a multitude of different motions are multiplied, and diversities among men and the discord of their wills arise, from there spring wars and contentions which contribute to the destruction of things and to their ends. And whatever may be said by certain people who are ignorant of their Creator—who disposed all things in an orderly fashion and made nothing without a cause—this was the reason why these three things were given to the three superior planets as primary principles in the first significance, preceding those which follow from the second significance, which are signified by the other attributed planets.

And thus, as the **Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> testifies, the first motion is moved from the center, and the third motion is moved toward the center. And the second, middle motion is naturally attributed to the **Sun**, which is the greater light <note>original: "luminare maius"</note>, and to its effects; and that motion is "from the center" by relation because he is akin to that motion; and he is placed circularly in the order of the circles in the middle of the others, and whatever is referred to him is between the first motion and the third motion. And because his motion is less slow than the superior planets and less swift than the inferior ones, for this reason he is called the significator of kings and the wealthy, or of magnates and others who excel and wish to dominate; and because he participates with the first division and

<column-break/>

the significance of his meaning is weighed more strongly in the second division than any other, and he succeeds Mars in the order of the circles.

¶ The third motion, however, is attributed to the three inferior planets toward the middle motion on account of their distance from the first motion, which is above the middle motion; and their effects are upon "hurried" things <note>original: "rebus festiuis"; things that happen quickly or pertain to the moment.</note> and those whose length is not expected; and because of their swift motion, they have an affinity with fast things, and although in a certain way they savor of the first motion, they nevertheless have an affinity with the third motion. And their natural motions are considered according to the three divisions of the motions of the three superior planets.

For the significance of marriage and of the garments that arrange bodies and similar things is given to **Venus**, because of her correlation to Saturn. For just as Saturn is the first and highest of the three superior planets and governs the principles of things of great and long durability, so also Venus is the first of the three inferior planets, and according to her are considered the beginnings of things whose great durability or length is not expected; and she succeeds the Sun in the order of the circles.

¶ To **Mercury**, however, is given the significance over things signifying the perfection of things that do not endure for a long time, such as numbers, writings, measurements, sculptures, and the like; although some of these may last a long time, they are only made for the memory of things so that the forgetfulness of men may be corrected. And since his significance is akin to the significance of Jupiter and correlates to it, which signifies the perfection of long-lasting things. For just as Jupiter is the middle among the superior planets, so also Mercury is the middle among the inferior planets, and he succeeds Venus in the order of the circles.

¶ To the **Moon**, indeed, is given the significance over mobile things that change quickly, and over pilgrimages <note>original: "peregrinationes"; can also refer to foreign travel or wandering in general.</note>, and over all things undergoing rapid change and whose end hurries; and her significations are correlated to the significations of Mars. For just as Mars is the third and last of the three superior planets and signifies the end of long-enduring things, so the Moon is the third and last of the three inferior planets; and she is akin to the third division signified by Mars, and signifies the end of things reaching their end quickly; and thus she succeeds Mercury in the order of the circles, as will be said more broadly below in the treatise on nativities.

Nor should you believe these significations to be attributed to these three planets except by reason of the need of those whom natural necessity drives toward them—such as the rites of men, oppositions, conditions, laws, and those living according to their fables <note>original: "appologos"; likely referring to stories, moral tales, or traditional accounts.</note>—all of which are perfected by number and writing and apparently reach their due action, as much in those things pertaining to wars, contentions, and journeys, as in other mutations which do not receive perfection except through motion. And these aforementioned significations were attributed to the said three inferior planets because they are like secondary things by relation to the motion or to the first being; and because of that which they consequently follow from there.

And because from their significance and that of the others, there is a foreknowledge of the effects of those things which are to come universally according to their course, through which one arrives at the particular knowledge of them—which aforementioned conjunctions we can weigh if we wish to find them correctly, namely of Saturn with Jupiter and Mars in the aforesaid places. However, concerning these motions and their significances, it will be spoken more broadly in the treatise on nativities and more precisely <note>original: "ad vnguem"; literally "to the fingernail," meaning with great precision.</note>.

### Chapter 3: On the conjunction of Saturn and Mars.

The third conjunction is that of Saturn and Mars, which occurs at the beginning of <term>Cancer</term> <note>The zodiac sign Cancer is traditionally considered a "water" sign and the "home" of the Moon.</note>, either in its first degree or at least in its first <term>term</term> <note>A "term" is a specific sub-division of a zodiac sign ruled by a particular planet.</note>; this happens once every 30 years. ¶ But you might ask why the conjunction of Saturn and Mars is only considered at the start of Cancer, when they also join at the start of other signs and other <term>triplicities</term> <note>original: "triplicitatum"; a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> just as they do in Cancer. To this, it can be answered that their conjunction was more heavily considered at the start of Cancer than elsewhere because it is the most destructive of all the conjunctions they make. Although all their meetings are "evil," the one they make at the beginning of Capricorn is less malicious because they "receive" one another, which diminishes their malice. <term>Capricorn</term> is the "dignity" of both—being the <term>house</term> of Saturn and the <term>exaltation</term> of Mars. <note>In astrology, a "house" is where a planet is most "at home," and an "exaltation" is where its power is amplified in a positive way.</note> However, Cancer is the <term>detriment</term> of both Saturn and Mars, which is their greatest <term>impediment</term>. And when "malefic" planets are impeded, they become even worse, increasing their malice and their obstruction. In other signs, they do not have such a manifest detriment. And although they may wound or offend in other signs, they do not cause as much harm as in that one. For it is then that the greatest changes in the world occur, and the greatest accidents, which do not happen in other conjunctions they make elsewhere. Indeed, they change kingdoms, or terrible wars arise from which follow suffocating killings, wicked captures, the destruction of kingdoms, conflagrations of fire, and much shedding of blood, famine, death, infertility, and a multitude of pestilences.

If the planets are **oriental** <note>original: "orientales"; rising in the east before the Sun.</note>, their significance will happen quickly, depending on how close or far they are from the Sun. If they are **occidental** <note>original: "occidentales"; setting in the west after the Sun.</note>, their effects will be prolonged and delayed. You should also consider the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the conjunction.</note> of their conjunction down to the minute. Look at the number of degrees of longitude between them and the Sun, from which you will determine the timing by assigning 30 degrees to each sign. If the ascendant is a **fixed sign** and the planets are occidental, it signifies the number of *years* until the event occurs based on the distance between them and the Sun. If they are oriental, put *months* in the place of years. If it is a **common sign** and they are occidental, put *months* in place of years; if they are oriental, put *weeks* in place of months. If it is a **movable sign**, put *weeks* in place of years if they are occidental; if they are oriental, put *days* in place of weeks. When you give one sign for a year, give a month for 2 degrees and 30 minutes; a week for 20 minutes and 30 seconds; and a day for 2 minutes and 21 seconds. These times will bring about their significance if you have correctly calculated the ascendant of the conjunction.

¶ You must also consider whether the <term>angle</term> of the first house is "straight" or "remote." For if it is straight—meaning it is exactly one sign and makes only one house—these things will happen in the specific and equal times I told you. If it is remote, it happens differently. If that angle contains fewer than 30 degrees, the effect will be delayed; this happens if one sign spans across two houses, as occurs frequently. But if it contains more than 30 degrees—meaning it includes an entire sign that is not named, or otherwise contains more than 30 degrees—the effect will be hastened and accelerated. For example, if the 1st degree of Leo is the first house and the 27th degree of the same sign is the second house, then this sign creates two houses and delays the effect by a tenth part, just as a tenth part of it falls into another house. If more of it fell into the other, it would delay it more. If a ninth part fell into another house, it would delay the effect by a ninth part of the time; if an eighth part fell, it would delay it by an

<column-break/>

eighth part; and so on for the other parts of the sign. And if a sign were "intercepted"—for example, if the 28th degree of Pisces was the first house and the 3rd degree of Taurus was the second house—then all of Aries would be included in the first house. This would hasten the effect according to the number of degrees the first house takes beyond 30. In this case, there are 2 degrees of Pisces and 3 of Taurus; thus the effect would be hastened by a sixth part of its time, just as a sixth part of a sign falls into that house more than it should according to the "straightness" of the angles. Understand this for every proportion of the sign. Similarly, if there are so few degrees between them and the Sun that they cannot form a whole sign (meaning less than 30), and the ascendant is a sign that rises in less than two equal hours, it signifies *days*. If there are enough degrees to make a whole sign (30), and the ascendant is a sign that rises in exactly two hours, it signifies *months*. And if the ascendant sign rises in two hours, it signifies *years*, maintaining the proportion of degrees and minutes as I have said.

<margin>Effects according to the nature of the signs.</margin>

¶ It is also to be known that the effects of their conjunctions will mostly fall upon those things signified by the sign that was ascending at the hour of their mid-conjunction, or by the sign in which their conjunction occurred. If they are in the **Eastern** part when their conjunction is completed—meaning they meet in the same minute or are joined to oriental planets—those effects will happen in the East. If they are in the **South** and joined to southern planets, they will happen in the South. If they are joined to **Western** planets or are themselves occidental, they will happen in the West. And if they are in none of those parts but are **Northern** or joined to northern planets, they will happen in the North. 

¶ **Cancer**, as has been said, is the detriment of Saturn and Mars because it is opposite **Capricorn**, which is the house of Saturn and the exaltation of Mars. Every seventh sign from the house or exaltation of any planet is said to be that planet's <term>detriment</term>. ¶ **Aries** is the opposite of **Libra**, which is the exaltation of Saturn, but it is not the opposite of any dignity of Mars; rather, it is his own house. ¶ **Taurus** is the opposite of **Scorpio**, which is the house of Mars, but it is not the opposite of the house or exaltation of Saturn. ¶ Therefore, their conjunctions in the beginnings of other signs or other triplicities are lesser than their conjunction in the beginning of Cancer and are less malicious. ¶ **Gemini**, indeed, is not the opposite of the house or exaltation of either of them.

### Chapter 4: On the fourth conjunction, of Saturn and Jupiter.

The fourth conjunction is that of Saturn and Jupiter, which occurs once every 20 years, such that they make 12 conjunctions in each triplicity. That this is true—that they make 12 conjunctions in each triplicity—is clear if you look closely at the truth of it. ¶ For 12 multiplied by 20 (or 20 by 12, which is the same) makes 240. Thus, they join 12 times in 240 years, making one conjunction every 20 years. In this way, they pass through all the triplicities before they return to the same point where they made the first conjunction, totaling 48 conjunctions. Therefore, they make 12 conjunctions in 240 years; and 240 multiplied by 4 makes 960, and then their conjunction returns to...

# Chapter 5: On the fifth conjunction, of the Sun with the other planets.

The fifth conjunction is that which occurs when the Sun meets the planets at its entry into the first minute of Aries, or when the other planets meet each other at that time. This has its own meanings: sometimes small, sometimes great; sometimes good, sometimes bad; sometimes middling, as will be fully explained in the treatise on <term>revolutions</term><note>A "revolution" refers to a yearly horoscope cast for the moment the Sun enters Aries, used to predict world events.</note>. It would be long, laborious, and neither philosophical nor orderly to touch upon it all here. And you should similarly consider the Sun's entry into Aries, its <term>ascendant</term><note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> at 그 hour, and its exact minute in every year in which one of the aforementioned conjunctions of Saturn with the other planets is due to occur; for in such a year, the joining of the Sun with the planets shows greater significance than in others.

# Chapter 6: On the sixth joining.

The sixth joining is that of the Sun and Moon at the same minute, which happens once at the start of every lunar month <note>The New Moon</note>, and their opposition, which happens in the middle of every lunar month <note>The Full Moon</note>. These likewise have their various meanings, as will be discussed in the treatise on <term>plants</term><note>original: "plantis"; this likely refers to a specialized text on the astrological timing of agriculture, or is a scribal error for "planetes" (planets).</note> and also in the book of revolutions, for I shall tell you there what seems useful.

# Chapter 7: On the "combust" and "uncombust" hours after the conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, which some call *albuiz* or *abtuth*.

Certain ancient wise men—from whom I do not wish to deviate—have said that after the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, starting from the very minute of their contact, twelve hours are born which are called <term>combust</term><note>original: "combuste," meaning "burnt." In astrology, being "combust" usually means a planet is too close to the Sun, weakening its power or making it dangerous.</note>. After those twelve combust hours, there are 72 hours called "uncombust"; and after those 72 uncombust hours, there are 12 more combust hours; and so it continues until the degree and minute of the next following conjunction. These wise men said that they divided those 12 combust hours into three equal parts, giving four of those hours to each part. 

And they said that for anyone who begins to wage war or goes out to battle in the **first four hours**, he should fear the death of his own body. 

And he who begins to wage war or goes to battle in the **second four hours**, he should fear capture, wounding, or some blow, though without the loss of his life. 

And he who begins to wage war or goes to battle in the **last four hours**, he should fear the loss of his property and of those who were with him, and he may also lose the persons of his helpers. 

Furthermore, he who begins to plow or goes out to plowing in the **first four hours**, he should fear the loss of the fruits expected from that plowing. 

And he who begins to plow or goes out to plowing in the **second four hours**, he should fear a great loss in all things he possesses, and even in his body, though without loss of life. 

And he who begins to plow or goes out to plowing in the **last four hours**, he should fear the lessening of his seeds.

### Regarding the twelve-parts of the Moon.

In the same way, there is another division of these hours called the "12 hours of the Sun and Moon," or the "12 of the Moon." This is a matter to be strictly observed. Specifically, you must know the hours and minutes of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, take 12 hours after the conjunction, and divide them into three equal parts—giving four hours to each part. You must give the first division to the Sun, who is the first

<column-break/>

lord of the first triplicity, namely the **Fire** triplicity. You must give the second part to the second lord of the same triplicity, which is Jupiter. And the third you must give to the third lord of that triplicity, which is Saturn. You must judge the matter to belong to those lords as I shall explain to you in what follows. 

Next, you must give the next 12 hours (following those you gave to the lords of the first triplicity) and judge the matter according to the lords of the second triplicity, namely **Earth**. Give the first 4 hours to Venus, who is the first lord of the second triplicity of Earth. Give the second 4 hours to the Moon, who is the second lord of the same triplicity. Give the final 4 hours to Mars, who is the third lord of that triplicity. 

Then you must give 12 hours to the lords of the **Air** triplicity (the third) after those 12 you gave to the lords of the second triplicity. Give the first 4 hours to Saturn, who is the first lord of the third triplicity. Give the second 4 hours to Mercury, who is the second lord of the Air triplicity. Give the final 4 hours to Jupiter, who is the last lord of the same triplicity. 

Then you must give another 12 hours to the lords of the fourth triplicity, namely **Water**. Give the first 4 hours to Venus, who is the first lord of the fourth triplicity. Give the second 4 hours to Mars, who is the second lord of the same triplicity. Give the final 4 hours to the Moon, who is the last lord of the fourth triplicity of Water. 

And you must do this with every single triplicity until the arrangement returns to the Sun and reaches the degree and minute of the next following joining. You shall consider all these hours according to <term>inequality</term><note>Unequal hours (also called planetary hours) vary in length depending on the season, as they divide the day and night into 12 equal segments regardless of the actual time of sunset.</note> and not according to equality. And because of this, Ptolemy said: *"Observe the twelve-parts of the moon,"*<note>original: "serua duodena lune"</note> for this is the "twelve of the moon" that he meant. 

For whenever the Moon is in any of those twelve-parts, its state and disposition will be according to the nature of that planet to which that third part of the twelve was assigned. Therefore, one must avoid the twelve-part of the Moon based on the disposition of that planet to which those 4 hours are attributed; that planet should not be placed on the side of the person for whom you are choosing a time, if you can ever avoid it. Unless it happens by someone's misfortune that the start of his war or his journey to war falls into one of those prohibited combust hours; for then he should fear the danger mentioned above. These four hours from the "twelve of the moon" will be even more severe if the planet is poorly positioned at that time; in that case, there would be no remedy, even with a good <term>election</term><note>The practice of choosing the most astrologically favorable moment to begin an undertaking.</note> for war; only God could turn it away. Nevertheless, the aforementioned 12 combust hours are to be avoided more strictly, since they take precedence over these. 

In this way, 12 degrees of these twelve-parts reach each planet, dividing them equally among the planets; thus those degrees total 84 among all of them, because 12 multiplied by 7 makes 84. Then the eighth "twelve-part" returns to the Sun, and the divisions of the twelve-parts are made again as was said before until the second joining is reached. 

Finally, the wise men said that after the aforementioned 12 combust hours—in which it is not good or useful to do or begin any of the things mentioned—there are 72 "uncombust" hours in which one can begin or do what one wishes, unless something else hinders it; and so on until the second conjunction. Therefore, you must take care in your judgments, and especially in those things I mentioned to you, to see that the beginning of any matter you or anyone else intends to do or start does not fall into any of those prohibited hours, whether it be a journey or anything else, and avoid it as much as you possibly can.

Having dealt with conjunctions and with the hours that are <term>combust</term><note>A planet is "combust" when it is so close to the Sun (usually within 8.5 degrees) that its power is thought to be weakened or "burnt up."</note> and non-combust, although it may not seem to follow the general order established here, I will mention how to find the degree of the <term>ascendant</term><note>The sign and degree rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of an event; the most critical point in a horoscope.</note> for someone whose birth time is not known with total certainty. This is so that judgments can be made that seem to show accuracy, even if they are not perfectly certain in themselves. This often happens because a mother, a nurse, or other midwives do not know the exact hour of a child’s birth, nor do those present at an event know the exact time; instead, they have a general idea of the truth that is not far off—perhaps by an hour or half an hour or so. 

Thus they might say, "this boy was born around the third, sixth, or ninth hour," or perhaps they say "around midnight," "around dawn," or "around the first sleep," as laypeople are accustomed to saying. Or, regarding another matter, they might say a certain thing happened around such an hour—namely, when banners were given, or a building's foundation was laid, or some other arrangement. In such cases, certainty cannot be given to you for that hour through those initial reports, but the approximate hour is provided to you. 

In order for you to find the certain hour of that birth or event, you must <term>equate</term><note>To "equate" or "rectify" means to mathematically adjust the planetary positions to find the true moment of an event.</note> the planets for that hour as closely as you can, so that you do not deviate from the hour the midwives or mother or someone else reported by more than one equal hour. See what sign was rising then, and consider whether that birth (or the beginning of whatever matter it was) was <term>conjunctional</term> or <term>preventional</term><note>A "conjunctional" birth occurs after a New Moon; a "preventional" birth occurs after a Full Moon.</note>. Look at the degree in which that conjunction or prevention was made, and consider which of the planets is stronger and more powerful by its multitude of <term>dignities</term><note>Dignities are various positions in the zodiac where a planet gains strength, such as its Home or Exaltation.</note> or strengths in that degree. Look at how many degrees that planet has traveled through the sign in which it is located, and you shall make the degree of the ascendant match the degree of the sign where that planet is—namely, the planet that was the <term>Almuten</term><note>The "Almuten" is the planet that holds the most combined dignity and influence at a specific point in the zodiac.</note> in the degree of the previous conjunction or prevention.

**For example:** It seemed to you, according to the calculation you made for the uncertain hour you had from the first reports, that the ascendant would be the 4th degree of Aries by your estimation (as I said), based on what you could grasp about the birth or the matter that was not quite certain. Let us say the conjunction or prevention had been in the 10th degree of Aries, and the strongest planet in that degree—the Almuten—is the Sun (due to its many dignities, as has been said elsewhere). Therefore, look at the Sun at that hour and see in what degree of whatever sign it is; let us suppose it is in the 17th degree of Aquarius. You must now change the ascendant that you first found by estimation and make the ascendant of Aries (which first seemed to be at the 4th degree) become the 17th degree. Thus you will verify the ascendant you are seeking. And if you had found by your estimation that the ascendant was at a higher degree than the Almuten planet is in its sign, reduce it to the quantity of its degrees; for instance, if it were the 24th degree or more or less, reduce it to 17, just as the Sun is in its sign. Understand this regarding any planet, and according to that ascendant, arrange the other <term>houses</term><note>The twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope, each representing a different area of life.</note>. But because I shall, God willing, write a special treatise for you on nativities in which I will set forth all these things and explain them to a hair's breadth, I will not stay here longer now, so that a more direct order may be preserved.

To judge concerning the future, as is said elsewhere, is very difficult, nor can the future be judged with absolute certainty to a hair's breadth; it can, however, be judged so close to the truth that the judgments are sufficiently similar and approach the truth, not differing much from it except imperceptibly. And although it is very difficult to judge the future, the labor is not to be abandoned, as we strive to know whatever can ever be reached of judgment by the human mind. 

And because lower things are ruled by higher things—as everyone unanimously confesses and as is true, as is said elsewhere—from the disposition of the higher bodies, something can be known through the measurements of their movements, which have been found by experts to a hair's breadth and clearly proven. We can judge concerning the future and what may happen from those movements and predict things to come. Hence, this art has its <note>original: "precepta"</note> principles; for the principles of astronomy are its science, and its end is judgments, as is touched upon elsewhere. This stands against those who strive to reproach astronomy, who seem to want to say it is nothing; for it would not be an art if it did not have its own principles. Indeed, it is an art, as is said elsewhere, which no one denies; therefore it has an end, and its end is judgment. The astrologer considers judgments through himself, and judgments arise from the <term>accidents</term><note>Temporary conditions or qualities, as opposed to essential nature.</note> that are impressed upon lower things from the movements of the higher bodies and their qualities because of their effects upon them.

-> The first consideration is in those things which move a <-
-> person to make a question: and there are three movements. <-

The first is the movement of the soul, when someone is moved by their own intention to make a question. The second is the movement of the superior bodies—namely, that what is asked is impressed by the stars themselves upon the matter sought, regarding what the future of it shall be. The third is the movement of free will, which can be the act of seeking itself; for although the soul may be moved to seek, it is not sufficient unless the superior bodies lead to the making of the question, nor is the movement of the stars sufficient unless it arrives at the act of seeking through the movement of free will.

-> The second consideration is in the manner which <-
-> anyone who wants to ask anything should observe. <-

And it is that when he wishes to interrogate the astrologer about present, past, or future things, he must observe this manner of seeking: namely, that he ought to pray to the Lord God, from whom every good thing takes its beginning, and with all devotion and a contrite spirit, beseech Him that He grant him to arrive at the knowledge of the truth of those things about which he intends to ask. Then he should go to the astrologer with this intention of truth regarding what he wants to seek and what he has proposed to interrogate. And when he has retained his intention in his heart for a day and a night or more—not acting upon every flighty movement of the mind, as many unskilled people are sometimes accustomed to do, as is said elsewhere—then He who said "ask" and who "gave so that you might ask" will "add so that you may find." In this manner, I believe every interrogation ought to be made, unless it should perhaps be a sudden case...

# The Third Consideration is to see in how many ways the planets act upon the lower world through the diversity of the qualities of the aforementioned movements. There are 16 ways by which the diversities of actions and effects happen to all things that are made and perfected: those that are not made and not perfected, and those that are partially made and perfected and partially not made nor perfected, which will be discussed below.

# The Fourth Consideration concerns the causes that help things to be made and perfected, those that prohibit things from being made or perfected, and those causes that destroy things after they have been perfected, which happens frequently. These occur in 16 ways, as I have said, according to the 16 diversities of movements, etc. The first of these is the arrival or perfection of things, which the philosophers call **perfection** <note>original: "alocohol," from the Arabic *al-qubul*</note>. The second is deterioration, which they call **impairment** <note>original: "aliber"</note>. The third is conjunction or returning, which they call **application** <note>original: "alittisal"</note>. The fourth is separation or disjunction, which they call **separation** <note>original: "alincherat"</note>. The fifth is the carrying of light, which they call **translation** <note>original: "annecad"</note>. The sixth is a gathering or bringing together, which they call **collection** <note>original: "algemēi"</note>. The seventh is forbidding or prohibition, which they call **refusal** <note>original: "almanā"</note>. The eighth is **reception** <note>original: "alcohol"</note>. The ninth is the emptying of the course, which they call **void of course** <note>original: "gasralcohol"</note>. The tenth is granting or permission, which they call **permission** <note>original: "galaalocir"</note>. The eleventh is the return of virtue or disposition, which they call **renewal** <note>original: "alteat"</note>. The twelfth is the pushing of virtue, which they call **pushing power** <note>original: "dalpha alchoa"</note>. The thirteenth is the pushing of disposition, which they call **pushing disposition** <note>original: "dalsaaredbit"</note>. The fourteenth is revenge or strength, which they call **fortitude** <note>original: "alcoeuaꝫ"</note>. The fifteenth is **weakness** <note>original: "adirof"</note>. The sixteenth is the state of the Moon, which they call **the Moon's distress** <note>original: "gnaymel alchamaur"</note>, which is a bad state as the ancient wise men said, and is the Moon's defectiveness.

# The Fifth Consideration is in how many ways such a state of the Moon occurs. The philosophers said this happens in ten ways. To me, however, it seems that seven more can be added, and thus there will be 17 ways in which hindrances and damages occur in all things that are hindered—in all beginnings, in all questions, in all journeys, in all births, and in all things we wish to do or intend to do. The first of these is when the Moon is <term>combust</term><note>Burned up by the Sun's heat and hidden by its light.</note>, that is, within the rays of the Sun: less than 15 degrees behind the Sun when she is approaching it, and less than 12 degrees ahead of it when she is moving away from it to emerge from under its rays (since it is possible for her to appear from under its rays then). It is a greater hindrance to her when she goes toward the Sun than when she moves away from it; for when she moves away and is separated from it by five degrees, she is said to have escaped, though she is not entirely free—just as when a fever leaves a sick man: although he is weak and broken, he is said to be free because he is now secure in the health to come. The second is when she is in the degrees of her <term>fall</term><note>A sign where a planet's influence is most weakened or "descending."</note>, namely in the third degree of Scorpio or in all of Scorpio and in all of Capricorn; or if a planet is joined to her in its own fall—that is, if a planet is in its fall or the Moon's fall, such as if she joins the Sun while he is in Scorpio or Capricorn, or if the Sun were in his own

<column-break/>

fall, namely in the fourth [degree] or in Libra—that is, in its 19th degree—or in all of Libra; or if she were joined to Mars while he is in Libra or Taurus or in the 28th degree of Cancer or all of Cancer. Understand the same for all other planets. The third is when she is in the <term>combust degrees</term><note>Specific degrees in the zodiac considered volatile or harmful.</note>, the worst of which are the 12 degrees before the degree directly opposite the degree where the Sun is, in whatever degree the Sun may be. The fourth is if she is joined to any of the <term>malefics</term><note>Saturn and Mars, the planets traditionally associated with hardship.</note> or in their opposition or <term>square aspect</term><note>An angle of 90 degrees, considered a point of tension.</note> without perfect <term>reception</term><note>A supportive relationship where one planet is in a sign ruled by the other.</note>—as if she were joined to Saturn or Mars. It would be otherwise, however, if a perfect reception intervened, for then they hinder less. In all other places, they hinder her in the aforementioned aspects and in bodily conjunction, unless she were in places where the malefic has two of its minor <term>dignities</term><note>Astrological "strengths" based on a planet's position in specific degrees (terms, faces, etc.).</note>, such as Saturn in the last four degrees of Aries where he has his term and triplicity, or in the last four degrees of Gemini where he likewise has two dignities. Or as Mars in the last 10 degrees of Pisces where he has face and triplicity. Understand the same for all other signs and places where they have two of those minor dignities. The fifth is if she is with the <term>Head of the Dragon</term> or its <term>Tail</term><note>The North and South Nodes of the Moon, where eclipses occur.</note> so that there are fewer than 12 degrees between them, since that is the limit within which the Moon is eclipsed. The sixth is if she is in Gemini, which is the 12th sign from her own house <note>The 12th house is traditionally associated with hidden enemies and self-undoing.</note>. The seventh is if she is in the bounds of the signs which are the <term>terms</term> of the malefics, except for the last six degrees of Leo which are the terms of Jupiter; but in its first six degrees she is hindered, for they are the term of Saturn. You might perhaps say that she is hindered in the first six degrees of Cancer, which are the term of Mars; yet she is not hindered there as in other terms of malefics, for something is taken away from the harm because Cancer is her house and her greatest strength. The eighth is if she is in the 6th, 8th, 9th, or 12th [house] from the <term>ascendant</term> without being received; or if she is joined to a planet in any of those houses; or if she is in the 3rd, because the 3rd is among those falling away from the angles; but because she is said to "rejoice" in that house, she is not so hindered there as in other cadent houses. The ninth is if she is from the 15th degree of Libra to the end of the 15th degree of Scorpio, which 30 degrees are the <term>Via Combusta</term><note>The "Burned Way," a region of the zodiac (late Libra to early Scorpio) traditionally viewed as highly unfortunate.</note>. The tenth is if she is <term>void of course</term><note>Moving through a sign without making an aspect to any other planet.</note>, namely joined to none of the planets by body or by aspect, or if she is "wild" or "feral," which happens when she is void of course and in a place where she has no dignity. The eleventh is if she is slow in course, for then she is likened to a <term>retrograde</term> planet. The twelfth is if she is in the waning of her light, so that nothing or little is seen of her as she goes toward combustion, which happens at the end of the lunar month. The thirteenth is if she is <term>besieged</term> between two malefics hindering her. The fourteenth is if she is in <term>azimene degrees</term><note>Degrees associated with lameness or physical disability.</note>. The fifteenth is if she is in <term>pitted degrees</term><note>Degrees where a planet’s power is said to be "swallowed" or weakened.</note>. The sixteenth is if she is in <term>smoky degrees</term>. The seventeenth is if she is in <term>dark degrees</term>—concerning all of which you have the tables noted above in the first treatise of this work.

# The Sixth Consideration is another way of weakening the planets, not much different from the one said above, which happens in ten ways. The first of these is if a planet is falling from the angles and from the ascendant so that it does not aspect it. The second is if the planet is <term>retrograde</term><note>Appearing to move backward in the sky; a sign of instability or reversal.</note>. The third is if it is <term>combust</term>, which is 15 degrees before the Sun and fewer after it; the "inferior" planets <note>Mercury and Venus.</note> are hindered more when they are after the Sun and less when they are before it when they are <term>direct</term>; but when <term>retrograde</term>, it is the opposite. The fourth is if any of them...

it acts like a hospitable welcome that mitigates harsh aspects.</note>. ¶ The **Fifth** is that it be "besieged" by two malifics: that is, that it separates from one and is immediately joined to the other without a perfect reception by house, exaltation, or two minor dignities, which are **term**, **triplicity**, or **face**. ¶ The **Sixth** is that it be joined to a planet in its **detriment** <note>original: "descensione"</note> or its **fall** <note>The "fall" is the sign opposite the planet's exaltation, where its power is most diminished.</note>, which is the opposition of its house or exaltation. ¶ The **Seventh** is that it be joined to a **cadent** planet <note>A planet in a house that "falls away" from the main angles of the chart (the 3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th houses), weakening its ability to act.</note> or from the Ascendant; or that it separates from a planet that was receiving it and joins another that does not receive it. ¶ The **Eighth** is that it be **peregrine**: this means it is in a place where it has no dignity whatsoever; or that the superior planets are followed by the Sun, or the inferior planets follow it <note>This refers to being "under the beams" or "combust," where the Sun's light overwhelms the planet.</note>. ¶ The **Ninth** is that the planet be with the **Head of the Dragon** or its **Tail** <note>The North and South Nodes of the Moon, which were thought to have powerful, often disruptive, effects.</note> without latitude. ¶ The **Tenth** is that the planet be "impeding itself": that is, that it be in the seventh house from its own house, or not received. These are the ten impediments of the planets by which obstacles are created in nativities <note>Birth charts</note>, in interrogations <note>Horary questions</note>, in journeys, and in all works which we intend to do or begin. You ought to know all these modes of planetary impediments.

¶ There are also other modes which you ought to know, some of which I will mention to you that seem more necessary: for it would be grave—indeed, most grave—to consider all those modes. It would be impossible for you to apply them all at once, as I said. But I will tell you those that are most necessary for you, and without which you cannot judge perfectly. Others I may perhaps name for you, but I will not explain them all lest they cause you boredom. Some are very strongly good, some stronger good, some strongly good, some weakly good, some weaker good, some very weakly good; some are hidden, some manifest. Similarly, some are very strongly evil, some stronger evil, some strongly evil, some weakly evil, some weaker evil, and some very weakly evil.

### The Seventh Consideration
is that you should guard yourself against those ways in which an astrologer can err, of which the wise have noted four. ¶ The **First** is if the questioner does not know how to ask the question. ¶ The **Second** is if the astrologer takes the shadow <note>Measuring time via a sundial</note> in an uneven place or with a false instrument. ¶ The **Third** is if he is ignorant of whether the Sun has already receded from the line of the Midheaven, or whether it is on the line, or before it, or after it. ¶ The **Fourth** is if the "fortunes" <note>Jupiter and Venus</note> and the "infortunes" <note>Saturn and Mars</note> are equal; in such a case, you should not accept any question if you can avoid it. To me, however, it seems that three other modes can be added by which an astrologer can err. ¶ **One**, namely, if the questioner comes to him for the purpose of **testing** <note>original: "temptandi"</note> him, as some occasionally do who say: "Let us go to such-and-such an astrologer and ask about such a thing, and we will see if he tells us the truth," just as the Jews did to our Lord Jesus Christ. ¶ In **another way** it similarly seems the astrologer can err: if the questioner does not ask with genuine **intent** <note>original: "intentione"</note>, as some do who, when they meet an astrologer or when they are going about their other business, think of some matter they want to ask the astrologer about, and thus they ask on a whim <note>original: "ex prouisu"</note>, and then error can fall there. ¶ And you might say: "How can I know whether the questioner asks with intent or not, or asks for the sake of testing me or not?" To which I say to you that it seems a very arduous and difficult thing; but I have experienced this many times and found it to be true: I looked at the hour of the interrogation and I saw its Ascendant, and if I found the line of the eastern horizon <note>The Ascendant</note> to be

<column-break/>

at the very end of one sign or the beginning of another, I would say that he was not asking with intent, or that he was asking for the sake of testing me. I found many who confessed to me that it was so, and they afterwards reputed me to know more than they believed before, and they placed faith in the art where they had not placed it before. And when I found an Ascendant like that, I would say to him: "Brother, do not weary me unless you ask with genuine intent; for I suspect you wish to deceive me by not proposing this question as you ought. But if you wish me to labor for your cause, provide for me for my labor." And immediately, if it was a deception, he would leave. ¶ In a **third way**, the astrologer can err if the **Lord of the Ascendant** and the **Lord of the Hour** <note>The planet ruling the specific planetary hour of the day.</note> are not the same, or if the Lord of the Ascendant and the Lord of the Hour are not of the same triplicity, or are not of the same complexion as the Ascendant. If you find it so, the question will not be **radical** <note>A "radical" chart is one that is considered fit for judgment, having "roots" in reality.</note>, as I have experienced many times. ¶ I have recited this to you so that you may know which people you ought to look for: for as the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle, though here referring to astrological wisdom.</note> says, the answer will be according to the quality of the questioner's concern, and according to whether he comes to you under necessity, sad or thoughtful, and hoping that you can and know how to answer him the truth regarding his question. For those people, you may look [at the stars] securely.

### The Eighth Consideration
is that you see and consider how many of the aforementioned modes or considerations you ought to use in judgments, which are thirty. Namely: the **16** mentioned above regarding the impediments of the Moon; the **10** by which the planets are impeded and weakened; and **four** in which the planets **rejoice** <note>original: "gaudent," referring to "Planetary Joys," specific places in a chart where a planet's nature is most comfortable.</note>, as I told you above in the chapter on the joys of the planets. ¶ Of these four, the **first** is to see the place in which each planet rejoices: such as **Mercury** which rejoices in the Ascendant (1st house); the **Moon** in the 3rd; **Venus** in the 5th; **Mars** in the 6th; the **Sun** in the 9th; **Jupiter** in the 11th; and **Saturn** in the 12th. ¶ The **second** is that a planet be in its own house in which it rejoices, as has been said elsewhere: **Saturn** rejoices in Aquarius; **Jupiter** in Sagittarius; **Mars** in Scorpio; the **Sun** in Leo; **Venus** in Taurus; **Mercury** in Virgo; and the **Moon** in Cancer. And let it not annoy you if I occasionally reiterate some of these things which were said elsewhere, for it is easier for you to see what you want where it is needed than to search elsewhere. ¶ The **third** is that the **diurnal** planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Sun, and Mercury) be with the diurnal ones in the East and be oriental of the Sun and near the eastern line; and the **nocturnal** planets (Mars, Venus, Moon, and Mercury) be with the nocturnal ones in the West and occidental of the Sun, especially near the western line. ¶ The **fourth** is that the **three superiors** (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) be in the masculine quadrants, which are from the cusp of the 10th house to the cusp of the 1st, and from the cusp of the 4th house to the cusp of the 7th. And that **Venus** and the **Moon** be in the feminine quadrants, which are from the cusp of the Ascendant to the cusp of the 4th, and from the cusp of the 7th house to the cusp of the 10th. **Mercury** indeed rejoices with the masculine planets in masculine quadrants and with feminine planets in feminine quadrants.

You, however, ought to consider in your judgments those things which they considered in theirs, and moreover whatever else you can consider concerning the contingencies. For you ought to consider and see, when you erect a figure <note>A 'figure' is a horoscope or birth chart.</note> for any **significator** <note>The planet that represents the person or the specific question being asked.</note> of a thing sought, whether begun or to be begun or to be done: if any of the **fixed stars** <note>Stars that do not move through the zodiac like planets; they were believed to exert intense, specific influences.</note> which is of the same nature as itself is in the place in which it [the planet] has its **house** or **exaltation** <note>These are "essential dignities," signs where a planet is particularly powerful, like a king in his own palace.</note>, and is with it in the same minute; for then that star will help such a significator in such a way and to such an extent that it will complete the matter even beyond the intention of the one seeking, beginning, or doing it. And this is the **strongest hidden helper**; for he will not know from where this [success] happens to him. 

If indeed that star is with the significator in the same degree from one minute up to 16 minutes ahead, or up to 6 minutes if **retrograde** <note>Moving backward from our perspective on Earth, which usually weakens a planet.</note>: it helps, but not as much. And this is the **stronger hidden helper**. If indeed it is with it in the same degree from 16 minutes up to 50 minutes, it will help again less: and this is the **strong hidden helper**. If indeed it is in the same degree in a place where the significator has two of its **minor dignities** <note>Lesser sources of power called Term, Triplicity, or Face.</note> in the same minute or from one up to 16, it will help him clearly less: and that will be the **weak hidden helper**. If indeed it is in the same degree far from the significator by more than 16 minutes up to 50, it will help him still less: and this will be the **weaker hidden helper**. ¶ If indeed it is in a place where the significator does not have any dignity, it will help him some, but almost imperceptibly: and this will be the **weakest hidden helper**.

minutes onward, it will harm then again less: and this will be the **strong hidden harmer**. ¶ If indeed that star is in the house or exaltation of the significator, not in the same minute but another, and it is up to 16 minutes, it will harm still less: and this is the **weak hidden harmer**. ¶ But if the star is with the significator in the house or exaltation from 16 minutes up to 50, it will harm again less: and that will be the **weaker hidden harmer**. ¶ If indeed the star is with the significator in the same degree in any of the **major dignities** <note>House or Exaltation.</note> from 50 minutes up to the end of that degree, it will harm again less: and this is the **weakest hidden harmer**. ¶ However, the fixed stars which are of the natures of the planets and those of their opposites will not be named here, for it would be a long discourse; but in the treatise on **Revolutions** <note>The study of the "birthdays" of years or cities to predict annual events.</note> I shall tell you some which you will need to consider in every revolution; some all to you in the treatise on **Nativities** <note>Birth charts.</note>; some others in the treatise on **Rains**; if God’s goodness grants me life with bodily integrity to finish this work.

### Concerning the aforementioned ways in which they are strongest good and so forth, and which are strongest evil.

I do not wish to forget, however, to tell you the ways of which I made mention above—namely, which are the **strongest good**, etc., and which are the **strongest evil**, etc. And all those are manifest <note>Visible and obvious to the astrologer.</note> and not hidden, whether they be good or evil. 
¶ The **strongest manifestly good** is when the planet that is the significator of any matter is in its own house, in an **angle** <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses, which are the most active areas of a chart.</note>, in the very minute with the **cusp** <note>The exact starting point or "doorway" of a house.</note>, moving directly and with swift course, **received** <note>A type of celestial hospitality where one planet hosts another, providing support.</note>, and free from all impediment—which very rarely happens. ¶ The **stronger manifestly good** is that the significator be in its house or exaltation in an angle, one degree before the line [the cusp] or two after; free from evils and received—which happens more rarely. ¶ The **strong manifestly good** is that the significator be in an angle in its house or exaltation, three degrees before the line or five after it. 
The **weak manifestly good** is that the planet be in two of its minor dignities in the angles, 5 degrees before or 15 after, or that it be in its house or exaltation in a **succedent** house <note>Houses that "follow" the angles (2nd, 5th, 8th, 11th), which have moderate strength.</note> to an angle, free from evils. ¶ The **weaker manifestly good** is that the significator planet be in its house or its exaltation, or in two of its other minor dignities, in **cadent** houses <note>The 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th houses, considered the weakest and most difficult positions.</note> while aspecting <note>Forming a geometric relationship with.</note> the **Ascendant** <note>The eastern horizon, representing the person asking the question.</note>. 
¶ The **weakest manifestly good** is that the significator planet be in any of its major dignities or in two minor ones, not aspecting the Ascendant, or in one of the minor ones only while aspecting it, or linked to a planet aspecting the Ascendant and having testimony in it. 
¶ The **strongest manifestly evil** is that the significator be in a place where it has no dignity, no **joy** <note>A specific house where a planet is traditionally said to "enjoy" being.</note>, not received, **besieged** by two malifics <note>Trapped between Mars and Saturn.</note>, falling from an angle into a cadent house from the Ascendant; and all the more strongly if it is joined with any of the evil fixed stars. 
¶ There are also other ways besides the aforementioned ones that help, and others that harm, both hidden and manifest, and it shall be through the conjunctions and aspects of the planets—all of which it would be long to narrate individually here. I do not make mention of them now; however, it shall be done regarding some of them in this treatise; for the sermon would be prolonged and generate boredom for the listener and reader. Nor do I make an example for you of all the aforementioned things on account of the excessive length of words. But all things further for you concerning the considerations or chapters which principally look to the first face of judgments.
