# ¶ Here begins the treatise on elections according to the sayings of the wise.
## The first introductory chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a scholar or physician seated in a study with various books and instruments.</image-desc>

Since, after the <term>judgments</term> <note>original: "iudicia"; refers to predictive astrology or the answering of specific questions</note>, we require <term>elections</term> <note>original: "electionibus"; the practice of choosing a specific moment in time to start an activity to ensure a favorable outcome</note> more than all other parts of astrology, and since these are matters that occur to us daily—and without them we cannot perfectly reach the full utility of the many judgments we must explain every day—it seems appropriate to me to create a special treatise about them, following the footsteps of our wise ancestors. An election is the choosing of a desired thing through prior counsel. To "elect," therefore, is a desire resulting in the intellect from an act of <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberi arbitrij"</note>. And although I have occasionally encountered many fools and "dressed-up" idiots <note>original: "ydiote tunicati"; likely referring to unlearned people who wear the robes of scholars without the knowledge</note> saying that an election is worth nothing and is utterly non-existent, the truth of elections and the other parts of astrology nevertheless remains firm, nor is their truth diminished because of such people.

For through elections we can obtain many good things and likewise avoid many evils that are destined to come according to the stars. I do not say that an election "makes" the event happen; rather, it "removes the hindrance" that prevents the event from happening. For if an astrologer judges that someone going against enemies will have victory based on a question asked, unless that seeker has a good election for moving his army against his enemies, he might succumb because of an evil beginning to his journey; or at the very least, much of the good signified to him through the initial judgment would be diminished. But if he has a good election under a good and strong <term>ascendant</term> <note>the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, he will arrive at the good end of the matter signified by the judgment and will overcome the enemy resisting him.

For it is impossible that those things which are done by right reason and by law should not have firmness and reach a good end. For the Most High and glorious Creator of all made the heavens and the incorruptible stars out of the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "qnta essentia" or quintessence; in ancient physics, the pure, celestial element that makes up the stars, distinct from the four earthly elements</note> so that they might rule and govern the inferior, corruptible things made of the four corruptible essences, namely the <term>elements</term> <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>. And He made the stars for the sake of humans, so that help might be provided by the stars to humans and other lower things. That which is made for man ought to serve man. If anyone says it is not so, one should not argue with them, as they understand nothing and believe nothing; let them be dismissed as masters of error and heretics against the truth. If they are ignorant of the truth, it is because they are intent on monetary gain; this deprives them of knowledge and blinds their minds and hearts.

The stars are established in the eight sensible and moving heavens. Those which are in the <term>First Moveable</term> <note>original: "primo mobili"; the outermost sphere of the universe in Ptolemaic cosmology</note>, which are called by philosophers [the fixed stars], are like the form, while the corruptible things are the matter. The planets, however, exist and operate as a certain medium through which the higher things act upon the lower. Nevertheless, they formally carry out their operations. Because matter is a certain infinity and forms are made from matter, that is the reason why the form of no rational thing is simply assimilated to the form of another; not only between two individuals, but even the species are nearly infinite to us. If God made the stars for humans, what utility would follow from them if they did not work and impress various things upon the lower world? We see them doing this daily and manifest; for in one place they sometimes work good, and at other times we see them in that same place doing the opposite of what they first worked, which only happens because of the diversity 

<column-break/>

of their motions and positions. Because of the different qualities of their motions and the different positions of their bodies, various changes occur in the world. We see the planets move with different motions, and according to those different motions, they leave impressions on lower things in different ways; and those things are changed and altered according to those impressions. They are heated and cooled; they are dried and moistened. For when Mars and the Sun are joined together, if it is summer, the heat exceeds moderation. If it is winter, the cold is diminished and it returns to a temperate state. But if the Sun is joined with Saturn and it is winter, the cold is intensified. If it is summer, the heat is diminished.

Therefore, when the astrologer knows those diversities of motions through his inquiry, and knows those impressions which are made on lower things because of those motions—and since those motions are sometimes of a good quality and sometimes bad—he can choose the good when the qualities of those motions are good and take hold of it. And afterward, he can choose the evil that is signified by those qualities when they are bad and avoid it. For as has been given elsewhere, a planet does not signify the same thing when it is <term>retrograde</term> <note>appearing to move backward</note> as when it is <term>direct</term> <note>moving forward</note>; not the same when it is slow as when it is fast; not the same when it is <term>stationary</term> as when it is progressive; not the same when it is <term>combust</term> <note>too close to the sun, which was thought to "burn up" the planet's power</note> as when it has escaped; not the same when it is <term>void of course</term> <note>making no further aspects</note> as when it is joined to another; not the same when it is in foreign dignities as when it is in its own. It is not the same when it is in an <term>angle</term> <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a chart, positions of strength</note> as when it is in a <term>cadent</term> house <note>the 3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th houses, positions of weakness</note>; not the same when it is free as when it is hindered.

Therefore, since the astrologer knows through the experts of this science when a planet is well-disposed, an election can then be made for good. And since he knows when a planet is poorly disposed, an election can be made and [the evil] avoided, according to what the astrologer finds to be true. And good or bad hours can be chosen, just as our Lord Jesus Christ chose when he said, "Let us go into Judea again," etc. <note>original: "eamus in iudeā iterum"; a reference to John 11:7, implying Christ chose the timing of his travels</note>. And the evils that are destined to come according to the dispositions of the aforementioned motions and their evil significations can be avoided. This applies to all the beginnings of those things we intend to do: in travels as well as in the betrothals of women and the celebration of nuptials; in buildings as well as in destructions; in plantings as well as in uprootings, and in every single thing we wish to do or intend to avoid. 

Thus the stars work different things in lower beings according to the diversity of their various motions; and the astrologer, through good elections, can avert many evils which would have happened to a person according to the motions of the stars unless they had taken precautions. Hence, critics cannot strike down astrology nor the elections of things by the light path they have taken for themselves. They can, however, somehow argue against those things which seem "likely," but all can be defended. For example, if they were to say that elections were not intended for every lowly person: that is in a way true, but not simply so. For we do not believe that any lowly person can choose a time for themselves by making an interrogation; but if a question is asked about a matter—what might happen to them—we can certainly then choose, having taken the <term>significator</term> <note>the planet representing the person or the matter in the chart</note> of the election from the question they asked. For through their question, that which was thought to be destroyed regarding the significator of their <term>radical nativity</term> <note>birth chart</note> is renewed. And in a way, elections seem to be common to all. For an election is not of a spontaneous thing nor a certain thing; nevertheless, it belongs to anyone who has counseled with themselves or whom another has counseled, and it is a matter for which counsel was the preamble and reason and intellect provided the lead. For magnates and nobles—those, namely, who are fit for a kingdom—they can choose [times] both over their births and over their international...

It explains the cosmological basis of astrology, asserting that planets act as a medium between the heavens and the earthly elements to influence human affairs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion on "elections"—the art of choosing the most auspicious time for an action. The author is refuting critics who claim that everything is decided by God's will alone, arguing instead for the reality of "Fortune" as mapped by the stars. He then transitions into the specific requirements for successful astrological elections.</meta>

...petitions, even without these things, always and indifferently regarding all their beginnings, whether in journeys or other matters. However, when you choose for common people without a <term>question</term> <note>original: "interrogatione"; a formal request for an astrological reading</note>—and especially if there are many of them together, as sometimes happens with those wishing to travel by land, provided there are several, as in pilgrimages and similar cases—you cannot choose for them as you would for a single person. This is because the fortunes and misfortunes of the "roots" of their <term>birth charts</term> <note>original: "radicum natiuitatum"; the planetary positions at the exact moment of their birth</note> differ. Consequently, a <term>significator</term> <note>a specific planet designated to represent the person or the action in the chart</note> that is beneficial for one of them might be harmful to another. Thus, you cannot have a single election that is useful to everyone at the same hour, for nothing can perform two natural and contrary operations at once and at the same time, according to the same thing and toward the same result.

And that things are so is evident from this: we sometimes see several people go out together at the same hour for some business, and for some it turns out well, while for others the opposite occurs. Therefore, if they all had <term>interrogations</term> <note>specific astrological questions cast for a specific moment</note>, one should choose for those whose questions signified good, and one should not choose for those whose signified the contrary, as with the others. It is true, however, that a good election either helps or at least does no harm, provided it is not contrary to the "root" of the person's birth. Nor should elections be rejected because of this; rather, they should be observed according to the order shown to you. Those for whom good planets were the significators will rejoice in good days and be glad in them; in bad days, they are sometimes saddened. Those for whom bad planets were significators rejoice in days when they should not seem to do so, and they are saddened on good days and feel unwell. This is only because the "bad" planets conquered in the root of their birth chart. For the "bad" <note>the "malefic" planets, traditionally Mars and Saturn</note> only benefit the just; they do not harm strangers. But the "good" <note>the "benefic" planets, traditionally Jupiter and Venus</note> always benefit the just and never profit strangers. This is the reason why elections are more likely to help than to harm. Therefore, do not despise these things I tell you; if you consider them well and observe them carefully, you will be able to perceive the utility of elections, where they originate, and how and why they are valuable for things. 

For I want you to know that fortune rules in everything, although certain "clothed" idiots <note>referring to unlearned people who wear scholarly robes</note> say that fortune does not exist, but only what God wills. Their wise men, however, disagree with this in secret, even if in public they seem to agree with them—which is more out of fear that their <term>orders</term> <note>likely religious orders or social ranks</note> might be disparaged than because they believe those people speak the truth. If fortune did not exist, who would be so foolish as to be unable to acquire all necessary things for himself abundantly by his own judgment? But we see the opposite clearly every day. Do I not see certain wise, upright, and intelligent men who, for the most part, have nothing to eat? And certain fools who, if a wolf took seven out of ten sheep, would not even know if they were missing or not, yet they flow with an abundance of everything necessary? These people [the critics] actually impose madness upon their Creator, lying that He is not just, and they fall into an abominable heresy.

### Chapter two: regarding those things which are considered in this treatise.

**In** this treatise, which is called "Of Elections," you must know these five things: namely, if the elections we make contain any utility within them. Similarly, it behooves you to consider the principle of every thing which anyone intends to do or begin, and why it is so. And whether things that begin are destined to come to completion or not. And if there should be a completion, whether the end of that which we begin will be good or bad in the future. To <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology</note>, who before other wise men was the rectifier of this science, it seemed that the fruit of this art would be judgments, with elections not excluded; indeed, they are counted in the fruit of this science. For it is necessary that a large part of the fruit of astronomy be the election, because when we choose the beginning of any matter...

<column-break/>

...we can know through that election the beginning, the middle, and the end of the matter itself, as it ought to be. For if we choose for someone at an age fit for it so that they might beget a son—or even if we do not choose for them, but we know the hour of that conception, whether that concept be rational or non-rational—we will know what will happen to it in the mother's womb up to the day and hour of birth. And if we know the hour of birth, we can tell them what will happen to them after birth until the end of their life according to the natural order, and what ought to happen to them. For God gives to the newborn what the stars minister. And although the matter is the same in them, the operations are many and diverse, just as happens in the limbs to which the First Cause gave the power of each according to its operations; for it is not His concern to prohibit anything, although some who are ignorant of astronomy do not admit this. 

Similarly, when we choose for someone wishing to sow or plant, we will know what will happen to that planting or that sowing according to the administration and significations of the stars. **Sarcinator** <note>original: "Sarcinator"; likely referring to Sahl ibn Bishr (Zahel), a famous 9th-century Jewish astrologer</note> seemed to wish that we should not choose for common or mediocre people unless it was based on their birth or their interrogation; yet he did not totally forbid us from choosing for them. But it seemed safer to him to choose based on birth charts or on interrogations; just as it is good to choose based on births or interrogations. But if we sometimes cannot have either of those, the election is not therefore to be forbidden. And he said that we might choose even without them, nor are they contrary to him for this reason. Sarcinator wanted to be certain, so that he could not be criticized, because he wanted to choose based on birth charts (which are rarely available) or on interrogations concerning their nature. **Daly** <note>original: "Daly"; likely Yahya al-Khayyat (Albohali), a student of Masha'allah</note>, however, wanted to be more liberal in this, in that he wanted to benefit everyone, although elections that are not made based on birth charts or questions are not as certain as those made upon them; nevertheless, he was confident that they ought to be of value, or at least they cannot harm. 

To me, however, it seems that we can choose for everyone individually, provided there is not a plurality for whom we choose. By "plurality," do not understand a community, but a private plurality, such as when some go together joined in pilgrimages and the like. For I believe the mediocre or common person has his own "root" in his birth just as a nobleman has his root, since each of them was born under an **ascendant** <note>the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>. If we have prepared the **Moon**, which is a participant in every matter, then we have the part of the journey or other matter universally prepared, which is from the radical things, and which will not allow the traveler to perish easily—even if the ascendant of the journey were contrary to the ascendant of the birth in which the Moon was a participant. And since the Moon is the strongest factor in journeys, she removes much of the contrary that might be signified by other planets opposing the traveler; for her signification in journeys is double the signification of any of the other planets. 

Hence, since she has such a large part in journeys and all other things, and is a participant in the birth of the traveler, and we have prepared her for the journey, it seems that a part of the root of the birth of the traveler or beginner has been prepared. Thus there will be prosperity for him on the journey, although perhaps not everything will turn out as prosperous as he would wish. Nevertheless, a good election will diminish and take away many evils that were destined to come according to the significations of the stars. And he for whom one chooses will grasp some good things which, without an election, he would not have grasped. For those who avoid elections that are not made based on birth charts or on interrogations...

...to me they do not seem entirely wise: for if they cannot have that good which they desire, they should not nevertheless scorn that good which they can have. ### Chapter Three: On the Root of Elections.

The root of our elections is the "adaptation" of their foundations, and foremost among these is the adaptation of the Moon: for as it is said elsewhere, she has a participation and significance in every beginning: in every journey, in every place, in every time, in every matter, and in every hour. It is similar with the Sun, which, as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> says, presides among the other planets like a king; and also the planet that signifies the matter we wish to begin. For example, if we wish to begin a war or anything else involving iron and fire, we must adapt Mars, who naturally signifies such things. If we wish to acquire money, we must adapt Jupiter, who naturally signifies it. If we wish to celebrate a wedding or similar pleasures, we must adapt Venus. Understand the significance of every planet in this way. Furthermore, we must adapt a <term>zodiac sign</term> that is of the same nature as the thing we wish to begin, so that it may represent it: as if we wish to make a journey by land, let us adapt an Earth sign; if by water, let us adapt a Water sign. And its "adaptation" means that it should be free from impediments and from <term>malefics</term> <note>planets like Saturn or Mars that were thought to cause harm</note> and their aspects, and you should place that sign as the <term>ascendant</term> <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the start of the action</note> for your election; or place the Lord of the Ascendant in it, or the Moon, or both if you can. These things are necessary in all common elections, whether they are made based on <term>birth charts</term> or <term>horary questions</term> <note>astrological charts cast for the moment a question is asked</note>, or in others if it can be done. Certain other things are opportune though not as necessary, such as adapting a masculine sign for men and a feminine sign for women.

### Chapter Four: On the Adaptation of Particulars.

After you have adapted the aforementioned universal things, you must adapt the particulars; specifically, after you have adapted the <term>luminaries</term> <note>the Sun and the Moon</note>, the Lord of the Ascendant, and the planet signifying the matter the beginner intends to do—namely, the <term>house</term> <note>one of the twelve divisions of the sky representing different areas of life</note> that signifies the matter upon which your election and the intention of the beginner rests. This is done in two ways: for in those whose birth charts you know and for whom you have "questions," you must adapt the house signifying that matter in the birth chart or the question. But for those whose birth chart or question you do not have, you shall adapt the house signifying that matter at the hour of the election or the beginning. In every election, you must also adapt the First and the Fourth houses and the Lord of each: the First and its Lord so that the person for whom you are choosing may be saved and protected; and the Fourth and its Lord so that the matter may be perfected and its end may be good and praiseworthy.

¶ And Haly said: adapt the house signifying that matter for this reason: because one and the same sign can become different houses, which will have different meanings according to the diversity of regions. For example, if Aries were the First House in Toledo, in that same hour at the <term>seventh climate</term> <note>a geographical zone</note> that same sign would be the Twelfth House; and at that same hour, that is, at that time, for a Corinthian or someone slightly this side of there, it would be 

<column-break/>

the Eleventh House. And so it goes unto the end of the habitable earth, diversifying the houses according to the difference of the longitudes of the regions and their distance from one another, giving to each 770 miles, according to how the ancient sages measured the earth, or perhaps according to the measurement contained in their books. Concerning this, I do not make a great fuss, except so that you may see the manner of the diversity of the houses, so that you may perceive their significance according to the diversity of regions; for that same sign which signifies one thing in one part of the earth can signify another thing, different from that, in another. And thus it seems that elections are not to be avoided in every way, even if they do not always have birth charts or questions.

And if someone should say that if we always make the <term>benefics</term> <note>the "fortunate" planets: Jupiter and Venus</note> strong and the <term>malefics</term> <note>the "unfortunate" planets: Saturn and Mars</note> weak in elections, and one of the malefics happens to be the significator of the birth chart of the person for whom we are choosing, we are doing the opposite of what we should do, and thus we become contrary to them when we ought to be useful. To this it can be answered that we ought to follow the footsteps of nature, which is always intent upon the better; and we, too, must be intent upon the better. For it is better, since we are ignorant of their birth charts and have no questions, that we adapt the benefics and weaken the malefics; for the weakening of the benefics is worse than the weakening of the malefics. For if we weaken all the benefics, it may be that no good remains in the election. But if we weaken all the malefics, we cannot weaken them so much that some good does not remain in it. For none of the malefics—even if one of them signifies good in a birth chart—signifies good universally, always, and everywhere.

For among the good planets, there are many who naturally and universally always and everywhere signify good: such as Venus, who always signifies betrothals, the celebration of weddings, and other affairs of women in every hour and in every land, and similar things; and the Moon, which has significance in the affairs of mothers and in all our other affairs, as is said elsewhere; similarly the Sun over matters of dignity; and Jupiter, who naturally, always, and everywhere, in every hour and in every land, is the significator of substance. And thus, whenever we fortify the benefics or the stars signifying what we intend, we reserve some good for the person for whom we choose, which does not happen with the malefics. Furthermore, the "naturally evil" planets are only two, namely Saturn and Mars; but the "naturally good" are five, namely Jupiter, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. Since the good ones are more numerous than the evil ones, they must prevail in strength; and thus we ought to consider the "much good" more than we fear the "not much evil." And in this, those who say we should not use elections are in error; for as someone says, an election cannot harm, but it can profit. For it is impossible that a good hour should not be good and a bad one should not be bad. Therefore, since we can discern the good from the bad, why should we not take up the good hour and avoid the bad? 

If someone wishing to go to battle—who perhaps was on the verge of going—sought counsel from you to choose a good hour for him, or asked you to see if that hour was good or not; and you saw the significator poorly disposed in that hour, such that if he went to battle then he would be killed; and you saw another hour in which he could go without danger—if you did not tell him not to go then but to wait for the hour in which he could go safely, or if you said "Go, for this hour will not harm you if God wills," would you not, if he went then and was killed, be made a homicide thereby? Know that it is so; I say this if you denied him counsel by your own fault: that is, if he wished...

For that election can be so strong that it not only averts the evil of one whose birth is unknown or about whom no question is asked, but even if evil is signified through the birth or the question, it could be averted from him by that very strong election. 

Similarly, if some traveler asked you which of three roads would be better and safer for him—on one of which it was publicly said that robbers never stood; on another, there were sometimes robbers and sometimes not; and on the third, there were always robbers—and you said to him: "Go by this way," namely the one where there were always robbers, "since you will not encounter robbers if God wills it," would you not, if he went by that way and was robbed, be held liable to him for the restitution of what he lost? This is because you could have taught him the way in which it was said there were never robbers, through which, even if he had been robbed, you would not be held liable to him. 

For an election works according to "more or less." And we sometimes see doctors give medicines to certain people sick unto death and for whom there is no hope of escape; yet it is possible that the power of the medicine is sometimes so great that nature is strengthened by it and the sick man is liberated. And if the medicine does not free the sick man, at the very least it will not harm him; and thus, a good hour is always to be chosen.

## Chapter five: that the election ought to agree with the nature of the thing for which it is chosen.

Yet, it is necessary that your election agree with the nature of the thing for which you are choosing. For the effects and impressions of the superior bodies <note>The planets and stars.</note> are not naturally adapted except to subjects fit to receive them. Nor can an election give anything to any subject except what is its own and what pertains to it according to the natural order of its species. For no one could choose such an hour for a man that would make him fly, nor one that would make him run as a hare or a fawn runs, nor even one that would make him travel 500 or 1,000 miles in one day. Rather, he must choose only for those things that can be adapted to him according to the natural order. For the Most High Creator of the world established an order for every creature according to its nature and according to what was suitable for it; for every creature and every individual can do only as much as its natural form permits. For power ought to correspond to form; nothing can have anything through its nature except what can be given to it, unless perhaps it be monstrous. 

Therefore, do not choose the impossible for anyone, since laypeople and even certain "tunic-wearers" <note>original: "tunicati"; likely referring to monks or friars who wore distinctive tunics or habits.</note> and almost everyone indiscriminately strive to mock astrologers and invent unheard-of lies for their derision. Do not choose an hour for an eighty or ninety-year-old woman to conceive, since old age prohibits it. Do not choose for a boy of ten or twelve years to father a child, since his age does not allow nor permit it. Do not choose for one wishing to ride

<column-break/>

a foal of two or three months, since its tenderness will not allow it. According to the saying: "No one happily dares what nature denies." Do not choose for one wishing to sow wheat in the plains of Italy in June or July; nor for one wishing to sow kidney beans or millet in Hungary or in Germany <note>original: "teutonia"</note> in the month of October or November, because the region or the disposition of the air does not desire it. Nor even choose for one wishing to sow on the seashore, because the place is not fit for this. For the actor would not produce anything except what proceeds from his own nature. Do not choose for one who does not know how to swim and wishes to throw himself into deep water, because he will drown. Nor even choose for one wishing to throw himself into a burning furnace, because he will burn. Nor choose for one wishing to throw himself from a high tower to the ground, because it will break his neck. Do not choose in the desert for one wishing to fight with a lion, because it will tear him apart. Do not choose for a weak man wishing to fight with many and stronger men, or for a few wishing to fight with many, because they will succumb. For violence will be done however you choose for an equal or for one slightly weaker. 

For natural reason does not incline except toward those things to which it naturally pertains. However, sometimes a few are chosen against many and the few win; but what happens occasionally should not be taken as a general rule. For it suffices for him for whom you choose if you choose for him against a fourth or third part larger than his own. For if it exceeds that, the election will not be very safe, because the force of the path often makes reason retreat. For the super-celestial bodies work nothing other than what was granted to them by nature. For they are of eight species: for every planet is of its own proper species; the fixed stars similarly are of their own proper species. And it could even be said that every fixed star was of its species and that the species are diverse, as are the operations and significations, although they are equally incorruptible. 

It is true, however, that I once chose for Count Guido Novello of Tuscany <note>Guido Novello (c. 1227–1293), a leader of the Ghibelline faction.</note> against the Florentines, who had expelled him from Florence and leveled all his castles that he had in Tuscany and had despoiled him of all his goods. He had on his side 3,200 knights and perhaps 13,000 footmen and 300 crossbowmen <note>original: "balisterios"</note>; and the adversaries had 5,300 knights and perhaps 12,000 footmen and 5,000 crossbowmen and more; and yet we battled them and defeated them entirely. And this was in the Valley of the Arbia at Montaperti <note>The Battle of Montaperti (September 4, 1260), a famous Ghibelline victory over the Guelphs.</note>. Nevertheless, I first had through a "question" that we ought to prevail, and afterward we had a very strong election in going to the battle. And I knew their outcome through private messengers sent for that purpose, which was bad, indeed worst. 

You, however, ought to consider in all your elections that the grace of nature and the being of each thing seems to be able to suffer it to be done so, and you will not err. For it is necessary for this—so that your election may achieve what you intend and he for whom you choose may reach a good end of the matter—to make sure you adapt all these things I tell you, if you can: namely the first house <note>The Ascendant</note> and its lord; the fourth house also and its lord; as well as both luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note>; the Part of Fortune; similarly the lords of the lords in which they were; and the house signifying the matter for which you choose and its lord; and the planet to which the Moon will first be joined after your election or beginning; and the lord of the fourth sign from the sign in which the Moon was, because he has a participation in the signification of the end of the matter; and also the lord of the fourth sign from the sign in which the Part of Fortune was; and the lord of the house in which the lord of the sign was where the Moon was—both in all the aforementioned things and in the building of cities or castles or houses and similar things. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions for "elections"—the practice of choosing the most astrologically auspicious moment to begin a task. Therefore, if you wish to adapt any **election** <note>The practice of selecting a specific time to start an undertaking to ensure a favorable outcome.</note>—for instance, if you wish to build a tower or a castle, or begin anything else—you must be focused both on the **matter** itself and on the **person** for whom you are choosing the time. For the **first house** <note>The Ascendant; the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment the work begins.</note> and its lord must be adapted for the person themselves. You must also adapt the first house, its lord, the **Moon**, and the **Part of Fortune** <note>A mathematical point in an astrological chart representing prosperity and success.</note> to the matter being started, so that its end may be good. Thus, if a thing is begun—whether it be a building, a journey, or anything else—and those **significators** <note>The specific planets or houses that represent the people or objects involved in the chart.</note> are well-disposed for you (or for the one for whom you are choosing), it will be good. But if they are all hindered, the result will be the opposite. And if the lord of the first house and the Moon are hindered, but the Part of Fortune is safe, it will be good for the thing for which the election is made, but not for the person to whom the thing belongs. However, the power of the Part of Fortune, though helpful, will not be so great that it can defend the business without it sharing in some of the hindrance.

### ¶ On demolishing any building.

If, however, your election is for the purpose of wanting to **demolish** a building—namely a house or a castle or some such thing—its significators must be weakened, and especially the **lord of the fourth house** <note>In astrology, the fourth house represents foundations, lands, and the "end of matters."</note> and the planet to which the Moon is joined. This is because that planet signifies what is to become of the matter. Above all other significators, **Mars** must be weakened; for Mars signifies the "reiteration" or rebuilding of a destroyed structure, and most especially in a way that goes against the one who is demolishing the building or who caused it to be demolished. But if the intention of the one demolishing is that he should rebuild it, or if his intention is to demolish it with ease and speed—or perhaps if he does not care whether the destroyed building is rebuilt or not—let the Moon be separated from a "malefic" <note>An unfavorable planet, usually Mars or Saturn.</note> and joined to a "fortune" <note>A favorable planet, usually Jupiter or Venus.</note> that is oriental, moving directly, or joined to the lord of the house in which she is located by a **trine** or **sextile** aspect <note>Harmonious angles of 120 or 60 degrees between planets.</note> while descending in her circle.

### ¶ Chapter Six: That the beginning of a thing is not before the thing is actually started.

Know also that the inception or beginning of any thing cannot be "before" that thing starts, nor is it necessary after it has already begun; rather, it is in the very **start** of the thing, as I shall tell you. It is not when the beginning has already been made, nor when it has not yet been made; it is not even when it is in the process of becoming; but only **when it is made**. For example, when we build a tower or a house or any other building intended to last, we seek out and cast the **first stone** and place it in its proper location. That first placement can truly be called the "beginning" of the building or the construction. If someone were to say that digging or measuring is the beginning of a building, it does not seem right to me. For every "beginning" constitutes the thing begun; it is **intrinsic** <note>Internal or essential to the thing itself.</note> to the matter we wish or intend to start. But that which is **extrinsic** <note>External or not essential.</note> is not part of the thing itself. For sometimes one can build without digging—as when we build upon a rock or similar surfaces—but without the first stone, we can never build the thing we wish or intend to start. It is clear, therefore, that the positioning of the first stone, the first stone itself, and its proper location constitute the intrinsic beginning of the thing and the building we intend to make, as well as the act of construction. Measuring and digging, though they are preparations for building, are not part of the building itself—no more than the gathering of stones or the mixing of lime. Yet, I do not forbid you from adapting all those preparatory acts if you can. If it is necessary for the building we wish to make to be founded upon timbers—as sometimes happens with bridges and similar things where the start cannot be made with stones—adapt the **first timber** that is placed in that foundation; that is the beginning of that building, for it is part of the structure.

<column-break/>

### ¶ When one builds without making a wall.

And if it should be another kind of building that does not have walls, let the beginning be the placement of the **first column** in the pit made for that purpose, once its placement is finalized and correct, and so on. And because it seems almost impossible to adapt all the significators I have named for you, if you cannot adapt them all, adapt those that you can. For you will not adapt so few of them that they do not benefit your election, even if not as much as you would wish. For if you could adapt them all, the matter would be blessed in every way; however, it will be "blessed" according to the number of significators you have adapted. Therefore, if you can, you shall adapt the first house and its lord, the Moon, the lord of the house in which the Moon is located, and the planet to which the Moon or the lord of the first house is joined; also the Part of Fortune and the lord of the house in which you find it, the planet signifying the thing you intend to do, and also the **Lord of the Hour** <note>The planet ruling the specific planetary hour in which the work begins.</note>. If you cannot adapt all of these, adapt the lord of the first house, the Moon, the planet signifying that thing, and the lord of the hour. If you cannot adapt all of those again, adapt the Moon and the lord of the hour. But if you cannot even do that, consider what your election is about: for if it is a journey or going out for hunting and the like, then you should adapt the lord of the hour rather than anything else, and make the Moon "fall" from the **ascendant** <note>Move the Moon out of the first house so it does not influence the person directly.</note> so that she is neither in it nor looking at it. But if it is something other than a journey or hunting, adapt the Moon as you wish, and it will profit you in the thing you intend to do or begin. If someone should say that we ought not to make elections so extensive as I have said (since almost everyone else seems to want to say something different), he could be answered thus: the **wise** <note>Referring to the great ancient and medieval masters of astrology.</note> wanted their elections to be so "blessed" that they would be perfect in every way. They considered elections that a person might not always be able to wait for until all the significators could be adapted as they described. But we, for the most part, do not have the time to wait; hence we must choose within the window of time we have and gather what good we can in our election.

### ¶ On strengthening the Sun.

However, you should always take care to strengthen the **Sun** in durable matters as best as you can, and especially for those of nobles and great men; for this is rightly done, even in other elections where you can adapt it. Nevertheless, elections (as I have mentioned to you elsewhere) are diverse: namely according to nobility, according to time, according to age, according to place, according to office or magistracy, and according to the nature and species of the thing to be chosen. In the cases of those whose **birth charts** <note>original: "nativitates"</note> we know, or for whom we have **interrogations** <note>Questions asked of an astrologer to produce a horary chart.</note>, we must not weaken any of the planets that have strength in the "root" of the birth or the interrogation of any of them. And **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel (965–1050 AD), a famous Arab astrologer whose "Book of the Skilled in the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard textbook.</note> said that these things agree in every beginning, except that for certain men we must place some of the following factors which are not to be placed universally for everyone else; for they are exceptions for them and are almost necessary in their affairs, as will now be told to you.

### ¶ Chapter Seven: How different planets are adapted to different persons.

These are not merely among those things to be followed, but are among the necessities and the "roots" [of the matter]. For whether you wish it or not, you must adapt these in the affairs of kings, powerful men, and the like—that is, in matters pertaining to the kingdom...

...and other lay dignities: the **Sun** is also to be adapted to Babylon and the Eastern Romans <note>The Byzantines</note>. **Mercury** is to be adapted to scribes and merchants; for it naturally signifies writings, the intellect, and such things due to its changeability: and to the Indians, since its strength is in that land. **Mars** is to be adapted to fighters <note>original: *pungilibus*, likely *pugilibus*</note>, butchers, bakers, smiths, and the like, since it naturally signifies contentions and those things which are worked through iron and fire; and to the Western Romans, since its strength is in those parts. **Jupiter** is to be adapted to secular religious people and to merchants wishing to trade justly, since it signifies substance—especially well-acquired wealth—and to those of Al-Iraq, since its strength is in the parts of Al-Iraq. **Venus** is to be adapted to women, since it naturally signifies the affairs of women; and to the Arabs, since it naturally signifies that nation, and its strength is in those parts. **Saturn** is to be adapted to Jews, farmers, old men, religious people who wear black garments, and the like, because of the heaviness of its motion; and to the Ethiopians, since it signifies that nation. 

Therefore, as has been said to you many times already, adapt those **significators** <note>The planets or zodiac signs that represent specific people or themes in a chart.</note> which you are able to, even if you cannot adapt all those you might wish; this is so that our **election** <note>The chosen time to start a project.</note> may increase some good and diminish some evil as much as we are able, even if we cannot do everything we wish. 

**Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> indeed said that in all our elections we ought to consider the **Lord of the Ascendant** <note>The planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> and the **Moon**, and make the significator of our matter the stronger of the two; and he praised this because it signifies what follows from that beginning. And he said that when the Lord of the Ascendant is fortunate—that is, joined with the **Benefics** <note>The "good" planets, Jupiter and Venus.</note>—but is weak (falling from an angle or from the Ascendant), and the Moon is strong (in the angle of the Ascendant, or in the succeeding house in the eleventh or fifth, aspecting the Ascendant) but is "unfortunate" (joined with the **Malefics** <note>The "harsh" planets, Saturn and Mars.</note>), we ought not to judge the matter as bad because of this. Rather, we ought to judge it as good, because he says that then the Moon has little participation in that matter. 

But if the Lord of the Ascendant is joined to your fortune, great weight should not be placed on the Moon; indeed, he said that sometimes it is necessary for us to "unfortunate" the Moon—that is, to weaken it—and to make the Lord of the Ascendant fortunate, as in hunting. However, **Zabel** <note>Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century Jewish astrologer and mathematician.</note> and **Abomar** <note>Likely referring to Abu Ma'shar or his son.</note> seem to say that the Moon should be made fortunate in hunting; but Haly said the Moon should be "unfortunate" in hunting, speaking idiomatically. For he himself understood that when he said "unfortunate," he meant "debilitated," because any planet can be strong and unfortunate, or weak and fortunate, through other factors. And as for what he said about placing it with the Malefics: it can be placed with Malefics without a total misfortune, and there are certain Malefics with which it is necessary for us to place it in hunting. Sometimes it is also necessary for us to weaken and "unfortunate" the Moon, such as in the investigation of a fugitive, as will be said elsewhere. Those others who said it should be made "fortunate" did not mean it should be made "strong."

## Chapter 8. What kind of end is hoped for in the thing we begin.

**Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most influential astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> indeed said that in order for us to know the **end** <note>The final outcome or result.</note> of our election, we must consider seven things. First, he placed the **Lord of the 4th House**, not as preceding the others in order, but as the most worthy, since it specifically signifies the end, and the end is worthier than the beginning. Second, he placed the Lord of the sign in which the Moon is found. And if the Moon is then in Cancer, it should be considered itself after the Lord of the 4th. Third, he placed the planet to which the Moon is first joined in the first conjunction it makes with

<column-break/>

any of the planets after the matter has begun. Fourth, he placed the Lord of the sign in which the **Part of Fortune** <note>A calculated point representing success and well-being.</note> is located. Fifth, he placed the 4th sign from the sign in which the Moon is then located. And someone else wished, as Haly said, to add the Lord of the 4th from the location of the Part of Fortune. 

But because all these things cannot easily be adapted at once and at the same time, I have told you these things. And although the Lord of the 4th naturally signifies the end of a matter which someone wishes to begin—whether it be a journey or something else—it sometimes happens that it does not signify the end, wherefore you must seek another. For example: the Lord of the 1st House signifies the matter as preceding the other significators, and the Lord of the 4th regards the end as well, as I said before all others—namely, if it "aspects" the 4th house. When some journey or building is begun, and the Lord of the 4th aspects the 4th, the end of the matter is sought from it. But if it does not aspect the 4th, seek it from the Lord of the house in which the Moon is; if that planet aspects the Moon, it signifies the end of the matter. If not, then seek the end of the matter from the planet to which the Moon is first joined after the matter is begun. If it is joined to someone, or seeks a conjunction with someone, then seek the end of the matter from the planet in whose house the Part of Fortune is located; if it aspects it, it will be the significator of the end of the matter. If not, the signification will then remain with the Moon and the house—not the house in which it is, but rather the [Lord of the] house will be stronger than the Moon in participation. 

And all the aforesaid significators have some kind of participation with it, as does the Lord of the 1st with them; but it <note>the Lord of the Moon's house</note> will be more authoritative than all of them. And he said that if the signification were given to the Lord of the 4th sign from the place of the Part of Fortune, it should be placed after all the others. And he said that if the Moon were joined bodily, degree by degree, to any planet in the sign in which it is, that planet will be the significator of the end of the matter, whether it has dignity there or not; and it shall be placed before the Lord of the sign in which the Moon is. 

If you find it so, consider then the participation of the aforesaid significators with the planet to which the Moon joins bodily in the sign in which it is, degree by degree. And return to the Lord of the 1st house, as it seemed to **Alchindi** <note>Al-Kindi, the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note>, since it signifies the seeker or the beginner and what happens to them from the start of that matter. And the Lord of the sign in which that [Lord of the 1st] is located signifies what happens to them in the **middle** of the matter. And if it is in its own house, it will signify the middle just as the beginning. And the Lord of the sign in which *that* planet is located <note>the host of the host of the 1st house</note> signifies what kind of **end** the matter has and what happens to the beginner from it. Therefore, see what the condition of those three is, and according to that, judge the state of the matter in each of the aforesaid times. 

Our wise men wished to adapt so many significators because if it had been possible, they said we could have perfected all our business according to our will. However, we cannot adapt everything just as we can say they ought to be adapted; nor do we always have the convenience of waiting so long that we can adapt them thus. For perhaps in the whole time of our life we could not make one election so perfect that it would not lack some of the aforesaid. It is necessary, therefore, that we adapt our elections as best we can; and if we cannot have everything we want, let us at least have the best we can get so that our labor is not in vain. For as that revered predecessor of ours, **Albumasar**, said—who was better in this art than the Latins ever had, and who studied at **Athens** when study flourished there, as he himself confesses in a certain book of his—it is impossible for us to adapt all twelve houses, because "evils" <note>the Malefic planets</note> cannot be removed from heaven. Therefore, it is necessary that we adapt those things we can adapt and do what good we can. And keep the method which I told you above in adapting those significators which you can adapt; and by doing so, you will follow utility.

And Haly <note>original: *Haly*; referring to the 11th-century Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel, whose work was a standard textbook in medieval Europe.</note> said that the adaptation of the house of the end of the matter—that is, the 4th house—is very necessary after you have adapted the other radical <note>The "root" or fundamental factors of a chart.</note> things: namely, the lord of the first house, the Moon, the lord of the 10th house, and the Part of Fortune. ### ¶ Chapter 9. How a sign should be adapted.

Haly said that we ought to adapt the sign signifying the matter which we intend to do or begin; and its adaptation consists in being remote from every impediment—that is, that it be free from misfortune <note>original: *infortunio*; referring to "malefic" planets like Mars or Saturn.</note> and from their square or opposite aspects. Nor should it be besieged by two evils <note>A condition where a planet is trapped between two malefic planets.</note> or by their rays, but rather be clean of them. In this way, the sign will signify good, and it will signify even greater good if some **fortune** <note>original: *fortuna*; a "benefic" planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> or its rays are within it; and it is even better if they behold that sign from a trine or sextile aspect <note>Harmonious geometric angles of 120 and 60 degrees.</note>. If more fortunes are in it or behold it, the more they are, the more its significance for good will increase. And he said that if the sign is as fortunate as has been described, even if it is falling from an angle <note>original: *cadens ab angulo*; "cadent" houses (3, 6, 9, 12) were considered weaker than "angular" houses (1, 4, 7, 10).</note> or is besieged by evils, it cannot be hindered for this reason; and if there is a hindrance, it will be so small that it will do little or nothing. But if the fortunes behold that sign from a fourth aspect <note>A square aspect (90 degrees), usually considered difficult.</note> or from an opposition, he said it will not be as profitable, and this is true. He also said that if both good and evil planets behold it or are in it together at the same time, it is a mixture of both powers; and one judges the goodness or malice of that sign according to the multitude of the strengths of the good or the evil planets. If, however, the fortunes and misfortunes behold it or are in it equally, it must be said of that sign as if there were nothing good or evil in it. And if the planet which beholds it or which is in it has some dignity <note>A position of strength, such as being in its own sign.</note> there, it will be good: for if it is a good planet, it will increase the good; if it is an evil planet, it will diminish the malice. And he said that the lord of that sign is to be adapted so that it has two significations there: one from the lordship it holds over it, and another from the good place in which it resides.

### ¶ Chapter 10. How a planet should be adapted.

Haly said that the adaptation of a planet is that about which nothing evil is said, from which all impediment is removed; but it is to be clean from the evils and their conjunctions and aspects. It should be **direct** <note>Moving forward, not retrograde.</note>, not **retrograde**, nor **combust** <note>Burned by being too close to the Sun.</note>, nor **cadent**, nor in a cadent sign or one otherwise hindered, nor weak in any other way. For if it is so disposed, it strengthens and makes fortunate the matter we wish to do or begin. It also strengthens the place signifying that matter and its end if it is the significator, whether it is a fortune or not. In whatever place it may be and in whatever sign, the beginning of that matter will always be blessed, as will the middle and the end. If it is clean of the evils and disposed as described, and strong and in a good place, it is said to be in the perfection of goodness; nevertheless, if any of the fortunes help it, it is said to increase its perfection. If the aspect of that fortune is "in front" <note>Approaching the planet.</note>, it will be better again; if it is "from behind," it does not increase it as much, though it still increases it. If, however, any of the misfortunes behold it, it diminishes something of its goodness, and it diminishes more if they behold it from the front than from behind. When we have adapted the sign and the planet which signify the matter we wish to begin as described, our election and its hour will be good and perfect according to how the sign or planet were adapted. And it is also appropriate, if possible, that the sign and planet from which we take the signifi-

<column-break/>

-cation should agree in nature with the thing we wish to choose. For a task to be done in water, or through water, or in the proximity of water—such as going fishing, sailing, making ships, building mills, digging wells, and the like—we ought to adapt an **aquatic sign** and a **humid planet**, or one signifying moisture. And if the election is on land or through the land, we ought to adapt an **earthy sign** and the planet which most agrees with it, such as going hunting on land, digging ditches, pulling stones or rocks from their mines, or making walls that are not intended to be raised high from the ground, and the like. And if the election is in things pertaining to the air or which are done in it—such as hunting birds with other birds like hawks, falcons, gerfalcons, and similar birds, or if we wish to build windmills or other very tall buildings that reach into the air—we ought to adapt an **airy sign** and the planet which most agrees with it. And if our election is in things pertaining to fire, or which are worked by fire or with fire, we ought to adapt a **fiery sign** and a planet agreeing with it, such as choosing for a smith, or bakers, and the like. ¶ And if the matter for which we are choosing is one we wish to be completed quickly, a sign must be adapted that agrees with speed and with a matter we do not wish to be prolonged—namely, a **moveable** <note>original: *mobile*; also known as "cardinal" signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn), which initiate change.</note> sign. This applies to the betrothals of women, because we wish to celebrate the nuptials shortly; and in works we wish to write, so that the work begun may be finished quickly; and in seeds, and the planting of vines, and in the retail sale of wine; and in all those things for which we desire speed and which we wish to be performed quickly. And if the election is such that we wish to act regarding four-footed animals, it is necessary to adapt a **quadruped sign** <note>Signs depicting four-legged animals: Aries, Taurus, Leo, Sagittarius, Capricorn.</note> according to the species of that animal; and we should place it in the house signifying those animals. For instance, if we wish to buy oxen or other larger animals that are **split-hooved**, or to deal with them—such as taming or castrating them, or doing anything similar that pertains to them—we should adapt the **12th house**. We should place in it, if we can, a sign signifying the aforesaid animals, such as **Taurus** or the last half of **Sagittarius**. And if we wish to deal with small animals, we ought to adapt the **6th house** and place in it a quadruped sign signifying those animals, such as dogs or birds with which we hunt, and also other birds and the like, such as the sign **Capricorn**, which signifies smaller split-hooved animals—and especially in smaller quadrupeds that are split-hooved, such as pigs, sheep, rams, she-goats, and he-goats. And we can also attribute these same small split-hooved animals to the 12th house when we deal with their affairs, except in the buying of them; because then they are signified by the 6th, just like other smaller things. They are also signified by the 12th in the case of mules and donkeys, as has been said elsewhere. And if you wish to go out to hunt split-hooved animals, such as deer, roe deer, and the like, one of those split-hooved signs should be placed in the house signifying hunting. And if the departure were for other animals that attack with claws or teeth, such as lions, bears, wolves, and the like, one of the signs signifying those animals should be placed in the house of hunting, if possible. But their lords should not be strengthened in hunting, but rather weakened, as will be said in its own place below. Haly also said that we ought to adapt **Aries**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius** <note>The "Fiery Triplicity."</note> in the deeds of kings and great men, which agree with them, and this is true; because that triplicity is more noble than the other triplicities by reason of its action, just as fire is the most noble element among the elements because of its action. And because the **Leo** is the strongest among those three animals, it is deservedly placed first in the affairs of kings because of their excellence among other men. **Aries**...

### Chapter 11. Again concerning the same.

**A**lbumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer and one of the most influential authorities in the Middle Ages.</note> gave us even more leeway; he was more perceptive in judgments than all other astrologers except for Ptolemy and Hermes, and he was also more eloquent than all of them. He said that when we wish to choose something, whether it be a journey or something else, and we find in the sign signifying the matter the lord of that sign or the lord of its exaltation, and it is "strong"—that is, free from impediments—we ought not to have any suspicion about the matter. Or if one of the luminaries is there, and if it is "received," it will be better than it could otherwise be.

And whatever planet from among the **fortunes** <note>The "benefics," Jupiter and Venus.</note> is in it, that will be good and useful; nor should one care whether it has dignity there or not. Similarly, it is good if a fortune is there, free from the aforementioned impediments, even if it has no dignity in that place.

And he said that the Sun and Moon should be received, provided the ascendant is not the sign of detriment for either of them. And Alchindi <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873), the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> said that the Moon should not be placed in the ascendant because its nature is contrary to it; but he preferred the Sun to be placed in it because it is not contrary to the ascendant's nature. This is because the Sun has the power to detect hidden things and reveal them, just as the ascendant detects and manifests to us those things which were covered and hidden below the horizon; thus the Sun shows things joined together and reveals secrets.

And [Albumasar] said that regarding the matter of the Moon, the opinion of Albumasar is more suitable and more in harmony with the words of Ptolemy than the opinion of Alchindi. He said that according to him, the Moon is hot and a "fortune," just like Venus. And Albumasar testifies to this where he speaks of journeys. And he said that Messahala <note>Masha'allah (c. 740–815), a Persian Jewish astrologer.</note> and his associates prohibited placing the Moon in the ascendant during a journey. And he said that Albumasar did not agree with the words of Messahala in this. He said that they judged the Moon to be cold and moist while the ascendant is hot, and that this does not help...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of "elections"—the art of choosing the most auspicious astrological moment to begin an undertaking. It focuses specifically on the placement of the Sun, Moon, and beneficial planets (fortunes) in the horoscope, citing the divergent opinions of major authorities such as Haly, Al-Kindi, and Aomar Tiberiades.</meta>

[...they came] together. And he said the second is as I have said elsewhere: that it has a significance over the beginning, and especially over the beginning of a journey <term>peregrination: traveling abroad or going on a pilgrimage</term>. And therefore they said it ought to be placed in a suitable house, which I believe to be the 10th, or the 11th, or the 3rd, or the 5th, although they themselves did not specify the place. And he said they claimed the Sun should not be placed in the **ascendant** <term>ascendant: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</term> because the Sun is considered "fortunate" only in **conjunction** <term>conjunction: when the Sun and Moon meet (New Moon)</term> and **prevention** <term>prevention: the moment of the Full Moon (the syzygy preceding an event)</term>. 

And he said that many disagreed with their opinion. And Haly <note>Haly Abenragel: a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> said that when any "fortune" <term>fortune: a beneficial planet, typically Jupiter or Venus</term> is in the ascendant, unimpeded and prosperous, it will be very good. And he said that what Aomar of Tiberias <note>Aomar Tiberiades: a Persian-Jewish astrologer of the 8th century</note> recommends most is that if a fortune is in the first third of the house of the ascendant, it hastens the matter. To him, however, it seemed that if a fortune were in the first degree of the ascendant, or shortly after that degree, it would be better and would make the ascendant more fortunate. In truth, what Aomar said was for no other reason than that it very rarely happens that a planet is found exactly on the degree of the ascendant; and for this reason, he placed its greatest strength in the first third of the ascendant. In the other two-thirds, he did not deny that the ascending degree was stronger than the others. 

Haly spoke of the ascending degree itself for greater certainty and caution. Those who said the Sun should not be placed in the ascendant intended this for when the Sun itself is an **infortune** <term>infortune: a planet that causes harm, like Saturn or Mars</term>, and that would be the time when it joins another planet bodily, or when it is in opposition to any planet within 5 degrees before the degree of opposition or 2 after. Therefore, to avoid every impediment to it, they located it elsewhere rather than in the ascendant. 

As for what Al-Kindi <note>original: "alchindi", a famous 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer</note> said about the Moon not being placed in the ascendant—and Messahala <note>original: "messahala", an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note> said the same—their intention concerned journeys or travels, since the Moon is naturally impeded from the full moon onwards until the conjunction; even before the full moon by 15 degrees: for in those 15 degrees it is impeded because of the opposition. From the opposition onwards until the third **dichotomy** <term>dichotomy: the quarter phase where the moon appears half-lit</term>, it is impeded because of the dryness <note>original: "ficitatē", likely a transcription of "siccitatem" (dryness)</note> that then prevails in it. And from the third dichotomy until the conjunction with the Sun, it is impeded because of coldness, and then it should not be placed in the ascendant of a journey because it afflicts the body of the traveler. Therefore, in order to avoid all its impediments and lest perhaps the elections should deceive them, they avoided placing it in the ascendant. 

What Haly and Albumasar <note>Albumasar: a 9th-century Persian astrologer influential in Europe</note> said in praising Ptolemy's <note>original: "Ptholomei"</note> statement—namely that the Moon should be placed in the ascendant because it is warm like Venus—it is true that Venus, though judged cold and moist, nevertheless has a certain hidden heat which appears in the fact that Venus signifies delights, cheerfulness, and games; and these are not without an admixture of heat. Similarly, the Moon also has a hidden heat and also has a [blank] which is manifest. It has the hidden kind like Venus; it has the manifest kind because when it is in the first dichotomy, it is in the nature of moisture; in the second dichotomy, it is in the nature of heat according to the first witness. And for this reason, those who placed it in the ascendant were confident, considering that heat and moisture are more noble than cold and dryness, and more profound in the operations of nature; they wanted these to be able to benefit more than cold and dryness could harm. Therefore, they did not find enough force in that impediment to prevent them from placing it in the ascendant. 

Although I have told you otherwise, I still bring it back to your memory: if you can fit together all things that the wise men have told you, it would be the ultimate good in your elections—which seems to me like something impossible. But since you cannot fit everything you want into one instance, fit those things that you can; at the very least, however, fit the Moon; and if you cannot fit her, make her fall from the ascen-

<column-break/>

-dant and fit at least the **Lord of the Hour** <term>Lord of the Hour: the planet ruling the specific planetary hour in which the work begins</term>; and it will be some help to you in your matter. 

¶ There are also certain other things that increase fortune, prosperity, and good: namely, the degree of conjunction and the degree of prevention that occurred before your beginning or the election you wish to make—so that it and its lord may be fortunate and clean from "evils" <note>evils: referring to the malefic planets, Saturn and Mars</note> and their aspects, if you can manage this. The place of **conjunction** is the degree in which the Sun and Moon were joined together. The place of **prevention** is the degree of the luminary which was above the earth at the hour and minute of the prevention <note>the full moon preceding the event</note>. And if one luminary is in the eastern degree and the other in the western degree, the degree of prevention will be the one in the east. 

For Al-Kindi said that conjunction here has significance over all things that happen between conjunction and prevention; and prevention here has significance over all things that happen between prevention and conjunction. Therefore it is necessary at the beginning of a nativity <note>nativity: a birth chart</note> and in every election, if it can be fitted: and to consider the place of conjunction or prevention so that we may know whether it was in an **angle** <term>angle: the four most powerful houses of the chart (1st, 4th, 7th, 10th)</term>, or in a **succedent** house <term>succedent: houses following the angles (2nd, 5th, 8th, 11th)</term>, or in a **cadent** house from the angle <term>cadent: the weakest houses (3rd, 6th, 9th, 12th)</term>; and what may be in that very degree of conjunction or prevention from the planets, or in the sign itself where the conjunction or prevention occurred—whether from good or evil planets, or from aspects, and who they are who aspect that degree with any aspect whatsoever; and similarly for all degrees of conjunction or prevention, whether they be under the Sun's rays or in their own light. 

Thus these things signify what will happen in the future concerning those things between conjunction and prevention, and between prevention and conjunction: which, if they are safe, signify the perfection of matters and their goodness. But if they are impeded, they signify their weakness and instability. It must also be considered that the Moon should not join with "infortunes" when it has separated from the degree of conjunction or prevention, but let it be joined with fortunes; and let the degree of conjunction or prevention be with fortunes in some angle. Also, let the Moon be going toward a conjunction with fortunes at the hour of conjunction or prevention if possible; for these things will signify the exaltation and goodness of matters, and their perfection and a praiseworthy end. 

If, however, the place of conjunction or prevention is impeded, and the Moon is joined to "evils" after separating from one of those two places, it signifies that although the beginning of the things done during those times may be praiseworthy, the end will be bad. And the conjunction of the Moon with the planets <unclear>is</unclear> stronger [than] the degree of conjunction or prevention. And if she is joined to fortunes after separation from those places, even though one of those places is in an angle with fortunes, <unclear>nevertheless</unclear> the beginning of those matters might be unpraiseworthy, yet the end will be praiseworthy and good. 

But if the place of conjunction or prevention was with "evils" as stated, and when the Moon was separated from them she was joined to "evils," it signifies that the beginning, middle, and end of those matters will be unpraiseworthy and bad—unless the lord of the sign in which the conjunction or prevention occurred is **oriental** <note>oriental: rising before the Sun</note>, in an angle, and in its own house, or exaltation, or triplicity, or term; or if it aspects that house. For if it is so, it will break all the malice of the others, since it has greater power in matters occurring during the aforementioned times than any of the aforementioned significators. If indeed it were in a house following an angle, perhaps the beginning of the matter would be weak, yet the end will show itself to be good. But if that lord were **occidental** <note>occidental: setting after the Sun</note>, or outside its aforementioned dignities, or cadent from an angle, or did not aspect that house, it will increase the malice of the others and matters will become worse. And if the place of conjunction is cadent from an angle, the things begun in that conjunction or prevention will be bad and of no use. All these things refer to the intention of Al-Kindi; but his intention was not absolute, but rather that I should make a good election in those things which he spoke [of].
