But if one is well or poorly disposed, and the other is neither well nor poorly but in a middle state, they will neither add nor diminish. And all these things are according to what the nature of that sign or that planet might be. And the wise men understood this regarding nearly a twelfth part <note>original: "duodecimam"; likely referring to the *dodecatemoria*, or 2.5-degree subdivisions of a sign</note> of the planets and the houses. And although you may not see much great utility in this chapter, it is nevertheless difficult; it is for your benefit that you know it, for it renders you in some way more eloquent in your art.

# Chapter 12: On the ninth-parts of the signs and what they signify.

Having made mention above of the twelfth parts of the signs in the preceding chapter—or rather, the nature of the twelve signs—the ninth-parts <term>novenaria</term> <note>Also known as *navamsas* in Indian astrology, these are 3°20' subdivisions of a sign</note> in each of the signs must not be omitted. For the ancient wise men said that we ought to know how far a planet has traveled in the sign in which you find it, by degrees and minutes; or how many degrees have ascended of the house whose ninth-part you wish to know. Then divide that sign into nine divisions, each of which will be three degrees and twenty minutes. You shall begin to take these from the beginning of the sign in which the planet is, or the degree of the house from which you began. And see into which ninth-part that degree has fallen. You shall give that first ninth-part to the lord of the **movable sign** <note>Also called a "cardinal sign": Aries, Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn.</note> of that ascending **triplicity** <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> (that is, of the aforementioned house). Give the second ninth-part to the lord of the sign which immediately follows the ascendant or the house. Give the third to the lord of the third sign which follows the second; and the fourth to the lord of the fourth sign; and the fifth to the lord of the fifth; and the sixth to the lord of the sixth; and the seventh to the lord of the seventh sign following the first; and the eighth to the lord of the eighth; and the ninth to the lord of the ninth. Always do this until you find the planet ruling the ninth-part, as shown in this example:

Suppose the ascendant or house from which you began is **Aries**, **Leo**, or **Sagittarius**. **Mars** is the lord of the first ninth-part, because he is the lord of the movable sign of this triplicity, namely Aries. **Venus** is the lady of the second ninth-part, because she is the lord of Taurus <note>The text says ".8." which may be a scribe's error for "Tauri"</note> which is the second sign from the first (that is, from the ascendant) and follows it immediately. The third ninth-part belongs to **Mercury**, as he is the lord of Gemini, the third sign from the first. The fourth ninth-part is the **Moon's**, who is the lady of Cancer, the fourth sign. The fifth is the **Sun's**, lord of Leo. The sixth is **Mercury's**, lord of Virgo. The seventh is **Venus's**, lady of Libra. The eighth is **Mars's**, lord of Scorpio. The ninth ninth-part is **Jupiter's**, lord of Sagittarius.

# Regarding the second triplicity.

If the ascendant or house is **Taurus**, **Virgo**, or **Capricorn**, the first ninth-part will be **Saturn's**, lord of Capricorn <note>The movable sign of the Earth triplicity</note>. The second ninth-part will be the same **Saturn's**, as lord of Aquarius. The third is **Jupiter's**, lord of Pisces. The fourth is **Mars's**, lord of Aries. The fifth is **Venus's**, lady of Taurus. The sixth is **Mercury's**, lord of Gemini. The seventh is the **Moon's**, lady of Cancer. The eighth is the **Sun's**, lord of Leo. The ninth is **Mercury's**, lord of Virgo. And you should understand this for the third and fourth triplicities if the ascendant or house is any of the signs of said triplicities, always beginning from the movable sign of that ascending triplicity and proceeding in order as was said.

To provide an example: suppose a planet or the start of a house is at the 21st degree of **Taurus**. Divide all of Taurus into nine divisions. The first division (the first ninth-part) belongs to **Saturn**, lord of Capricorn, covering 3 degrees and 20 minutes of Taurus. The second is the same **Saturn's** (lord of Aquarius), reaching 6 degrees and 40 minutes. The third ninth-

<column-break/>

part will be **Jupiter's**, lord of Pisces; there you have 10 full degrees. The fourth ninth-part is **Mars's**, lord of Aries, and you have 13 degrees and 20 minutes. The fifth is **Venus's**, lady of Taurus, and you have 16 degrees and 40 minutes. The sixth is **Mercury's**, lord of Gemini, and you have 20 full degrees. The seventh is the **Moon's**, lady of Cancer, and there you have 23 degrees and 20 minutes. Therefore, the planet or degree of the house necessarily falls into the ninth-part of the Moon. 

Whence it follows that the Moon is the lady of that ninth-part. According to how the Moon is then disposed, she will provide assistance to the ascendant and its lord, or to the house from which you began the matter, or the <term>Almuten</term> <note>The planet with the most dignity or "power" at a specific degree.</note> of the birth or the question; or she will take away from its significance. For if she is well disposed and the ascendant is well disposed, she will support the outcome for nearly a seventh part in a good way. But if both are poorly disposed, she will detract in a similar portion. If one is well and the other poorly disposed, they neither add nor diminish. Nevertheless, always consider the lords of the triplicity and the terms, because they always remain in their own being and significations, as was said above. I say nothing here of **Dorotheus** <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century astrological poet.</note>, because he seems to look to the consideration of the **faces** <note>The "faces" or "decans" are 10-degree subdivisions of a sign.</note>, about which enough was already said in the first treatise in the chapter on faces.

# Chapter 13: On the lord of the circle or orb of the signs.

The consideration of the lord of the orb or circle of signs in births is looked at in this manner: you must know the lord of the ascendant of any native and his first hour. You shall give the ascendant, its lord, and the lord of that hour to the first year of the same native, because both these two will signify what the state of the native will be in the first year of his life. Hence, if both are well disposed, his state will be good in that year; if the contrary, you shall judge the contrary. But if one is well disposed and the other poorly, then you can announce that the state of the native will be mediocre, unless the Moon or the lords of the triplicities or terms work against it. You can say the same regarding the health or infirmity of his body. 

Next, you shall look at the lord of the second house and the lord of the second hour and how they are disposed; for if their disposition is good, the substance <note>Wealth or possessions.</note> of the native will be well disposed in the second year; of the contrary, judge the contrary. If one is well and the other poor, the substance of the native will be moderately disposed. After this, look to the lord of the third house and the lord of the third hour; for according to their state, the state of the brothers will be disposed in the third year. And so, proceeding in order according to the disposition and being of the lords of the houses and hours up to the twelfth, you shall judge the significations of all the houses in their years according to the aforementioned method just described for the first, second, and third houses.

# Chapter 14: On the lords of the remaining 12 hours.

You shall consider the order of the twelve remaining hours after the aforementioned ones successively, just as you considered the previous ones and their lords. For you shall give the 12th hour <note>original: ".12. horaz"; likely the cycle of planetary hours</note> and its lord to the first house; it will provide assistance to the ascendant, its lord, and the lord of the first hour in increasing the good by a 24th part, if both (the hour and its lord) are well disposed, as well as the ascendant and its lord. But if the ascendant and its lord are poorly disposed, it will diminish a fourth part of their malice. If the lord of the 13th hour is poorly disposed, it will diminish a 24th part of the good and increase the evil by as much in the first year. And so understand the rest of the hours by proceeding successively in order. For according to how they and their lords are disposed...

thus it will help or hinder the disposition of the other indicators <note>original: "significatorum"</note>, but according to the significations of the 12 houses. In their years, just as it can be seen to come from the nature of things in those years: just as it was said regarding the 13th or 9th lord who gives the ascendant of the testing <note>The text likely refers to the "profection," or annual advancement of the chart</note> 14. 2. 18. or the 9th lord giving the second house, and so on in order. And according to this method, you shall provide for all these houses and their lords, and all good things and their lords. For when the lord of these houses and these hours—as **Alchabicius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in medieval Europe</note> has testified to us—is the prince over all, he holds a sign every year over every sign of that year to which he is assigned, according to what the <term>Alcohoden</term> <note>The planet that determines the length of life</note> holds. And he disposes the significations of the native according to whether he himself was well or poorly disposed, by adding or diminishing in good or evil through the parts named above. And Alchabicius said that some astrologers place the lord of the ascendant of the root <note>The "root" or *radix* is the original birth chart</note> of the birth as the lord over all in the first year; and in the second year, the planet which succeeds it, just as was said regarding the lord of the hours. This seems to me to be appropriately sustained; not that they are simply the lords of the sphere, but they are co-helpers of the aforesaid. It was said what some think, but what he himself put forward seems appropriate for you to know, although it may be a matter of greater labor than strength, it nonetheless renders you more profound in the science of perfection <note>original: "perfectionis," referring to the Profection technique</note>: the science of the place of your perfection through these eras and the quadrant of other things, as I shall recite to you in what follows. For it was said by the elders that **Alchabicius** says there were 51 solar years between the year of the profection which signifies the sect of the Saracens <note>The rise of Islam</note> and the year of the <term>Hegira</term> <note>original: "alchigerat"; the flight of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, marking the start of the Islamic calendar</note>, which was the first year of the years of the Arabs. And the ascendant of the year of the profection of the said sect in that region was the sign of Gemini; and the perfection of that same year reached Virgo. And between that first year of the years of the Arabs and the first year of the years of **Yazdegerd** <note>The era of Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanid king of Persia, beginning in 632 AD</note> of the Persian region, there were three thousand and 224 days. Therefore, when you wish to have knowledge of this matter, take the years of Yazdegerd and turn them into days, as is explained in the book of the courses of the planets; and add upon them the days which were between the first year of the Arabs and Yazdegerd, and divide this by 365 days and a quarter part of one day. And however many divisions result, that many will be the solar years; and whatever remains in months and days will be from the incomplete year. That quantity which was collected from those years are the solar years from the beginning of the years of the Arabs. Therefore, cast away one sign for every year and begin from Virgo; and to whatever sign the number leads you, that will be the sign which the year of the world has reached from the ascension of the profection of the said sect. To others, however, such as **Albumazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most influential Persian astrologer in the Middle Ages</note> and his followers, it seemed that we should add to the completed years of Yazdegerd 51 years, two months, 12 days, and 18 hours: from the years of the Persians which are without fractions and without the quarter of a day; and they extended these years into days and turned those days into solar years, as was said; and they began to cast away from the beginning of Libra. But if you wish to know the profection from the sign of the conjunction of such a sect, let the profection be made from Scorpio, since the conjunction of the planets which signifies the sect began from Scorpio. If, however, you wish for the profection from the ascension of the kingdom, subtract from the completed years of Yazdegerd 118 completed years and turn them into solar years, as I said before; and begin to cast away from Virgo. And it should be known that Muhammad was not a king as predicted, but a prophet; and thus the kingdom did not begin from his time, but began much later, perhaps 117 years after the aforesaid things; and the Arabs began to rule and the ascendant had returned to Virgo. And it seems that there is an error in this letter; for this is not so, but the kingdom of the Arabs was then changed to its blackness <note>Perhaps a reference to the Abbasid Caliphate, whose heraldic color was black</note>; it smells <note>likely meaning "it is evident"</note>; and this is found in the second figure of the three figures of the last distinction of the book *Alalraren*.

### ¶ Profection from the ascendant of the profection.

For the rotation of the conjunction from the watery triplicity to the fiery triplicity, subtract from the completed years of Yazdegerd 176 years; and turn those which remain into solar years. Take care to cast away from Leo, and the number that results in that same sign will be the profection of each beginning of those things which were aforesaid.

### ¶ Chapter Fifteen: On the direction of the significator.

Besides this is the direction of the indicator <note>original: "directione significatoris"</note>; this is when you direct an indicator <term>significator</term> which you wish toward some place of the signs; and you know what may be between them in degrees of direction, and you will take one year for each degree. When, therefore, you wish to know this, and that indicator which you wish to direct to some part of the circle is in the ascendant, subtract the ascensions of the degree in which the indicator is—by the ascensions of the region <term>oblique ascensions</term>—from the ascensions of that degree to which you wish to direct it; and what remains will be the degrees of direction. But if the indicator is in the opposite of the ascending degree <note>the descendant</note>, subtract the ascensions of the opposite degree in which the indicator is from the ascensions of the opposite degree to which you wish to direct it in 그 region; because the setting of any sign corresponds with the rising of its opposite. And it is to be known that the degrees of direction, for each of which one year is taken, are degrees of the equator <note>original: "equatoꝝ diei"; the equinoctial circle</note>; and the degrees which direct and toward which the direction is made are degrees of the oblique circle <note>the zodiac</note>. If, however, the indicator is in the tenth or in the fourth <note>the Midheaven or the Imum Coeli</note>, you will subtract the ascensions of the degree of the indicator from the ascensions of the degree to which you wish to direct it by the ascensions of the direct circle <term>right ascension</term>; and whatever remains will be the degrees of direction. But if the indicator you wish to direct is not in any of the angles, you shall look at its distance from the angle from which it is least distant: namely, from the angle of the tenth house or from the angle of the fourth house. If it is between the ascendant and the tenth, subtract the ascensions of the degree of the tenth house from the ascensions of the degree of the indicator by the direct circle; and if it is between the seventh and the tenth, subtract the ascensions of the degree of the indicator by the direct circle from the degrees of the tenth house similarly by the direct circle. And what remains from the quantity of these spaces, divide by the parts of the hours <term>seasonal hours</term> of that day of the degree in which the indicator was; and what results from that division will be the hours of distance from the angle. And if it is between the ascendant and the fourth house, subtract the ascensions of the degree of the indicator by the direct circle from the ascensions of the fourth house. **A**gain, if the indicator is in the fourth and the seventh, subtract the ascensions of the degree of the fourth house from the ascensions of the indicator by the direct circle; and what remains from the quantity of hours, divide it by the parts of the hours of the night of the degree in which the indicator was; and this is if the indicators are in one quadrant of the circle and not in different ones. And if the indicator is in the middle of the eastern circle, which is from the tenth even to the fourth of those which succeed the ascendant, subtract the ascensions of the degree in which the indicator was from the ascensions of that degree to which you wish to direct it by the direct circle; and what remains will be the significator of the direct circle, which you shall keep for yourself. After this, subtract the ascensions of the degree in which the indicator was, by the ascensions of the region, from the ascensions of the degree to which you wish to direct it by the ascensions of the region; and what results will be the indicator of the regions. After this, you shall look at the residue which is between the indicator of the direct circle and the indicator of the regions; and you shall take a sixth part of 그 residue and multiply it by the hours of distance from the angle, and what results will be the equation. This is to say, if the distance is one hour, you take one sixth; and if it is more, you take more sixths, so that for each hour you take one sixth. And if the indicator of the direct circle is less than the indicator of the region, add that equation to the calculation; as Alchabicius says at length, who also clearly gives the method of directing.

# ¶ Here begins the treatise on rains and on changes in the air and those things which concern them.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing floral scrollwork and a profile of a human face.</image-desc>
Since it seems to me that in those things which preceded, I have sufficiently preserved the promises of those things which I announced at the beginning of this work, lest perhaps you say you have been deceived in anything, I think it will be fitting in this treatise—concerning the change in the air, and concerning those things which happen from those changes and what results from that occurrence, and concerning those things which we can perceive from this and to which the human mind can reach—that I should make mention as briefly as I can. Although the action of rains <note>original: "ymbrium"</note> and of others which are added from changes in the air is very specific and more particular than other specific matters, nevertheless those things which are known by skill and which ought to be known do not seem to me should be omitted: both according to the sayings of our wise predecessors, and those things which may further be seen to be useful according to the truth, so that it may run as surely as possible, nor deviate from their opinions according to what seemed best to our reverend predecessors **Haly**, **Al-Kindi** <note>OCR: "lencuo"; likely Al-Kindi, a 9th-century philosopher who wrote extensively on weather prediction</note>, **Ptolemy**, and others who have striven to elucidate the noble path to these things. Therefore, with brevity, by which the proposed knowledge can be reached more quickly, I intend neither to make a great approach to the beginning of this, nor to make you burdened with long speech; but rather to lead you more quickly to those things desired for the matter and to faithfully apply your mind and intention to them.

## ¶ Those things which are set forth first in this work.

In those things which regard this work, all planets and the mansions of the moon <note>the 28 divisions of the lunar cycle</note> and certain other things should be considered fundamentally, as is required. As has already been said, it is necessary to consider the moon above all others: and let its conjunction with the sun be considered, as well as their opposition, and also their quadratures <note>aspects where the sun and moon are 90 degrees apart</note>; and then to the aspects of the others and their bodily conjunction, and also the increase and decrease of the light of the luminary itself: and the speed and slowness of its course, and its rising, ascent, and descent, and likewise its setting; furthermore, consider those things which seem to relate to generation and corruption from their motions: for in the predicted times the effects of the changes of the air and their additions are more easily grasped, as will be shown more extensively in the following sections, God granting. **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, a prominent 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> also saw that the moon's similar return into the south and north and its application, and whatever figures may happen, suggests this same thing; the acts of all these, and the efficacy of the moon itself and its endurance for animals and the budding things of the earth, which the senses perceive and the common person judges, will be very easily distinguished.

## ¶ On having knowledge of the "fortunes" and "infortunes" and of all temperate or changeable things.

Since the knowledge of the change of air aims for full foresight, it must be known which of the planets are "fortunes" <term>fortunes</term> <note>the "benefic" planets that bring balance and favorable conditions</note> and which are "infortunes" <term>infortunes</term> <note>the "malefic" planets that bring harshness or disruption</note>: similarly, you must know which now tend toward fortune and which now toward infortune. For as the ancient wise men unanimously confess and it is true, **Jupiter** and **Venus** are by nature fortunes and workers of fortune. But **Saturn** and **Mars** are by nature infortunes, for by their nature they bring about misfortune, as the same wise men affirm: and it appears most

<column-break/>

manifestly from the experiment of truth. They said that the **Sun**, **Mercury**, and the **Moon** are common and temperate: that is, the Sun is sometimes a fortune and sometimes an infortune; but Mercury and the Moon are changeable, so that they are converted to the nature of those to whom they are joined, whether they be fortunes or infortunes.

## ¶ To know when rains signify they are coming and when not.

In having knowledge of future rains, it is necessary for you to consider the conjunction of the Sun and Moon as touched upon above, and if any of the planets are then joined with them, or look upon them with any aspect: for if **Jupiter** or **Venus** is bodily joined to them, or if Jupiter looks upon them from a trine or sextile aspect <note>harmonious angles of 120 or 60 degrees</note>, and none of the infortunes <note>Saturn or Mars</note> were present with them, nor cast their rays toward them, or if after the moon's separation from the sun Jupiter looked upon it, he will undoubtedly deny that rains are coming. If, however, the aspect of Jupiter to the luminaries <note>the sun or moon</note> should be a square <term>quartus</term> or opposition <note>challenging angles of 90 or 180 degrees</note> without the admixture of infortunes, it will signify that rains will be light or as if none at all. And if any of the infortunes looked upon them without the aspect of any fortune, or after the bodily conjunction or through opposition the Moon was first joined to them, you can announce without doubt that rains are coming. For it is the property of the fortunes naturally to refine the air and to clear it from thick vapors, and likewise to resist the malice of the infortunes; and from the goodness of the fortunes, the infortunes strive to resist: since the nature of their gravity and impurity accords with the thick vapors gathered in the air, they generate weights which, descending to the lower parts because of that gravity and the impurity and thickening of the air, bring on powerful rains and also disturbance of the air. Nevertheless, although Venus is among the fortunate stars, yet because her nature inclines somewhat to the side of humidity, if she is mixed with any of the infortunes and no other fortune assists, she allows rains to be moved; yet they are not very notable unless perhaps she is found too weak and the infortunes strong, so that she cannot break their malice: yet she always alleviates something.

## ¶ On the prognostication of rains in general.

In the prognostication of rains, however, you should apply discretion and consider the locations, sites, times, climates, regions, and similar things which occur to you to be considered. For the changes of the air continue to be diversified in different ways: for it happens more often and more strongly that it rains and also snows due to the thickness of the air and the rushing of vapor in the mountains <note>original: "alpibus"</note> than in flat places; more in the seventh climate <note>the northernmost latitudinal band of the known world</note> through the predicted proportions than in the sixth; more in the sixth than in the fifth; more in the fifth than in the fourth; more in the fourth than in the third; more in the third than in the second; more in the second than in the first: and so you should understand regarding every climate and every region according to its being and according to its nature.

## ¶ Which mansions of the moon are moist, which dry, and which common.

You shall also consider in which regions and mansions of the moon the predicted conjunctions and aspects take place: for some of those mansions are moist, some dry, some common; some happy or fortunate, some unhappy or unfortunate, as I shall set forth to you following this. For the predicted mansions are 28, of which the first is called **Al-Butayn** <note>OCR: "albarain"</note>: the second **Al-Thurayya** <note>OCR: "altamazer"</note>, the third **Aldebaran**, the fourth **Al-Haq'ah** <note>OCR: "albachia"</note>, the fifth **Al-Han'ah** <note>OCR: "aluara"</note>, the sixth **Al-Dhira'** <note>OCR: "alciraa"</note>, the seventh **Al-Nathrah** <note>OCR: "albiathia"</note>, the eighth **Al-Tarf** <note>OCR: "altarfin"</note>, the ninth **Al-Jabhah** <note>OCR: "algetua"</note>, the tenth **Al-Zubrah** <note>OCR: "alaracen"</note>, the eleventh **Al-Sarfah** <note>OCR: "algarfa"</note>, the twelfth **Al-'Awwa'** <note>OCR: "alafraqe"</note>, the thirteenth **Al-Simak** <note>OCR: "alçamec"</note>, the fourteenth **Al-Ghafr** <note>OCR: "achafre"</note>, the fifteenth **Al-Zubana** <note>OCR: "alçebene"</note>, the sixteenth **Al-Iklil** <note>OCR: "altachils"</note>, the seventeenth **Al-Qalb** <note>OCR: "alchabin"</note>, the eighteenth **Al-Shaulah** <note>OCR: "haftiala"</note>, the nineteenth **Al-Na'am** <note>OCR: "abuaarca"</note>, the twentieth **Al-Baldah** <note>OCR: "albelaca"</note>...

### ¶ Chapter on rain and changes of the air.

Let it be known concerning rains and changes of the air, and concerning clouds signifying rain or dew, or concerning clouds signifying neither of those, and concerning future winds—as well as at what time, in what part of the year, and at what hour the event of these things or any one of them will occur, and their increase or decrease—it is necessary for you to be able to predict. As **Gafar** testifies that he received from the very clear teachings of the Indians, it will be necessary for you to know, according to the position of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, the hour of the <term>conjunction</term> and <term>prevention</term> <note>the New and Full Moon immediately preceding the event</note> of the Sun and Moon that immediately preceded the entry of the Sun into the first minute of **Libra** <note>The Autumnal Equinox</note>, and the situational disposition of all other planets in the circle, especially the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note>. And it also behooves us to consider, after the Sun enters the first minute of **Libra**, its progress until it has traveled the whole designated path, and moreover the other final degrees of **Scorpio**. These things happen in the middle of the seven <term>climates</term> <note>Ancient geographic zones divided by the length of their longest day</note>, because **Libra** and the first 20 degrees of **Scorpio** have significance over rains and winds and changes of the air in the entire fourth climate, as well as in the last half of the third and the first half of the fifth. And the Indians said, after finally rectifying the Sun and Moon at these two hours of meeting <term>conjunction</term> and <term>opposition</term>, or at the two aforesaid signs, it will be necessary to turn one's attention with great diligence to discerning the mansions. From here onward, therefore, it will be necessary to discern the mansions in this way: because

<column-break/>

wherever the conjunction or opposition of the luminaries occurs, from the beginning of **Aries** to the end of the signs themselves, you shall assign 13 degrees and 20 minutes according to equal degrees. And when you have determined the place of the conjunction or opposition, you will see whether that mansion is dry, wet, temperate, or common. You will also see in which mansions the other planets are found, just as was considered for the Moon. When you have done this, you will see to which planet the Moon applies or joins corporally after the meeting or prevention. For according to whether its joining or application with any planet in the circle occurs, so will its significance be over rain or no rain, or winds, or dew, or changes of the air. ¶ For if the Moon is joined or applied to **Saturn**, and he is good and well-disposed, and similarly in a wet mansion without any other application, you will be able to announce without a doubt temperate and early showers, as well as dark clouds filling the entire sky. And if **Saturn** is impeded or poorly disposed, he will increase the rains, winds, darkness of clouds, and all the aforesaid things in that category; and all things are shaped according to the situational places of the houses, mansions, predictions, conjunctions, aspects, or applications, as was given above when we spoke of the complexions of the lunar mansions themselves. And if **Venus** and **Mercury** add their testimonies and their powers, they will greatly increase what has been said, and all the more strongly if their conjunction or application has occurred.

...will be in the angles <note>The "angles" are the four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> or from the angles, then the conflicts of the winds and their fury will be feared, as well as the ruin of certain houses and the breaking or uprooting of certain trees.

### On the hour of rains, showers, and winds.

<margin>c:</margin> To know the timing of the aforesaid events, you must know the hour of the conjunction <note>The New Moon, when the Sun and Moon meet.</note> (if your consideration is based on the conjunction) or the hour of the "prevention" <note>original: "preventionis"; refers to the Full Moon immediately preceding a conjunction.</note> (if your consideration is based on that). You must see by how many degrees the completion of the conjunction, or the application, or the "prevention" or square aspect <note>original: "tetragoni"; an aspect of 90 degrees, usually considered stressful or active.</note> is distant from the predicted place. For the effects of the rains or the change in the air will arrive within as many days or hours as there are degrees, depending on which signs the aspects, applications, or conjunctions occur in. For if they are in **fixed signs**, they will signify days; if in **common signs**, hours; <margin>a:</margin> and if in **movable signs**, they will also signify hours. But you must distinguish what the aforementioned common and movable signs portend: the event will be hastened by a sixth part if the Moon’s course is fast or if its increase in light is not lacking. But if only one of these is present, the event will be hastened by some amount less than that. However, when you find the Moon in the opposite degree of the conjunction or "prevention," or in a square aspect, or if its course is slower according to the sign or place in which it is, the event will be delayed. When the Moon, after its meeting with the Sun, applies to one of the **fortunes** <note>The "benefic" or helpful planets, Jupiter and Venus.</note>, and that fortune—through some aspect—beholds Saturn and receives him into one of its dignities <note>A "dignity" is a sign or degree where a planet has specific strength, like its "home."</note>, it is even better if it receives another and is received by it; these things will alter the predictions, exceeding moderation and signifying delay, and the event will be prolonged by a sixth part of its total duration. But if the Moon applies to it from a square aspect or opposition, and nothing else hinders the effect of the rains, no delay will be interposed; and especially if the two "inferior" planets <note>Venus and Mercury, which orbit between the Earth and the Sun in the Ptolemaic system.</note> testify to them and provide their aid as has been said, then they agree, and will not waver or be diminished.

### When Saturn prohibits rains.

If Saturn remains in a **dry mansion** <note>The 28 lunar mansions were categorized by their elemental nature: dry, humid, temperate, etc.</note> and the Moon applies to him in a dry mansion, and no aid from others is given to them, rains will not occur, even though clouds may frequently disturb the air.

### On the application of the Moon with Jupiter.

And if the Moon applies to Jupiter from the aforesaid places or similar ones, or is with him in the same place or mansion that is **humid**, and Venus and Mercury provide their testimony, then clouds with dews and soft rains (or almost none) will be signified. But if Venus and Mercury do not provide their testimony to them, the rains will cease entirely. But if one of them goes toward them and the other does not, something of rain will happen, though it will be modest. And then, if Jupiter applies to Saturn, it will signify a coming rain that does not exceed moderation. But if the Moon, after separating from the Sun, applies to Mars from the aforesaid places or mansions, and Venus or Mercury beholds them with the testimony of some masculine planet, and such an application is in an angle or from an angle and in a humid mansion (or from a humid mansion), it will signify a massing and mixing of clouds. It will portend few dews or almost none; yet it can signify thunder and lightning; and also, in times and regions suited for it, there will be thunderbolts without a multitude of rains, provided that Mars then applies to Saturn or Jupiter—for if he is then applied to them, he will indicate future rains. And **Gafar** <note>The Latinized name for the Persian astrologer Albumasar (787–886 AD).</note> said this also occurs as something to be noted: that Mars increases the significance of showers from any aspect; and the Moon and the star <column-break/> to which she applies here entirely helps in generating rains. For that same thing is now, properly and principally, the gathering. And he said if it happens otherwise, it does not signify this, and even ruins it; but the clouds which Mars produces have a saffron brightness <note>original: "croceum candorem"; a yellowish-white light.</note> from above, not without whiteness.

### On the application of the Moon with Mars.

<margin>a:</margin> Again, if the Moon has withdrawn after its conjunction with the Sun and applies to Mars and Saturn simultaneously, and she herself remains in a humid mansion, it portends future immoderate rains. If she approaches only one of them and the situation is the same, or to both while they are in temperate mansions, she will signify rains. But if she is in a humid mansion and those two are in dry ones (or vice versa), she will greatly mitigate the coming showers. <margin>c:</margin> Likewise, when the Moon is joined to the Sun and is touched by Jupiter as if at the same time, or approaches him through an aspect, and both of them (or one of them) receive her, they will prevent showers from remaining, so that they do not <margin>e:</margin> flow forth. And **Gafar** said the Moon is finally in the best place, namely under one of the centers of the locations dedicated to this significance; because a fortunate planet makes its own fall <note>The "fall" is a position of planetary weakness.</note> and perverts the leadership [of the weather] if it has already responded to some configuration of the fortunes. And he said all these occasions must be noted. And he said the clouds that are then generated will be white and portend many and inconsistent dews.

### On the application of the Moon with the Sun.

<margin>o:</margin> And if you find the Moon attempting a union with the Sun, and none of the others behold them or join with them bodily, it prohibits showers from coming. But if any of the others then apply to them and are in a humid mansion—and even more so if this is in an angle and the Sun is outside his dignities and strengths—and applies to Saturn and Mars together (or separates from one and <margin>g:</margin> applies to the other), it will announce strong rains to come. But if it applies to only one of them and does not separate from the other, there will be showers which signify a half, or at least a third, or at least a quarter of what was induced in the aforesaid cases. In the aforesaid cases, the clouds will be between grey-blue <note>original: "glancas"; likely *glaucas*.</note> or saffron and semi-wrinkled and dense, not easily dissolved; but after they have been released and humbled, they will announce a serene <margin>i:</margin> sky. If the Moon, after her separation from their presence or aspect, joins the Sun from a trine aspect <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious.</note>, their significations will come into action according to the nature of the houses or mansions in which they are. And **Gafar** said that from a meeting or opposition, it shall by no means be called an "application."

### On the application of the Moon with Venus.

<margin>f:</margin> If the Moon, after her separation from the Sun, applies to Venus, and Venus is in water signs or air signs (but less in air signs) and in humid mansions, she will undoubtedly announce coming rains; and even more greatly, certainly, and unspeakably so if Mars and Saturn behold them. But if only one of them beholds them, their significance will be somewhat less than this, nor will it be necessary for Mercury to provide any help in any of the aforesaid cases; but if he does provide it, he will increase the future rains. But if the aforesaid "evils" <note>The malefic planets Saturn and Mars.</note> do not look harshly upon them, but Jupiter beholds them or the Moon is otherwise fortunate, the rains will cease without doubt and will not happen. But if Venus applies to any of the three "superiors" <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> in the same node <note>The point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>, and no other significance of Venus hinders it, she will portend future rains that are neither constant nor modest. And the aforesaid will happen more strongly if their application exists from a humid mansion or a water sign. But if Venus is free, fortunate, and strong, and is not found joined in the same node and with the Moon, nor is she in a water sign or humid mansion, or even...

## On the application of the Moon with Mercury.

**You must also observe** whether the Moon is joining with the Sun or separating from it after their conjunction. If it first applies <note>Term: "Application" refers to a planet moving toward an aspect or conjunction with another.</note> to Mercury in the same place and in a **humid mansion** <note>Term: "Mansion" refers to the 28 Lunar Mansions, segments of the sky the Moon passes through daily.</note> without the aspect or conjunction of any other planet, it will indicate continuous rains without any delay in time. But if she is joined to him in a way that does not exceed the usual measure, you can announce it as certain. If indeed Mars and Saturn together testify to their conjunction, you should not doubt to announce horrendous, threatening, flooding, and persistent rains. And if Venus still participates in the aforesaid conjunction through any of her dignities <note>In astrology, "dignity" refers to the strength a planet has based on its position in a specific sign.</note> in the predicted places, one should fear that the rains may exceed all measure. But if at the hour of the conjunction of the Moon with the Sun, Mercury is in the same place—the node and a watery sign <note>The "watery signs" are Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces.</note>—and also applies to Venus in a humid mansion, it will indicate rains exceeding measure. If, however, you find the aforesaid conditions in other signs and mansions, you can announce a moderate amount of rain as certain. And Thidius <note>Likely a reference to a historical astrological authority, possibly a corruption of an Arabic name.</note> said: likewise, if Mercury is in a watery sign and a humid mansion, looking toward Venus or located in the same node or "nerve," the rains will exceed the limit. But if Jupiter or another of the **benefics** <note>The "benefics" or "fortunes" are planets like Jupiter and Venus, traditionally seen as bringing good or moderate influences.</note> aspects those aforesaid misfortunes more strongly, you shall judge the rains to be moderate. And if Mercury alone is applied to the Moon and signifies dew and rains, and he is alone in aspect with reception <note>Term: "Reception" occurs when a planet is in a sign or "house" ruled by the planet it is aspecting.</note> to him from his own house or exaltation or from two other dignities, Mercury will take on the nature and significations of Jupiter; he will not permit the Moon to exercise her own significations, and he will bring about clear air, though with a multitude of winds. The quality of those winds will be according to the nature of Jupiter or the other star to whose nature he was applied, if you find him applied conversely to some other. But if the Moon, after her separation from the Sun, applies to Mercury and Venus before the others in the aforesaid places, or even to Mars and Saturn as was said, the significations of the Moon will come to pass and manifest their own effects, unless I say Jupiter and the Sun work against them from whatever aspect or conjunction the aforesaid happens. And this occurs more strongly and ineffably if the conjunction is with the aforesaid **malefics** <note>The "malefics" or "infortunes" are Saturn and Mars, traditionally associated with harsh or destructive weather.</note>; they will increase the rains and dew similarly, and the air will become cloudy. And if the aforesaid benefics work against them and cancel the dew and rains, they still cannot prevent the clouds from being present. And you should by no means let the aforesaid slip into oblivion; but always keep them in the secrets of your mind so that you may be able to respond to them studiously and also use them for your own utility and foresight.

## On the application of the Moon with benefics or malefics.

**And** if the Moon, after her separation from the Sun, applies to any of the **benefics**, she prohibits coming rains. But if she joins any of the **malefics**, or has looked upon them from any aspect and her application departs from that malefic up to 5 degrees or less without the aspect of any benefic, she will announce future rains in that same week. But if the Moon, after her separation from the Sun, joins any of the planets and this happens in a humid mansion or even in any other place of the circle, and she herself is neither impeded nor receiving from anyone, she will moisten the air and signify clouds and dew and various rains and a filling of the air with clouds; indeed, she will cause changes of various winds and sometimes disturbances and lightning

<column-break/>

for this reason. But if after this, the Moon applies to any of the planets through which she is made fortunate, or if she applies to a benefic itself, it will amend all the aforesaid and convert them into their opposite. But if it is a malefic, or if the planet itself is "unfortunate," those things which were predicted will increase and grow so much that they will seem to be doubled. But if she herself is unfortunate and in a bad state and poorly disposed in the observation of evils, she will be found to be a strong and stronger promise, nor will she weary another from the observation of the aforesaid. And although from these things which are now and were formerly said it is manifest that the Moon converts into the nature of that planet to which she is applied (and this is true), yet it does not seem right to omit telling you again that if she is applied with the benefics or other stars that are joined to benefics as was said—or if she exists in her own dignities without any impediment of the benefics—she will not make the rains remain, even though she does not resist them. But if she is applied to the malefics as was said, she will announce future rains along with the benefics. **And** Gafar <note>A reference to Ja'far al-Sadiq (c. 702–765 CE), a polymath and prominent figure in early Islamic science and astrology.</note> said that the Moon's entire leadership with each star—as if exposing the outcome in the highest sense—assists in those things which seem necessary for having this knowledge which was written above in a congruent order; however, how it should be handled in opposition and squares <note>original: "tetragonis"</note> will now be explained hereafter.

## On the four squares of the Moon, the four dichotomies, or the four figures.

**In** this matter, it is necessary to look at seven places in the circle principally: first, the degree of the conjunction of the luminaries <note>The New Moon.</note>; its squares <note>Aspects of 90 degrees.</note> which are distant from it, one before and another behind by 90 degrees; the degree opposite to it <note>The Full Moon.</note>; and the degrees of its dichotomies <note>Term: "Dichotomy" refers to the Moon being half-illuminated, specifically the first and last quarter phases.</note>. The first of these is from the beginning of the month until 7 days, and it is the **first dichotomy**. The second is from the said 7 days until another 7, and it is the **second dichotomy**, which is also the degree of "prevention" <note>The Full Moon.</note>. The third is from those 14 days until another 7 (that is, 21 days), and it is the **third dichotomy**. The fourth is after these aforesaid until the following conjunction, which is the **fourth dichotomy**. Secondarily, you ought to look at ten other places besides the aforesaid: the first is three days before the hour of the Moon's conjunction with the Sun; the second is three days afterward. The third is three days before the first dichotomy; the fourth is three days after it. The fifth is three days before the "prevention"; the sixth is three days after it. The seventh is three days before the second dichotomy; the eighth is three days after it. The ninth is 12 degrees before the opposition, and the tenth is just as many after it. When, three days after the meeting, you see her around evening thin and clear and bright without a covering of clouds, unless she is hindered elsewhere by the malefics, she will signify clear air as long as she stays in that sign. But if she is thin and her color inclines toward redness, and her unlit parts are similarly bright and seem almost to tremble or move, she will show that winds are coming from that direction toward which she seems to incline. But if the Sun then remains in Capricorn or Aquarius and the Moon is found in Taurus or Virgo and has some agreement with Saturn, then cold winds will come; and all the more so if Saturn is then found in Capricorn. But if she inclines toward blackness or sometimes a greenish tint with some thickness or undoubted coarseness, she will indicate clouds threatening rain and even rains themselves. In the other aforesaid places, according to the signs, mansions, and conjunctions or aspects of the planets with her, she will announce the future disposition of the air.

### ¶ On knowing the qualities of rain that lasts more than one day.

If you wish to foreknow the qualities of the air whose durations extend more than one day: as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose works formed the basis of medieval astrology.</note> said, you will consider the hours of the company of the luminaries <note>original: "societatū luminariū"; referring to the Sun and Moon.</note> in the chart, because each quality of the configurations that exists will signify for the most part from the hour of that configuration until the hour that follows it in the chart. Furthermore, it seemed to Ptolemy that we ought to consider the hour of the conjunction <note>Term: "Conjunction" is when two celestial bodies reach the same longitude and appear together in the sky.</note> of the luminaries and its minute, but to cast the chart for the ascendant <note>Term: "Ascendant" is the sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> of that minute and establish the four angles; and to see which of the planets is then the strongest <note>Term: "Almuten" (almuter) is the planet that holds the most "dignity" or power over a specific point in a chart.</note> over that ascendant. For that planet will preside over the entire disposition of the air until the Moon reaches another angle of the said chart—namely, according to the proper disposition of the air as it was arranged through the Almuten, unless something else contrary works against it, which it will behoove you to consider by your own skill, keeping in mind what was told to you above; and he will say more. You must also consider when the Moon enters the minute of your said angle; and you will see which of the planets was the Almuten over that ascendant when it happened then; since that planet will preside over the disposition of the air until the Moon reaches the third angle of the said chart of conjunction, which will be disposed according to the Almuten of that ascendant. Again, you will watch when the Moon enters the first minute of the degree which will be opposite the degree of the named conjunction; which, according to how the Almuten of the ascendant was disposed, will thus dispose the air for better or worse until the Moon reaches the first minute of the fourth angle of the said chart, unless something else contrary works against it. Afterwards, you will consider when the Moon reaches the minute in which the aforesaid conjunction occurred: which will then dispose the air according to the disposition of the planet that was the Almuten over the ascendant when it happened then, until the Moon reaches the minute of the following conjunction, unless something else works to the contrary: namely, that some of the "malefics" <note>Term: "Malefics" usually refers to Mars or Saturn, planets associated with challenging outcomes.</note> hinders the said Almuten, or if it is itself in a mansion or sign contrary to the nature of any of the aforesaid ascendants and their offshoots; or if the season itself also works against it—namely, by adding or subtracting [moisture] according to what Ptolemy testifies. This is just as if that lunar month were in summer and there were significators signifying humidity or rain; the rain and humidity will then be less abundant. If, however, it is in winter and there were significators signifying little humidity, more rains will follow from there than seem to be signified, and vice versa. **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> however seems to have said that Ptolemy divides the lunar months into only four divisions—that is, according to the four quarters <note>original: "dichotomiae"</note>—but if you remember well, enough was explained above. And always make the Moon a participant with the Almuten of the ascendant of any of the aforesaid angles according to what you find in its place, whether in dry, humid, or common signs or mansions. Furthermore, you must attend to the Sun and Moon when the Sun first enters the first minute of **Libra** from that minute until it has traveled through the 20th degree of **Scorpio**, observing how it stands with either good fortune or misfortunes; and in which mansion the Moon is then running, and in which sign it is, and the positions of the other planets; and with which of them either of the luminaries applies; for according to those signs which appear then, the air will be disposed until the entry of the Sun into **Aries**, though with an admixture of the significators that occur in the present conjunctions of the luminaries until then. And so says **Albumasar** <note>original: "Gafar"; referring to Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note>; for when these things I have set down are more fully executed, no variation or ambiguity concerning the change of the air will occur. One must likewise watch the Moon, whether she runs in a dry or equal mansion and applies to Venus or Mercury; or as Albumasar testifies, if she stays in watery signs and is applied to Saturn or Mars, it indicates future rains. And he said that the Moon and Mercury are stars signifying dews. Also, he said that if the Moon is situated in all good signs

<column-break/>

and they look upon her and are moved: if the Moon also applies to the same from such a place, it indicates showers. And he said that if the Moon applies to or looks upon dry or equal places, it will bring about entirely moderate rains. And he said the Moon, by her singular and proper nature, brings clouds and white, thin mists.

### ¶ On the circles that are formed around the Moon and Sun, and also around the stars, both wandering and fixed.

One must also observe the circle <note>Refers to atmospheric halos.</note> that is formed around the Moon, and whether there is only one or several: if there is one and it is clear, and if it is thin and bright and of short duration, and if it is removed and disappears gradually and slowly, it will signify fair weather and bright, pure air. If, however, there are several, they will signify a winter wind. But if they are declining toward a bright redness, and when they appear to be fragmented <note>original: "frustratiz"</note>, they will indicate a disturbance of the air being caused from any side by the occasion of winds. If indeed they are murky with thickness and are dark, let him predict a disturbance of the air through cold, winds, and snow. And Ptolemy said: if they decline toward a black greenness, they will signify winter air which happens by the occasion of both—namely, through winds, cold, and snow. And he said that if there are several circles, there will be more signs according to what we have said before.

And Ptolemy said: a circle will appear around the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> and the fixed stars around the bright ones, because they will signify by the colors of their circles as they resemble those of the stars they surround. And he said that we should also observe the fixed stars, such as the **Pleiades** <note>original: "p[re]sadeo"</note> in appearance, and their offshoots; and let us inspect the collections of those stars into which even the present stars approach in conjunction—let us grasp the color and the qualities or the number of the wandering stars themselves. For when they appear with a greater light and are of a greater quality, they will signify coming winds blowing from that part in which they are situated. Also, you can see concerning certain stars in the air which are called the **Manger** <note>Term: "Praesepe," a star cluster in the constellation Cancer.</note> and its neighbors, which appear as if nebulous; when they appear while the air is clear, if they are hidden or small in light and thick, as Ptolemy testifies, they will indicate a disturbance of the air and a multitude of rains. But if you see them decline toward brilliance and clarity, it is necessary to announce that there will be strong winds. And Ptolemy said the manner of those stars which at certain times reach out from their positions or other signs is similar.

### ¶ On comets and tailed stars.

Truly, the comets <note>original: "comate"</note> which are called tailed stars, when they appear, will signify winds and dryness of the air, especially if they appear somewhat nebulous; and the strength of their signification will be according to their multitude or fewness, and their length or shortness.

### ¶ On the "hurling" of stars.

In the "hurling of stars" <note>Term: "Iaculatio stellarum" refers to meteors or shooting stars.</note>, watching in clear times what they see as if stars were moved and falling: those movements and hurlings, from whatever part they come, will announce that wind is coming from that part. And the more numerous and thick the hurlings are, the more their significance will increase and hasten. If, however, they are from different parts, they will portend disordered winds from here and there. But if you see such signs appearing from everywhere, they will produce and cause a disturbance of the air from all sides, as well as thunder and likewise lightning. You can say nearly the same thing when you see light clouds that resemble tufts of wool.

### ¶ On the significations of daytime and nighttime qualities.

In investigating the daytime and nighttime qualities, we must always consider the body of the Sun in its...

At the second hour, at the very minute when [the Sun] begins to appear above the horizon, one must begin to observe and look closely to see whether its body rises clear and bright; for if it is so, it indicates a serene day in that time. But if you see it through a glass <note>A piece of darkened glass or crystal used to observe the sun without blinding the eyes.</note>, you will be able to judge accordingly. When it sets, we shall see the same for forecasting the qualities of the night's weather. If its body is of diverse colors, as **Ptolemy** says, or if it declines toward a fiery redness, or if the sun or the rays proceeding from it or around it are red, or if the clouds surrounding it decline toward redness through extreme brightness, and its rays are extended long and separated from one another outside the circle, it signifies that a very strong wind will arise from the angles in which these signs we have mentioned appear. But if they rise black, or declining toward greenness they fall into a mist, or if there are one or two circles around it, or if it has clouds around it which are called "mock suns" <note>original: "soles"; these are parhelia, atmospheric optical phenomena consisting of bright spots near the sun.</note>, and their rays are declining toward greenness or are black, they indicate wintry air and rains.

### On the rainbow when it appears, in what times and what it signifies.

You should also look at the rainbow <note>original: "yridem"; from 'Iris', the personification of the rainbow.</note> and in what times it appears, and in what times its appearance will be. For if it appears in clear times, that clear weather will not be of long duration or great dryness; for although its significance is not then so necessary, it nevertheless hardly or never fails to signify wintry air or rains. This happens because the vapors which were thin begin to thicken; for mostly, indeed almost always, a rainbow does not appear unless the vapors are thinning or thickening. But if there is clear weather in a wintry time, it will demonstrate fair weather to come, because the vapors then begin to be thinned and dried out and brought to nothing, as **Ptolemy** said. Generally, we add that for the most part, the colors themselves appearing in the air will indicate qualities similar to the outcomes signified by the aforementioned colors.

### On the investigation of the year when there ought to be rains.

When you care to know whether the year will truly be rainy, you will consider the Sun's entry into the first minute of Libra <note>The Autumn Equinox.</note> as was touched upon above, and what its state is until it has traveled through the 20th degree of Scorpio. You shall also look at what the state of the Moon is with the other stars in those times, for the significance of that year is gathered from them. Therefore, look at that entry [to see] which of the planets the Moon is joined to or first joins by an aspect <note>Term: "Aspect" refers to the specific angular relationship between two celestial bodies (e.g., square, trine).</note>. For if that planet is oriental <note>Term: "Oriental" describes a planet that rises before the Sun in the morning.</note>, as **Jafar** <note>likely Abu Ma'shar (Albumasar), known in Latin as Jafar, a leading Persian astrologer.</note> testifies, it shows the end of the year, month, or week to be rainy. But if it is occidental <note>Term: "Occidental" describes a planet that sets after the Sun in the evening.</note>, it declares the beginning of the rains by its favor; for this application <note>Term: "Application" is when a faster-moving planet approaches an aspect with a slower one.</note> is especially invited when made with Venus or Mercury in the aforementioned signs. But if she is applied to them, one being oriental and the other occidental, it will demonstrate great rains coming in the middle [of the period] and throughout the whole year. And [Jafar] said that a multitude of rains is especially threatened by the said Venus and Mercury when they hasten to enter Scorpio, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. And I say this more strongly if their application is from moist places or mansions <note>Term: "Mansions" refers to the 28 Lunar Mansions, segments of the zodiac used in medieval astrology.</note> when the Moon is within them. When these things are so, they will show general but useless rains. And if the Moon is applied to another [planet] which is seen by a southern aspect, as long as such an application lasts and until the completion of the application or aspect or conjunction, the multitude of rains will not cease.

### On the application of the Moon with Saturn and with the other planets.

**Ptolemy** said that if the Moon is applied to Saturn, it will signify

<column-break/>

the coming of soft and gentle or temperate rains, unless Mars or Mercury work the contrary. For Jupiter has clear air and proper winds; likewise, he helps the conjunctions of the other stars. However, the community or mixture of bodies, as was said above, will exhibit its efficacy, but also the leading and alternating colors of the clouds and the variations of the air, these things being weighed and balanced, it will be permitted to observe throughout the whole year with all difficulty removed. But if the Moon is applied to Mars, he will signify clouds between saffron and red and having whiteness above, and thunders as well as lightnings, and even in times fit for this, thunderbolts, unless Jupiter works the contrary. But if you see her applied to the Sun, it will indicate saffron clouds and great rains having large drops of water. If, however, the Moon is applied to Venus, it will generate soft and continuous rains and many dews, almost like mists. But if the Moon is applied with Mercury, it will show rains and fierce winds, and the harshness of the upper regions, and dispersed and diverse clouds resembling smoke.

### On certain extraordinary signs.

There are certain other extraordinary things which I do not remember finding in the sayings of any of the philosophers, but I have seen them many times and for the most part they are true; they especially have a place here in the entire sixth climate <note>Term: "Climate" refers to a latitudinal zone in medieval geography; the sixth climate included parts of Northern France, England, and Germany.</note>, and on the side of the fifth, and in the south of the seventh. Namely, when the sun sets, although in other parts the air appears bright and the time serene, where its body sets there may be a cloud like a cloth <note>original: "mappa"; a sheet or cloth-like cloud formation.</note>, which will signify winds or rains or both in that same night or on the following day. For if that "cloth" is thick and dense, and the air near it is bright and the time serene, it will for the most part indicate winds. But if there is any little cloud like a smudge near the cloth, like a painting, it will more likely indicate rains. But if it sets in a clear sky and after its setting until the completion of twilight the air appears red, it will signify that the weather will be serene in the same night and similarly on the following day. And **Cyprian** <note>Probably a reference to an astrological or weather authority, possibly Pseudo-Cyprian.</note> said: you shall consider what sort of weather it was on the second day of the Sabbath <note>Monday.</note>, for you shall expect the state of weather that was then to hold until the entry of the Sun into Aries. And **Gerard of Sabbioneta** <note>A 13th-century Italian translator and astronomer.</note> said: you shall see that when thick and dark clouds from the northern part are directly under the Arctic pole or somewhat declining toward the western part and are touching the horizon, then it will rain almost immediately. But if in the same part clouds appear in heaps <note>original: "monticulate"; like little mountains.</note>, like the bed of a river, and are separated from the horizon, they will signify a clearing of the air. Also, if you see lightnings in the same part below, they show the first disturbance of the air, so that the arrival of that disturbance will not be delayed easily beyond eight days, unless a great dryness should work the contrary. And **Alan** <note>likely Alan of Lille (Alanus de Insulis), a 12th-century scholar.</note> said: you shall also see if clouds have risen from the plain and especially diverse ones have sought the higher mountains toward the north: for it will be a sign of rain coming on the same day or at most on the following. The same is accustomed to happen when thick and dense clouds have surrounded the summits of mountains, announcing coming winds at that time. And the aforementioned things will happen more strongly if the clouds are extended by an eastern or northern wind. But if the clouds seek the plains from the mountains, you shall announce a sign of the lightening of the air and its improvement, unless much humidity works to the contrary; and much more so if it is moved by a western wind. There is also another occurrence which many times—indeed, for the most part—I have seen to be true: that if a rainbow appears in the morning, it then indicates rain, unless a great dryness of the air works the contrary. But if it appears around evening, then the weather will become serene, unless a great humidity of the air works the contrary. Also when there is a great density and frequency of stars, or an extreme rarity...

...if it has appeared, it will signify a change of the air in a short time. These occurrences, although they are for the most part true, are nevertheless not inevitable <note>original: "necessaria"; in a scholastic context, this means they are probable tendencies rather than absolute certainties.</note>.

### On the occurrences whose durations are somewhat prolonged.

**Y**ou will see in these occurrences whose durations are somewhat prolonged—I believe—the Sun, when you see it in the southern part; and if Venus is hidden under its rays <note>This refers to the planet being "combust," or so close to the sun that it is invisible.</note> with the Moon applying to it, or to the other of them (especially Venus) through conjunction or through an aspect, on that same day, and indeed at that same hour and even the minute in which such a conjunction occurs, you shall announce that rains are coming to that land. You may say the same if you find Mercury in the southern part with the Moon applying to it; or if it does not apply to it through conjunction, let it be joined to it in a direct diameter through opposition, and all the more strongly if the Moon is then found in Scorpio. You may say the same if Mars and Venus are joined together in Scorpio. And **Gafar** <note>likely Jafar ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi, known as Albumasar, a Persian astrologer.</note> said that with the Sun being in Aquarius and the Moon applying to it, or positioned in its opposition while Venus stays in the same place, rains will be present at that very hour. And he likewise said that the application of Mars to the Sun, or of Venus, with the Moon running in their opposition or in a square <note>original: "tetragono"; an aspect of 90 degrees, usually considered tense or active.</note> while Venus is combust <note>original: "adusta"; literally 'burnt', meaning too close to the sun's heat.</note>, makes a certain judgment regarding rains. If indeed, as has been said, Venus applies to the Sun and Mercury is joined to it, or at least to Venus itself, it will announce that rains are coming on that same day. Furthermore, if you find the Sun in Libra, and Venus in Sagittarius, and the Moon joined to them (especially to Venus) minute by minute <note>meaning a precise astronomical alignment.</note>, it will show that there will be showers in the land in which it occurs on that same day. But if the Sun is in an angle <note>one of the four cardinal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, or Imum Coeli.</note> or in its exaltation <note>a position in the zodiac where a planet's influence is most harmoniously amplified.</note>, and the Moon remains in Leo, it will show that many showers are coming on the day and hour of their conjunction or application. What I said about Leo can also be judged of Sagittarius, for according to the testifying authors, they are said to be "images of the river" <note>likely referring to the celestial associations of these constellations with water or flow in certain traditions.</note>. However, Leo produces a greater multitude of showers than Sagittarius; in its multitude, it thus makes them thicker. The same is accustomed to happen in the first face <note>a "face" or "decan" is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note> of Taurus. Sagittarius, however, does not produce such great rains of water in its thicker drops. And these predicted things will happen more strongly and certainly when the Sun is in Sagittarius or has looked upon it; and the Moon has looked upon Mercury or applied to it, and has followed Venus itself; and the efficacy of all these will be revealed on that same day. Similar things to the aforesaid will be generated in the houses of Mars and in the houses of Venus: large drippings, flashes of light <note>original: "coruscationes"; refers to heat lightning or flashes without immediate thunder.</note>, thunder, and hail will appear. And **Gafar** said again: the Sun running in Pisces or in Aries with the Moon staying in Virgo or Libra or in Sagittarius will offer an abundance of showers on that day, even in vaporous places. Likewise, if Venus and Mercury are joined to the Sun in any of the aforesaid places outside of Leo, and the Moon applies to them—all the more if it has applied from Leo—it will show flashes of light and thunder, although with little rain or perhaps none. And all the more if the Sun is with any of those in a direct diameter <note>an opposition (180 degrees).</note>, whether it be direct or retrograde <note>the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note>; but it is found more so then if it is retrograde. If, however, the Sun is in an angle, or in Aries, or in Leo, or in Libra, or Scorpio, and the Moon is in a direct diameter (that is, minute by minute) to it or opposed to Venus, it will signify luminous flashes of light as well as thunder after the rains or drippings. And all the more strongly if the Moon opposes it from Leo; for then, with flashes and thunder, if the air has been disposed to this, it will demonstrate the generation of lightning bolts <note>original: "fulgura"; specifically the striking bolt as opposed to the flash (coruscatio).</note>. And **Albumasar Trax** <note>possibly referring to Albumasar and 'the Thracian' as two sources, or a specific variant of Abu Ma'shar's name.</note> said in a similar way that in regions subject to the equinoctial line <note>the equator.</note> and in the second climate <note>the 'climates' were latitudinal zones used by ancient and medieval geographers to divide the world.</note>, these things are said; in the fourth and the third there will be a mediocrity of them; in the fifth and sixth they will be more remiss. But if you find the Sun or the Moon in Pisces and Mars looks upon them without the benefit of any fortune <note>a 'fortune' is a beneficial planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> from a square

<column-break/>

or from an opposition, they will signify an abundance of rain, lightning bolts, thunder, and flashes of light. And **Trax** said the same thing: even the Sun in Aries or Scorpio and the Moon in Leo prefigures this in their assembly alone.

### On the consideration of the places of rains.

**A**lthough you may have grasped the other considerations mentioned before, you should not forget to consider the "places" of rains, which are Cancer, Leo, Capricorn, and Aquarius. For if you find the Moon in any of those signs and it is joined to Venus bodily <note>original: "corporaliter"; a conjunction where they occupy the same degree.</note> or applied from some aspect (especially from a square or from an opposition), you shall announce that showers are coming; and all the more when their conjunction has been fulfilled minute by minute a degree or less before. The first half of Capricorn, however, is less [rainy] than the others preceding it; the last part, however, is considered to signify more cold than rain. Nevertheless, you shall consider all these things with discretion.
On the signs and places signifying smaller rains than the signs and places aforesaid.

**T**here are, however, certain other places in some signs signifying smaller rains than the aforesaid: these are the last term of Aries, and this is because of certain humidities which are found in those terms; also among the places signifying few rains are Gemini, Virgo, and Libra.

### In which arrival of the planets rains are signified.

**I**f, however, immediately after the arrival of the Moon, it is joined to Mercury and Venus and Mars, or to any one of them bodily or through some aspect, it will announce that rains are coming, unless Jupiter has predicted otherwise. If, however, it applies to Mars or Venus, it signifies that rains will occur on the same day. Likewise if to Mercury, following the tracks of that one to which Mercury is attached.
If you wish to know concerning any month whether it be rainy or not.

**W**hen you wish to know beforehand whether rains are to be in any month, you shall raise the figure <note>an astrological chart or horoscope.</note> appropriate to it at the beginning of each one, and you shall adapt the twelve cusps <note>the starting points of the twelve astrological 'houses'.</note> to it. You shall look at the hour and minute of the arrival of the Sun and Moon, and you shall see how the planets then look upon them, or to which planet they apply, and from which places and from which mansions <note>refers to the Lunar Mansions, a division of the ecliptic into 28 parts.</note> that application comes. For if they apply to stars that induce rain and from humid mansions, they will indicate wintry rains. If, however, they look upon planets signifying rains from dry places, their significance will be for a third or a fourth part less than the aforesaid. You shall also look to see if Venus is joined with Saturn; and all the more if Venus has transferred the light of Mars or of Mercury the author <note>original: "auctoris"; likely referring to the planetary ruler of the sign.</note>; for then you will be able to announce future rains without doubt. And if besides this the aforesaid planets have some application with the Sun, they will indicate rains of some sort; for the nature of the Sun in this case declines more toward dew than toward dryness. You shall also look to see if the Sun and Venus have run together in the same node <note>the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>, and if they are in a mansion of the nature of either of them, and with this both or either of them are joined to some star that is the distributor <note>original: "diatrizi"; likely a corruption of 'distributrix' or 'almuten', the planet with the most power in a specific location.</note> of the place which they have obtained; and if it has remained in a good place in the figure and has received the one joining it to itself, without doubt a significant shower is signified. Furthermore, when the Moon has drawn the degree of its arrival with the Sun, and has been joined to Jupiter and Mercury together or to either of them in a watery or airy sign—and all the more if it be in the southern part, and even more strongly if a reception <note>an astrological condition where two planets are in signs ruled by each other, indicating cooperation.</note> has entered between the aforesaid planets—great rains will show themselves, and they shall in no way be delayed.

### On the conjunction of the Moon with the planets and on the conjunction of other planets individually with each other.

**Y**ou shall look in the forecasting of rains if any of the inferior planets is joined with any—

## Jacobus Canter the Frisian to Joannes Müller, student of the sidereal science. Hearty greetings.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q containing the portrait of a man in a scholar's hat and gown, set within a circular frame.</image-desc>As often and in how many things the studies of learned men have been helped, my sweetest Joannes, by your fellow countryman Erhard Ratdolt <note>Erhard Ratdolt (1442–1528) was a famous pioneer printer from Augsburg, known for his beautiful technical and astronomical books.</note>—whom almost no learned man is ignorant of—so far and wide throughout almost the entire world are the volumes printed by him seen. Especially indeed those which almost no one else of the same craft has dared to touch: which show the mathematical discipline, most hidden in our age. For in printing books of this sort, this man has always stood out as most studious, as if he were the tutor and parent of the mathematicians whom I mentioned. Therefore, by his labor and expense, many volumes were once printed in arithmetic, some in music, and not a few in geometry, but very many in astronomy. Among which, by Hercules, this is not the least, which has come into the light in this latest time: the work of **Guido Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous European astrologer of the 13th century.</note>, containing everything that could be desired by an astronomer, but especially those things which regard the divine method of judgments [astrological predictions]. For in these, this man first spent his labor. Indeed, inspired by the divine power, he predicts the fates like a prophetess of Apollo <note>original: "phebadis instar"; referring to the Pythia or Sibyl.</note>. His volumes testify to this and show it; his own homeland of Forlì testifies to the same and proclaims it with a great voice. Which, during the time of Pope Martin IV when it was besieged for a long time, he saved unharmed by explaining to his fellow citizens the most suitable time for going out to meet the enemy. Likewise, in our own age, whoever follows his precepts predicts future things most truly, as if they were privy to the fates. I rejoice greatly, therefore, and I now congratulate those who, having despised common things, direct their journey toward divine and celestial things. But to you especially out of all, my Joannes, because by your merits you are most dear to me, and because you are most studious of this business. Have now, therefore, the most correct way to the counsels of the gods, by which you cannot be deceived; you have a most faithful guide. Proceed therefore as you have begun, happy and eager: and all the more because that Erhard whom I mentioned at the beginning, behold, has relieved you of great labor and now shows you a much easier and more open path, since he has placed an index at the front of this book. You will therefore one day use this convenience, nor will you consume a long space of time, as is usual, in seeking what you wish to know. Farewell, and love me. At Augsburg, May 28 <note>original: "quinto klas Junias"; the fifth day before the Kalends of June.</note>.

## The same man's verses to the same man concerning the index recently added to this work.

->What was once the blind work of Guido Bonatti,<-
->When no page had its own titles,<-
->Look, Joannes, it now shines clearly divided by chapters,<-
->Now with its own light; it no longer hides as before.<-
->Indeed, rescued from ancient darkness, it radiates with the index,<-
->Soon like the sky gleaming with bright stars.<-
->Therefore, take care to apply your mind all the more to this Guido,<-
->Now that you see him made easy by this certain order.<-
